India win toss, bat first in Asian Games cricket final against Pakistan
items.description: Indian opener Abhishek Sharma struck a characteristic quickfire half-century as India made a strong start after being asked to bat first by Pakistan in the Asian Games men’s cricket final on Saturday. India reached 81-2 in their six-over powerplay at the Korogi Sports Park, with Abhishek smashing six sixes and three fours in his 30-ball 52. Pakistan did manage two breakthroughs, however, with Vaibhav Sooryavanshi departing for 15 off nine balls after attempting to reverse-sweep Saim Ayub’s spin and being caught behind. Sanju Samson was the other wicket to fall, dismissed by medium-pacer Ahmed Daniyal. India won the toss and elected to bat first in a final that pits defending champions against a Pakistan side chasing their first men’s cricket gold at the Asian Games. Pakistan reached the final after beating Bangladesh in the semi-final — the only match of their campaign not washed out by rain. Under captain Sahibzada Farhan, they have a settled batting core featuring Farhan, Saim Ayub, Hasan Nawaz and Abdul Samad. Their bowling attack will rely heavily on spinners Abrar Ahmed and Sufyan Moqim, with the surface having already offered assistance to slower bowlers. India, meanwhile, have Jasprit Bumrah leading their attack and Ishan Kishan in good form with the bat. Pakistan are seeking to end their wait for a men’s Asian Games cricket gold, while India are bidding to retain the title they won in Hangzhou three years ago. Teams: India: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson (wk), Shreyas Iyer (c), Ishan Kishan, Tilak Varma, Shivam Dube, Axar Patel, Washington Sundar, Ravi Bishnoi, Jasprit Bumrah. Pakistan: Sahibzada Farhan (c), Maaz Sadaqat, Usman Khan (wk), Saim Ayub, Hasan Nawaz, Abdul Samad, Arafat Minhas, Ahmed Daniyal, Saad Masood, Abrar Ahmed, Sufyan Moqim.

Rising Traffic: MMA2 explores slot system
items.description: By Dickson Omobola Operators of the Murtala Muhammed Airport Terminal Two, MMA2, Bi-Courtney Aviation Services Limited, BASL, have disclosed that they are engaging with airlines to adopt a Level 2 schedule coordination, or slot system, to better distribute demand across available capacity and match the growth in passenger traffic and the concentration of airline operations within particular periods of the day. Head of Corporate Communications, BASL, Ajoke Yinka-Olawuyi, in a statement, said while the slot system would better distribute demand across available capacity, the approach requires close collaboration between the airport and airlines. Yinka-Olawuyi stated that the challenge was to ensure that any adjustment to flight schedules takes into consideration the commercial realities of airline operations, including passenger demand and potential revenue implications. She said discussions with airlines were ongoing, with the objective of developing workable options that optimise available airport capacity while improving the passenger experience. She stated: “While security screening is an important component of the passenger journey, managing passenger flow effectively requires looking at the entire journey rather than focusing on a single point within the terminal. BASL has been engaging with FAAN on the deployment of adequate Aviation Security, AVSEC, personnel to effectively man the available screening infrastructure during peak periods. FAAN has acknowledged the operational challenge and is already working towards solutions. “BASL has also identified road traffic and access into the airport environment as another area requiring attention. Engagements have consequently been held with the Police Airport Command, Air Force authorities and other relevant security stakeholders to facilitate smoother movement of traffic into the airport and minimise delays before passengers reach the terminal. The response to growing passenger traffic also requires airports to look beyond conventional capacity expansion and explore technology-enabled solutions. BASL is currently in discussions with its service partners to further scale digitisation of key processes, with the objective of improving operational efficiency and reducing pressure on physical facilities. “Plans are also underway for the introduction of a No-Bag Zone, which will provide passengers travelling without checked baggage with a more streamlined check-in experience. The terminal is also looking towards the application of Airport Collaborative Decision Making, A-CDM, principles, which promote the sharing of operational information and greater coordination among airport stakeholders. The objective is to improve predictability, efficiency and decision-making across the airport ecosystem.” The post Rising Traffic: MMA2 explores slot system appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Car crashes into crowd in Australia, 10 injured
items.description: A driver lost control and crashed his car into a crowd of rugby league fans in the eastern Australian city of Newcastle on Saturday, injuring 10 people including children, police said. Thousands of supporters had gathered to farewell local rugby league side the Newcastle Knights ahead of their grand final match against the Sydney Roosters on Sunday. But the festive environment was shattered when an 18-year-old rugby fan “driving erratically” lost control of his vehicle and crashed into the crowd, police said. “He was revving the car, he was excited, he was a supporter, he was there for the joy of the moment,” Newcastle Mayor Gavin Morris told national broadcaster ABC. “Somehow he lost control of the car… and he’s gone into the crowd.” Two people were in a critical condition — a five-year-old girl and 67-year-old man. Two other young children were hurt, police said. The driver had been taken into custody. “One person made a decision in a split second that put everyone at risk,” said Jenny Aitchison, the roads minister for the state of New South Wales. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said “my thoughts are with everyone injured or involved in the horrible incident this morning in Newcastle”. “Rugby league brings people together, and this should have been a weekend of excitement and pride for Newcastle fans,” he wrote in a post on X. And Knights captain Kalyn Ponga said on Instagram: “We’re thinking of you, your families and everyone in our Newcastle community.” “Sending our love and support.”

items.title: IGP Disu: Recent figures point to rising Policing
items.description: By Evelyn Usman On February 25, 2026, IGP Olatunji Disu took charge of the Nigeria Police Force with a solemn promise not to squander the confidence reposed in him. Today, that pledge is being tested against the hard realities of policing Nigeria , the crimes fought, the reforms pursued , the officers disciplined and the continuing effort to rebuild confidence in the Force When the number one cop in Nigeria, IGP Disu assumed office as the 23rd indigenous Inspector-General of Police, he inherited more than a crime-fighting institution. He took over a Force grappling with the longstanding challenges of crime prevention, public confidence, internal discipline and operational effectiveness. Since then, the police leadership has sought to reshape its approach around intelligence-led operations, internal accountability, tactical restructuring and closer engagement with communities. A career officer with a strong operational background, Disu had served as Assistant Inspector-General of Police at the Force Criminal Investigation Department Annex, Alagbon, Lagos, before his appointment. He previously commanded the Lagos Rapid Response Squad from 2015 to 2021, served as Commissioner of Police in Rivers State and the FCT, and headed anti-kidnapping and anti-robbery operations in different parts of the country. He also led Nigeria’s first police contingent to the African Union Mission in Sudan in 2005 and holds a third-degree black belt in judo. From command rooms to the streets, the months since his appointment have provided an early indication of the direction of his administration. But beyond arrests, recoveries and operational figures, a more fundamental question remains: how much has changed in the daily relationship between the police and the people they are sworn to protect? Confronting the State Police Question Barely a week in office, Disu signalled one of the major policy issues confronting policing in Nigeria. On March 4, 2026, he inaugurated a committee on the implementation of state police, charging it with examining policing models, community security needs and the framework required for the establishment of state police. The committee’s brief included issues around recruitment, training, standards and accountability. Disu maintained that state police should not replace the Nigeria Police Force but complement the existing federal structure within a coordinated national security architecture. The move placed the IGP at the centre of one of the country’s most consequential policing debates, how to bring policing closer to communities while maintaining national standards and accountability. Confronting Impunity Within the Force Internal discipline has also featured prominently in the administration’s early months. Disu ordered the strengthening of the Complaints Response Unit and the Independent X-Squad, with emphasis on investigating allegations of misconduct. Commissioners of Police were also reminded of their responsibility for discipline and accountability within their commands. His administration also moved to address the “Keep In View”, or KIV, culture, a practice described within the Force as allowing criminal cases to remain inactive for prolonged periods. Reports on the reform effort said police monitoring mechanisms had identified cases requiring renewed attention, prompting directives for their activation and prosecution. The administration also began reviewing operational responsibilities in an effort to reduce interference in sensitive investigations. Dismissal Over Delta killing That approach was tested in April, following the death of a suspect in police custody in Delta State. Disu described the conduct as unlawful and a violation of human life. The officers involved were dismissed from the Force, while the case was forwarded for criminal prosecution. The IGP subsequently directed a nationwide audit of police arms and reinforced accountability measures for Commissioners of Police. The incident provided one of the clearest tests of the administration’s stated position on police discipline: whether allegations of misconduct would result in internal sanctions and, where applicable, criminal proceedings. Operational Scorecard If arrests, rescues and recoveries provide one measure of police activity, the figures recorded under IGP Disu, point to sustained operational pressure across the country. In April 2026 alone, intelligence-led operations nationwide resulted in the arrest of 280 suspects, comprising 28 suspected terrorists, 85 suspected kidnappers, 62 suspected armed robbers, 51 murder suspects and 54 suspected cultists. Within the same period, police rescued 189 kidnapped victims and recovered 140 firearms, 1,074 rounds of ammunition and 37 stolen vehicles. Operations continued into the following months In another operational update covering nationwide anti-crime operations, police reported the arrest of 1,198 suspects, including 151 suspects linked to murder and culpable homicide, 117 suspected armed robbers, 151 suspected kidnappers, 104 suspected cultists and 169 suspects for unlawful possession of firearms. The operations also resulted in the rescue of 166 kidnap victims and the recovery of 166 firearms, 1,475 rounds of ammunition and 47 stolen vehicles. By September, the Force’s reported cumulative figures since Disu assumed office stood at 1,643 suspects arrested and 1,066 kidnapped victims rescued. The breakdown included 251 suspected terrorists and bandits, 343 murder suspects, 566 suspected armed robbery suspects and 483 suspected cultists. The figures demonstrate the scale of police activity during the period, but they do not, on their own, establish whether insecurity has declined nationally or whether public confidence has improved. Those questions require broader indicators, including crime trends, case outcomes, response times and citizens’ experiences with the police. Broader Security Challenge The operational environment confronting the Force remains complex. Data covering the first half of 2026 recorded thousands of major security incidents across the country, including terrorism and banditry, murder and homicide, armed robbery and kidnapping. The North-Central recorded 1,662 incidents, while the North-West recorded 1,539. Zamfara accounted for 748 incidents in the North-West, including 322 terrorism and banditry cases and 222 murders. Benue accounted for 518 incidents in the North-Central In the South-South, 627 incidents were recorded, with Edo accounting for 126 kidnapping cases, while the South-West recorded 609 incidents, including 279 in Oyo State. The figures provide context to the environment in which Disu’s administration has operated. They should, however, be distinguished from the IGP’s personal operational scorecard, particularly because the first-half data covers a period that began before he assumed office. At the Joint Security Press Briefing in July, the police highlighted the dismantling of organised criminal networks, rescue of kidnapped victims, disruption of arms-trafficking channels and increased cooperation with the Armed Forces, INTERPOL and other security agencies. New Tactical Architecture Disu has also sought to reshape the Force’s tactical response to violent crime. The administration established the Violent Crime Response Unit, VCRU, as a restructured tactical formation designed to respond to violent crime on the basis of verified intelligence. The units are placed under the command of Commissioners of Police in their respective states, with emphasis on accountability for their operations. The IGP also approved new counter-terrorism bases in Madagali, Adamawa State; Ikot Odo, Cross River State; and Ode-Remo, Ogun State, as part of efforts to close identified security gaps. The changes suggest an attempt to move the Force’s tactical response towards more specialised and intelligence-driven operations. Returning Policing to Community Beyond tactical operations, community engagement has remained another plank of the administration. Disu met with the leadership of the Police Community Relations Committee on several occasions and described the group as an important partner in intelligence gathering and community policing. He also directed Commissioners of Police to strengthen engagement with traditional rulers, religious leaders, youth groups, market associations and other community stakeholders. The administration has emphasised the need for police officers to maintain direct channels of communication with communities, including making official contact numbers available to community leaders. The underlying proposition is straightforward: intelligence gathering becomes more effective when citizens are willing to communicate with the police. But translating that proposition into sustained public confidence remains one of the more difficult tests facing the Force. Welfare and Promotions Checks by Saturday Vanguard showed that personnel welfare has also featured in the administration’s agenda. More than 33,000 police personnel were promoted during the period, including 17,952 junior officers. Speaking to newly decorated senior officers, Disu described the promotions as a strategic investment in leadership and charged the beneficiaries to maintain discipline and reject corruption.The administration has also spoken of improved welfare, housing and pension arrangements for personnel. For a Force whose operational effectiveness depends heavily on the morale and conditions of its personnel, welfare remains closely connected to the broader question of professionalism. Beyond the Numbers The figures tell one part of the story. They show arrests made, victims rescued, weapons recovered, tactical formations established and personnel promoted. But policing is ultimately experienced beyond statistics , at the police station, on the highway, at checkpoints, during investigations and in communities where citizens either seek police assistance or avoid contact with law enforcement. A review published by The Eagle Online noted the administration’s emphasis on bringing command closer to operations and strengthening internal oversight, while cautioning that the larger test remained the credibility of the institution. That distinction is important. Operational successes can demonstrate capacity. They do not, by themselves, resolve longstanding questions about accountability, professionalism, police-community relations and public confidence. Building Momentum About eight months into his tenure, IGP Olatunji Disu has provided clear leadership and strategic direction for the Nigeria Police Force.. His administration has prioritised intelligence-led policing, internal accountability, tactical reorganisation, structured engagement on state policing, sustained community partnership and enhanced personnel welfare, pillars that are gradually reshaping operational effectiveness. While national crime data for the first half of 2026 highlights the enormity and complexity of Nigeria’s security challenges, the Force under Disu has shown renewed capacity, coordination and resolve in confronting them. What will define the next phase is not arrests and recoveries alone, but follow-through: progression of cases, justice for victims, handling of police misconduct, community response, and whether reforms initiated at the top filter down to everyday policing. The early months have set a direction. The task ahead is institutionalising it. Vanguard News The post IGP Disu: Recent figures point to rising Policing appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Delta’s Schools of Sorrow: Trapped in decaying, unsafe public school classrooms
items.description: *Children, teachers wait for ‘conducive learning environment’ promised by government By Egufe Yafugborhi The classroom has no roof. The walls are cracked, windows disappeared. In another block, there are no doors. In yet another, the toilet has collapsed. Read Also: Death in Delta: More questions on ‘transfer fee’ saga that consumed Adeda Yet, every morning, children still come. They come carrying exercise books, pencils and the dreams their parents have entrusted to public education. Some sit on bare floors. Others squeeze into few surviving desks. Teachers stand before them and improvise, teaching lessons on education, discipline and a better future in environments that appear to mock the very idea of a conducive school. Across several communities in Delta State, this is the uncomfortable reality behind the government’s fresh promise to rehabilitate and reconstruct public schools. August 31, 2026, the Delta State Government announced Governor Sheriff Oborevwori’s resolve to, within two weeks, embark on massive rehabilitation or reconstruction of primary and secondary schools across the state’s 25 local government areas. Commissioner for Works, Rural Roads and Public Information, Charles Aniagwu, said the Ministries of Basic and Secondary Education had been directed to assess schools and determine those requiring intervention. Aniagwu said the governor has “directed that the two ministries immediately come up with the scope of these different schools that need to be rehabilitated so that the government will immediately proceed to put them in order for the purpose of our children having much more conducive learning and indeed teaching environment.” But, for children already trapped in these structures, the question is not whether they need a conducive learning environment. It is how long they must wait for one. At Otor-Edo Primary School in Ughelli South LGA, community President-General, Kenedy Egone, described a school that has moved from mud-house beginnings to a roofless and unsafe structure. “Our children sit under leaking skies to receive lessons. As the rains peak, there may soon be no place for them to learn at all,” Egone told Vanguard. According to him, Delta SUBEB engineers, years before, had visited for assessment, while the community was subsequently informed that “the job has been awarded. A year later, no contractor has shown up.” Egone plea is simple: “Otor-Edo Community should not be made to wait for another generation to enjoy what other communities take for granted. All we seek is to be seen, be heard, and to be remembered.” That plea echoes in schools far beyond Otor-Edo. At Ugbuwangue Secondary School in Warri South LGA, classrooms are in disrepair, with some abandoned and the remaining usable spaces overcrowded. A veranda has become a staffroom, while a security/gatehouse doubles as the Principal’s office. The school’s water system has collapsed, rendering toilet facilities unsafe. At Martin College, Isele-Uku, Aniocha North LGA , an all-girls school, the library and WAEC hall are in appalling condition, while a laboratory and several classroom blocks have fallen into disrepair. At Ogodor Community Primary School, also in Aniocha North, cracked walls on dilapidated classroom blocks raise fears of looming collapse. At Adonte Secondary School, Aniocha South, classrooms are inhabitable, bereft of desks. Abah Unor Secondary School is no less piteous – abandoned, dilapidated classroom blocks and no school furniture. Then there is Ojeta Secondary School, Abraka. Good governance advocate, Kelvin Williams, asked a question that hangs over the entire situation: “Ojeta Secondary School, Abraka — Where Is The Dividend Of Democracy?” Williams said: “There are teachers here. There are students here. There are young people who come here every day hoping to receive the education that will shape their future.” Then he added: “Students are struggling without adequate chairs to sit on. There are classrooms without proper writing boards. The buildings are visibly old and deteriorating, while parts of the roofing have been damaged. “Teachers are working under difficult conditions, with inadequate facilities to properly teach and carry out their responsibilities,” he said. Williams’ demand is unequivocal: “We are not begging for charity. We are demanding what belongs to the people.” At Urhuoka Primary School, Abraka, a classroom has collapsed, its roof lying on the ground. At Urhuoka Secondary School, the toilet has collapsed and the staff block inhabitable, with the roof falling off. For some teachers, speaking publicly about the conditions is itself considered dangerous. One teacher told Vanguard: “Even crying out or allowing concerned persons to come capture the images to do the outcry for the piteous learning conditions for us has become a risk to our jobs. “You can be sacked for talking, so most times it’s suffering and smiling for us as we must work against all odds. “And that doesn’t encourage us to give our all in teaching the children. Morale is low when you don’t have a desk to teach children sitting on bare floors to learn, no safe toilet for convenience. It’s a terrible learning environment.” The consequences are not merely about discomfort. On 3 October 2024, a dilapidated six-classroom block at Eghereka Primary School, Ewu, Ughelli South, collapsed under heavy rain. Primary 2 pupil, Ojiyovwin Salvation, died while three others were injured. As if beautifying the tragedy and passing the blame on the innocent children, the state government admitted the roofless structure had not been in use for more than a decade. The incident remains a grim reminder that dilapidation in schools can become a matter of life and death. A pupil confronted during tour of some of the schools captured the frustration of children caught between poverty and deteriorating public education: “We know where befitting private schools are. Our parents can’t afford those, but government and parents say education is key.” Then came the plea: “So we just want a place to learn to become good leaders of tomorrow. That’s why we beg the government to give us good, conducive schools to learn.” The infrastructure decay is also profound at Imode Prumary School, Otu-Jeremi Secondary School, both in Ughelli South and several other place. The random tour of schools also revealed part of the rapid rot of the structures is shabby construction with inferior materials. There is also inhindered vandalism and theft of props, particularly desk and furnitute due to absence of engaged security guards, leaving the schools porous after school hours. Aniagwu said Delta has more than 1,300 primary schools and over 430 secondary schools, explaining that the assessment would determine where intervention is needed. “It is from these numbers that we have they are going to look at which ones are necessary for us to be able to touch… to make both learning and teaching conducive,” he said. For the children waiting inside the cracked walls, however, the assessment is not the destination. They have waited through leaking roofs, missing desks, unsafe toilets and crumbling classrooms. What they are waiting for now is simple: a school that does not make learning itself a struggle for survival or a death wish. items.title: Rizwan, NCCIA tight-lipped after player appears for questioning
items.description: LAHORE: Pakistan’s wicket-keeper/batter Mohammad Rizwan appeared before the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) here on Friday in a case concerning allegations of online betting, gambling and leaking of team information from the dressing room during the Test series in England earlier this year. Neither Rizwan nor any NCCIA official were ready to respond to media queries after the cricketer came out of the agency’s office after more than three and a half hours of investigation conducted by four NCCIA officials. Rizwan, 34, was served a notice by the NCCIA under the Criminal Procedure Code Section 160. When asked how the conduct of the agency’s official was and what questions he faced, a smiling Rizwan said: “I am deaf (in this connection), the conduct (of NCCIA officials) was good. I am feeling hungry; so let me go” before leaving the venue. It may be mentioned here that the NCCIA had confiscated Rizwan’s mobile phone in England on Aug 30, reportedly, having some secret information. The agency had promised that it will return the phone in three hours but it was not given to the player before he was summoned for inquiry on Friday. It is still not clear if the NCCIA has returned Rizwan’s phone. And there is no information if the agency will again summon the player. It is learnt Rizwan was summoned for his face recognition, which is necessary for daily forensics of the phone. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

items.title: 2027: Why Nigerians must vote for working system
items.description: By Prisca Sam-Duru A 33-year-old Cameroonian woman living in the UK recently shared an experience that stayed with me. Thirty weeks pregnant and home alone, she felt what she thought was labour pain and dialled UK a emergency number. In less than three minutes, she said, four medics were at her door with full delivery equipment, ready to deliver her baby in her apartment. It turned out to be false labour alarm. They still took her by ambulance to the hospital for checks. That is what a working system looks like. Now place that beside Nigeria’s maternal mortality reality, where women still die because help comes too late, or never comes at all. Then you will understand how far behind we are. A few months ago, my neighbour’s house caught fire at night. The entire street came out shouting to alert the rest of the residents, fetching water, breaking walls to stop the fire from spreading. People called emergency numbers they knew. No fire service came. Through the night, it was residents and local vigilante who did the job of trained firefighters. At the end, we lost the brother of the house owner. In the UK for instance, fire alarms are checked routinely. Once a fire starts, the alarm triggers and within minutes firefighters are on site. In Nigeria, we have heard too many stories of fire trucks arriving after everything is burnt. Even when they do, they arrive, with no water in their tanks leading to reports of their being chased away by an angry crowd. What a country. In most English cities, you’ll hardly see police officers chasing bad guys on the road and creating trouble for road users. Also, you’d be surprised to find out that there are roundabouts without either traffic lights or traffic warden, yet, there is hardly any chaos. Road users, even cyclists, obey traffic rules. In Lagos, we have LASTMA, Road Safety officials at junctions that already have traffic lights, and the roads are still chaotic; drivers cursing, danfos blocking and driving one way, Korope bus and keke drivers driving like there’s no tomorrow while okada riders weave through like snakes, causing confusion. The difference is not magic. It is system. Another general election is approaching. What do we really want as Nigerians? Our politicians travel abroad as if it is their ancestral home. They enjoy 24-hour electricity, prompt emergency response, good roads and functioning hospitals. They return home, loot the treasury, and travel out again to spend it. And the cycle continues. It is high time Nigerians asked a simple question: Do we want to start walking the path of development, or continue serving politicians who impoverish us? Recently, we saw political thugs stopping a presidential candidate they oppose from campaigning in some states. The same thugs who are impoverished by bad governance. The same young men whose purchasing power has been reduced to almost nothing. In Benue, where communities have been repeatedly attacked and people massacred at different times by killer herders and bandits, we saw a self-styled strongman declare that Benue belongs to the President, while many of his people cry out to foreign countries for help. Where is the democracy in that? Why should any Nigerian be prevented from campaigning anywhere in his own country? Will stopping a presidential candidate from campaigning give Benue State people better life? Ask anyone who has lived in the UK, when last power blinked, let alone went out for hours. The answer would be never. In my own community in Lagos, we have battled epileptic power for over 15 years since we moved in because of an old, weak transformer. Last year, residents levied themselves over a hundred thousand each to buy a new one. We celebrated as if we had won the World Cup. From the transformer, cables, poles, everything was paid for from our pockets. Sadly, one year later, that transformer is yet to be energized by the electricity distribution company. Yet, people still receive outrageous bills. In saner climes, you simply enjoy uninterrupted power and pay at month-end. How the power gets to you is not your business. Here, we buy the equipment and still pay for darkness. In my street, we grade the road ourselves. Every house digs its own borehole. This has gone on for so long it now feels normal. It is not. At 66, Nigeria is experiencing more retrogression than progress. Insecurity has made people unsafe in their homes. Hunger has eroded the masses’ purchasing power. Corruption has spread from the political elite to the streets. People adulterate food with poison just to make profit, fueling strange illnesses. A working system would have checked that. At least the late Dora Akunyili proved that Nigeria can work when patriots are in charge. In Nigeria, citizens provide for themselves every basic amenity government should provide — light, water, road, security. And instead of demanding good governance, thugs fight fellow citizens for politicians who will never remember them after elections. We throw refuse into gutters and block drainage. We eat in moving vehicles and throw the waste out of the window. Perhaps, what is left is for Nigerians to throw waste from an aeroplane mid-air; that is, if its possible. We have lost regard for the rule of law because those who should enforce it have thrown morality away. A hungry, angry, hopeless people will hardly act orderly. If the system works, people will behave better. Come 2027, we need a fresh start Nigerians must vote without tribal or religious sentiments. We must vote for good governance. For a government that will reorient the people, restore our image at home and abroad, make politics less about profit and more about service. A government that will put Nigerians first, not the pockets of a few. We have a choice to make: continue with the status quo, or vote for a system that works. The post 2027: Why Nigerians must vote for working system appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ebonyi widow ostracized, banned from community water, market cries out
items.description: •Says, some people are after my late husband’s land; monarch dissociates himself, disbands women’s group By Jeff Agbodo ABAKALIKI — Mrs. Njideka Ngwuta, a widow from Nsokkara community in Ezza South Local Government Area of Ebonyi State, experienced the worst embarrassment of her life when a group of women from her community announced that she had been excommunicated and ostracised from the community for allegedly questioning the change of the women’s meeting venue. She alleged that the leadership and members of the Acharaukwu Development Union Women Wing (ADU) wrongfully accused and ostracised her without fair hearing or proper investigation. She alleged that the punishment was initiated by notable personalities in her kindred with the aim of banishing her and grabbing her late husband’s land and confiscating other estates belonging to the family. Read Also: How Nigeria declined into criminality, poor governance in 66 years The widow has therefore appealed to the Ministry of Women Affairs, the Governor’s wife and other well-meaning people across the country to urgently wade into the matter and conduct a thorough investigation into her plight. In her letter of appeal, titled, “Urgent petition against extreme harassment, ostracizing, and attempted forcible eviction by the leadership and members of the Acharaukwu Development Union, Women Wing (ADU), in Ezza South Local Government Area,” the widow alleged that members of Umunaza Kindred united against her and she had no one to speak on her behalf because all the adult male children of her husband’s family had died of strange diseases. Her petition reads: “I am originally from Achina, Aguata LGA of Anambra State but was married into the Ngwuta Anyigor family of Acharaukwu Nsokkara in Ezza South LGA about 27 years ago. The union is blessed with three children. Tragically, my husband is deceased, just like his brothers, parents and other prominent male relatives. Since the demise of my husband and his male relatives, nobody represents the family at the kindred level. That is why we have been maltreated. “I have been subjected to relentless torment by certain members of our kindred, Umunaza Kindred of Acharaukwu Nsokkara, who are hell-bent on dispossessing my family of the lands belonging to us. “My late husband had two brothers who got married and had children before the three brothers incidentally died under suspicious circumstances, leaving me and my co-wives as young widows with our young children behind. My parents-in-law are also deceased, and so the entire Ngwuta Anyigor family was left in the hands of widows and young children. Before my mother-in-law died in 2016, my co-wives and their children had left the village owing to numerous spiritual attacks and unexplainable deaths in the family, leaving only my mother-in-law, myself and my three children behind. “I had wanted to run away with my children from the village, but I could not leave my mother-in-law alone as she was old and needed care. I stayed behind and took care of her until she died and was buried. After her death, I realised that leaving the village with my children would mean that everyone in the family had run away, and that would lead the family name, compound and legacy into extinction. “I stayed back with my children, farmed on our lands and used the proceeds to train my children in school. As a result of my stay in the village, some of my husband’s nephews and nieces have returned and now live with me in the family compound,” she narrated. Mrs. Ngwuta, however, revealed that ever since she lost her husband and decided to stay back with her children, her husband’s nephews and nieces, as well as some members of her late husband’s kindred, Umunaza, have been trying to forcefully take over her husband’s estates and family lands and frustrate them out of the family compound. She expressed surprise that those at the forefront of the alleged land-grabbing were close to her husband while he was alive. She said, “despite my vulnerability as a widow without an adult male backing me in the family, I have consistently resisted these land-grabbing attempts. At the forefront of this oppression are some very close family members of my late husband, who share the same kindred with my late husband. When they attempted to forcefully take over my lands, I stood my ground, and the entire Acharaukwu community intervened, looked into the matter and rightfully decided in my favour. “Following their inability to take over the lands, these people have resorted to character assassination and blackmail. Sometime in 2024, two young girls from the same Acharaukwu Nsokkara came to my house around 9 p.m. and begged me to agree that I had sold some cassava to them. I immediately suspected that I was being set up by the same people who had been trying to take me out of my family, and I quickly refused and asked them to leave my house. “Owing to my fear of being set up on more unsuspecting events, I made a conscious decision to stop attending public events or gatherings held at private residences. This union conducts its meetings in each village from time to time, while the Annual General Meeting is held in August of every year. My own village is Effium, Acharaukwu Nsokkara, and the meeting is usually held at the Effium Playground. It is also worthy of note that, as of 2024, I was the Secretary of the Effium Unit of the Union. “Surprisingly, about three years ago, the then Chairlady of Effium Unit of ADU Women Wing relocated the meetings from the public playground where such meetings were always traditionally held, directly to the compound of one of my late husband’s relatives. “Understanding the clear danger this posed to my safety and liberty, I protested and formally informed the association that I would not attend any meeting in anyone’s compound. I expressed my legitimate fear of being set up and subjected to jungle justice for crimes I did not commit. “Rather than understanding my plight as a fellow woman and a widow, the ADU Women Wing leadership became infuriated. They went as far as reporting me to the Catholic Church where I worship. In an attempt to make peace, the Catholic Women Organization (CWO) of my church mandated me to apologise to the ADU women. In obedience to the CWO, I went with some members of the church to see the ADU women at Dr. Kelvin Nwankwo’s compound, but we were turned back at the gate, and Dr. Nwankwo specifically warned that we should not enter into his compound. I went back with the other church members, informed the CWO and the priest of the church and have since then maintained my resolution not to attend such a meeting in anyone’s compound. “They forcefully handed me a matchbox, indicating that I had been ostracised from the community. Furthermore, they passed draconian and illegal edicts against me to the effect that I had been completely banned from fetching water from any of the community streams or boreholes; forbidden from interacting or associating with anyone in the community; and banned from entering the markets to buy or sell anything. They threatened that I would be killed if I dared disobey their orders. “It is abundantly clear that this women’s group is being sponsored and weaponised by some people in Acharaukwu Nsokkara whose aim is to frustrate, humiliate and terrorise me into abandoning my late husband’s home so they can finally take over my family’s land.” “At the moment, my life and the lives of my children are in grave danger. My three children, my husband’s nephews and nieces have fled our home for fear of being harmed. I am currently living as a fugitive, sleeping in neighbouring communities because it is no longer safe for me to sleep in my own marital home.” Mrs. Ngwuta further alleged that one of her neighbours, Miss Rebecca Aleke, who visited her compound after she was ostracised, was later tortured and almost beaten to death for associating with her. Such action, she said, had left her traumatised and afraid of what might happen next. She is therefore calling on the wife of the Governor of Ebonyi State, Mrs. Uzoamaka Nwifuru, as her last resort to wade in and save her life and her home. “I also want the Governor’s wife to use her good office to promptly summon the leadership of the ADU Women Wing, Acharaukwu Nsokkara, to explain their justification for ostracising a widow like me, denying me access to basic amenities and issuing death threats against me,” Mrs. Ngwuta appealed. When contacted, President of the ADU Women Wing, Mrs. Leticia Ngele, and another member, Mrs. Eucheria Nwandende, confirmed that Mrs. Njideka Ngwuta was ostracised by the union, saying that Mrs. Ngwuta had always been at the forefront of carrying out barbaric acts against other women. However, the traditional ruler of Nsokkara Autonomous Community, HRH Eze Festus Ifesinachi Okonkwo, and a major stakeholder from the community, Chief Celestine Ekechi, condemned the action of the women’s group, noting that such an act was never part of their culture. The monarch admitted that he was aware of the case but noted that all efforts to resolve it had proved abortive, as even the letter of summons sent to the women was not honoured. Meanwhile, Ezeogo has disbanded the leadership of the Acharaukwu Development Union (ADU) Women Wing over the reprehensible action against the widow. Ezeogo Okonkwo, who submitted the ban order to the office of the Commissioner for Local Government and Chieftaincy Matters, said the action of the women’s group contradicted Section 002 of the 2018 Ebonyi State Violence Against Persons Prohibition (VAPP) Law. The traditional ruler, who frowned at the injustice meted out to the widow, ordered that Mrs. Njideka Ngwuta should, as a matter of urgency, return to her matrimonial home and reunite with her children and loved ones. He warned that further threats to her life would be viewed with seriousness and visited with the full weight of the law of Ebonyi State and the Federal Republic of Nigeria. He emphasised that the barbaric act was against the culture, customs and traditions of Nsokkara and Ezza Ezekuna people, noting that he was very annoyed with the leadership of the women for bluntly and flagrantly refusing to honour his invitation when he got wind of the matter. “The action, harassment and the inhuman treatment meted against Mrs. Ngwuta is a violent act which has caused her physical and emotional trauma and is condemned in its entirety, as it is an action perpetrated against her fundamental human rights and equally violates the provisions of Ebonyi State Violence Against Persons Prohibition No. 002 of 2018 (VAPP Law),” the monarch stressed, assuring that the palace had initiated an in-depth investigation to unravel the sponsors of the barbaric and heinous act in the community. items.title: Économie russe : sous pression budgétaire, les régions réduisent les indemnités versées aux familles des soldats morts en Ukraine
items.description: Mardi 29 septembre, le gouvernement de la région de Saratov, située sur la Volga, à la frontière avec le Kazakhstan, a publié un décret divisant par dix l'indemnité régionale versée aux familles des soldats tués au combat en Ukraine. Celle-ci passera d'un million de roubles (environ 10 600 euros) à 100 000 roubles (environ 1 060 euros) à partir du 1er novembre В Саратовской области в 10 раз сократили выплату членам семей погибших участников войны в Украине », Радио Свобода , 1er octobre 2026.'> 1 . Ces derniers mois, plusieurs régions russes ont réduit, voire supprimé, cette indemnité, restée jusque-là stable depuis le lancement de l'invasion en 2022. Depuis l'automne 2025, la république du Bachkortostan a réduit à trois reprises cette indemnité, qui est passée de deux millions de roubles (environ 21 200 euros) à 100 000 roubles (environ 1 060 euros). Les autorités des oblasts de Kirov et d'Omsk ont quant à elles divisé par deux son montant, qui est passé d'un million de roubles à 500 000 roubles au début de l’année, soit environ 5 300 euros. Dans l'oblast d'Irkoutsk, l'Assemblée législative régionale a finalement retiré le 20 mai une disposition, adoptée en première lecture, qui visait à diviser par deux le montant de l'indemnité Законопроект о повышенной выплате участникам СВО приняло Законодательное собрание Иркутской области », TK Gorod , 20 mai 2026.'> 2 . Selon l’économiste Janis Kluge, ces baisses sont remarquables car le montant des indemnités était resté stable depuis le lancement de l’invasion, en février 2022 Russian recruitment roundup, September 2026 », Russianomics , 10 septembre 2026.'> 3 . De plus, contrairement aux primes d’engagement, qui jouent un rôle direct pour inciter les hommes russes à signer un contrat avec l’armée, les indemnités versées en cas de blessure ou de décès ne constituent pas un engagement de vente. Comme l’explique Kluge : « Personne ne souhaite penser à sa propre mort lorsqu’il signe un contrat ». Ces baisses s’inscrivent dans un contexte de détérioration de la situation budgétaire russe au niveau des régions. Selon la Cour des comptes russe, 56 régions ont enregistré des déficits budgétaires au premier trimestre (contre 46 l’an dernier), et 74 régions (sur 85) ont fini l’année 2025 avec un déficit, selon l’agence de notation ACRA. Sberbank anticipe un déficit budgétaire cumulé des régions de 2 000 milliards de roubles cette année Сбербанк спрогнозировал рекордную « дыру » в бюджетах регионов на 2 триллиона рублей », The Moscow Times , 2 septembre 2026.'> 4 . En 2021, avant l'invasion de l'Ukraine, les régions russes avaient enregistré un excédent d'environ 400 milliards de roubles. Les indemnités régionales sont toutes largement inférieures aux sommes versées aux familles par l'État fédéral, qui dépassent 10 millions de roubles (environ 100 000 euros) par soldat tué. Pour le Kremlin, les familles des soldats tués en Ukraine ainsi que les vétérans représentent un enjeu politique de plus en plus important, alors que le bilan humain ne cesse de s'alourdir. Selon l'état-major ukrainien, l'armée russe aurait subi plus de 1,5 million de pertes, tués et blessés confondus, depuis février 2022. Les élections législatives de septembre ont vu l'élection à la Douma de 46 vétérans de la guerre en Ukraine, selon la présidente de la commission électorale centrale, Ella Pamfilova, soit un peu plus de 10 % de la chambre. En 2024, Poutine a lancé un nouveau programme, baptisé « Le Temps des héros » (« Время героев »), visant à préparer des vétérans à occuper de hautes fonctions dans l'administration. Trois personnes passées par ce programme sont aujourd'hui à la tête d'une région. L’article Économie russe : sous pression budgétaire, les régions réduisent les indemnités versées aux familles des soldats morts en Ukraine est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: ‘PUBG-linked’ bank robber arrested from home in Lahore
items.description: LAHORE: The police claim to have arrested a young man hours after he looted Rs700,000 by getting a “bank robbery task” from the PUBG game at Bhatta Chowk in Defence here on Friday. DIG Operations Faisal Kamran told mediapersons that the robbery took place at around 9:30am near Bhatta Chowk. He said a masked suspect entered the bank premises after taking the guard hostage. He then reached the cash counter, along with the hostage guard, collected cash and escaped the scene. The crime was committed within a few minutes. The DIG said that soon after looting the cash, the suspect drove back to his home which showed that he was not a habitual criminal. DIG says financial difficulties pushed UK-returned youth to commit crime by seeking help from the online game He said police teams were formed soon after receiving an emergency 15 call about the robbery, adding that the police traced him through the Safe City and private cameras and reached his house, located a few minutes’ drive away from the bank. The DIG said that the suspect was identified as Subhan, who had returned to Pakistan from the UK on Sept 16. He said the suspect was living alone in Lahore as his family was settled in the UK. He said that the suspect had been playing the PUBG game for the last many years. On the day of the incident, he got a ‘task’ from the game to rob a bank and acquired a mask and a pistol from somewhere to execute the crime. He said the police interrogated the suspect when he talked about the game, keeping in view such incidents in the past involving young men. He said that the arrested suspect also briefed the police about the methods described in the game to carry out a bank robbery. The DIG said that the suspect was planning to flee to Islamabad with the looted money when the police raided the house. He said the weapon, looted cash and a briefcase were recovered from him. He said that the suspect had changed his vehicle’s number plates to mislead the police. The DIG said the suspect had £1,200 when he reached Pakistan, however, he spent the entire amount and had been demanding more money from his family. When his family refused, he planned the bank robbery to overcome his financial constraints, he added. He said that according to initial investigations, he was influenced by online gaming and web series. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

items.title: Death in Delta: More questions on ‘transfer fee’ saga that consumed Adeda
items.description: •Teachers reveal how they pay for juicy postings By Egufe Yafugborhi, Akpokona Omafuaire & Ochuko Akuopha ASABA — SEPTEMBER 24, Unity Ekpevbughe Adeda, 54, left home for work like any other public servant. By the end of the day, the Deputy Director in Delta State Ministry of Secondary Education had been involved in a violent confrontation at his workplace. Read Also: Ebonyi widow ostracized, banned from community water, market cries out Taken to hospital, later returned home, yet rushed back, he did not survive. His death has since raised questions about what happened inside the ministry, allegations surrounding teacher transfers and the conduct of senior officials involved in the confrontation. For his family, however, the tragedy is painfully simple: a man went to work and died after an incident at the place where he was supposed to serve. The Final Hours Adeda’s sister, Ovwigho, recalled seeing him at the hospital after a colleague had brought him for treatment. “I saw him (Unity) tied up like a criminal. His entire body filthy, blood coming out of his mouth and nose, and his head was badly swollen,” she said. “My brother said the Commissioner (For Secondary Educatiion, Dr Kingsly Ashibogwu) had asked if he knew who he was. My brother responded by asking, ‘Am I obligated to know you? Must I know you?’ The commissioner took offense”, she added. According to her, Adeda later complained of continuing stomach pain after returning home. “He didn’t stay long before they declared him dead,” she said. The circumstances leading to the confrontation are now being investigated by the police and a state government administrative panel. A senior ministry official, who spoke on anonymity, gave Vanguard an account of the events. The official narrated, “Adeda is dead now, I don’t talk with Clementine Ufuoma Ojumah (one of the suspects), but because of what was happening I decided to beg her, that you are a Director, please ignore Adeda’s reaction.” The official alleged Ojumah, Director of Exams and Standards, used her vehicle to block the entrance of the premises. “Adeda who wanted to leave was prevented from going out, so he used the car to hit her Jeep,” the official alleged, adding efforts to calm the situation failed. The witness continued, “Immediately, the Commissioner came, Adeda heard and he started shouting at him. He (Adeda) accused top officials of collecting bribes and sleeping with women for posting (transfers). “Then Commissioner started blowing him, called his boys to joined and they tied him up and were beating him. Adeda was bleeding from mouth and nose. He was taken to hospital and later he died. This whole thing was avoidable but they didn’t listen to me.” Commissioner’s Denial The Commissioner, Ashibogwu, has denied ordering any assault on Adeda. He told Vanguard, “I didn’t. Rather, the man even assaulted me, assaulted people in the office. “I just came out from the church, and they drew my attention that the man came and was threatening their lives, to kill them. “As we were talking, I saw the man walking down, shouting from the gate, ‘I will kill you today!’ Before I knew what was happening, it was attack on me, physical, direct attack. I never ordered any person to touch him, I never touched him.” He said police officers who arrived at the scene did not arrest Adeda but advised that he be taken to hospital. “Police left. And his brother now took him to the hospital where they treated him and discharged him. Then later again at night, his body started becoming somehow, and before I got information this morning that he’s late”, he further claimed. The sharply different accounts are now before investigators. What about the transfers? Behind the confrontation are allegations concerning transfer of teachers within the state’s education system. A former colleague of Adeda, who worked with him before his transfer to Asaba, alleged that disagreements over transfer-related payments contributed to his movement. According to the colleague , “Adeda was not a trouble maker. He was pushed to his death. Adeda was transferred from Office of Chief Inspector of Education over allegations that he was not remitting funds of transfer rackets to Asaba.” He alleged Adeda was subsequently brought to Asaba to work under an official with whom he had previously had disagreements. “What happened that day was Adeda accusing the Directors and top brass of collecting monies in the recent transfer of teachers. This infuriated the Director and Commissioner,” the source alleged. Teachers also made allegations of payments for preferred postings. A teacher recently transferred from Ekredjebor, Ughelli North LGA, alleged: “The whole system is rotten. They collect money and transfer people to wherever they want. “The choice depends on what you pay. I was transferred and paid N50,000 before I was transferred back to where I wanted after two weeks.” A Principal, Patricia, alleged her inability to pay influenced her posting. “Transfer is to the highest bidder, because I am a widow and don’t have the funds. I was taken to a school in a remote village without WAEC accreditation and less than 200 students”, she said. Another teacher, Victoria, said: “I didn’t pay the N50,000 transfer fee, so I was transferred to a riverine school in Ewu. This has been the trend over the years, it is sad.” The allegations have not been independently established and are part of the wider issues requiring investigation. Police Take Over By September 30, Delta State Police Command had confirmed Ashibogwu, Ojumah and four others in custody as investigations progressed. Police spokesman, SP Bright Edafe, said “Ojumah turned herself in at the Command Headquarters Tuesday” The police investigation is expected to examine eyewitness accounts, video footage and medical records to establish circumstances surrounding Adeda’s death and determine individual responsibility. The family is also pressing for an autopsy. Oghenevwogaga Adeda, the deceased’s brother, said: “Arrangement for autopsy is already in place. The IPO on the matter is already asking that we get in contact with a pathologist.” For the family, the medical findings could be crucial to understanding how injuries sustained during the confrontation related to his eventual death. Otovwodo Demands Justice At Otovwodo, Adeda’s home community, grief has turned into public anger. Residents marched with placards reading “Justice for Adeda” and “We are peaceful people, all we want is justice.” President-General of the community, Prince Elvis Oharisi, said: “The community is grieved, and calling for justice. “The committee set up by the government, we are not satisfied with it. The community was not represented, the family never represented in that committee. So, that committee, we have no iota of trust in it”, he said. Youth leader, Umudi Ohwofasa, said: “It’s very, very painful for such a thing to happen to someone. We will continue the protest. I cannot be satisfied as we have not heard anything that will make us satisfied over this issue.” Women leader, Regina expressed the depth of the community’s grief. “A big man who has reached such height in public service. Someone we believed would help our children is the one they killed like a chicken. He is not a chicken, nor a goat, nor a cow — he is a human being”, she lamented. The sister-in-law, Julie Adeda, said: “He’s a very quiet person, and he’s the breadwinner of the family. We are looking up to him. I’m not suspecting any person, but the commissioner and the director have a case to answer. Let the law prevail in any angle.” The state government panel has commenced proceedings, while the police investigation continues. Governor Sheriff Oborevwori had earlier warned public officials against misconduct: “I’ve changed my style. This is not Sheriff of 20 years ago. So when you’re in government you must behave well,” the governor said. “If a Commissioner can be remanded in prison custody, nobody is above the law. Anybody who commits an offence, you want to do thuggery, we will hold you. We don’t play politics with that.” For the Adeda family, however, the issue is no longer about politics. It is about a man who left home for work and returned injured, before dying hours later. The competing accounts must now give way to evidence. If an assault is established and found to have contributed to Adeda’s death, those responsible should face the law. If the evidence establishes a different chain of events, that too must be made public. Likewise, allegations of financial manipulation of transfers must be investigated rather than converted into convictions by public opinion. For now, Adeda’s final day remains a story of a workplace confrontation, a family mourning and a civil service asking difficult questions about power and accountability. The police investigation, the autopsy and the government inquiry now have the responsibility of establishing what happened — and where the evidence ultimately leads. There is the danger of Adeda’s case becoming another political confrontation -one side defending government, another attacking it, and the facts becoming secondary to partisan narratives. That would be unfortunate. The central issue is not whether one political faction can exploit the tragedy against another faction. The central issue is accountability. If Adeda was assaulted and the assault contributed to his death, whoever was responsible should face the law. If the evidence establishes a different chain of events, that too should be stated publicly. The coming days will therefore test more than the police investigation. They will test the Delta State Government’s willingness to allow evidence speak louder than political influence. They will test the police’s ability to investigate people connected to power without fear or favour. They will test whether organised labour can secure meaningful guarantees for civil servants. And they will test whether the government understands that public confidence is not created by assurances alone, but by transparent action. For Adeda’s family, however, this is not an abstract question about governance. It is about a man who left home for work and died after an incident at the place where he was supposed to serve the public. The family wants answers. His colleagues want safety. The police say they want the facts. The government says it wants the circumstances established. Those objectives should not be in conflict. The most important outcome now is not a convenient narrative, a political victory or the protection of anybody’s reputation. The swollen face in the photograph leading to his death cannot answer all the questions. And until truth is established, the word “murder” remains an allegation than a settled fact. And the office where a public servant died should remain, above all, a crime scene and a place for evidence—not a battleground for political narratives. items.title: Five shop owners move court to include terrorism, murder charges in Gul Plaza fire case
items.description: KARACHI: A judicial magistrate on Friday issued notices for Saturday (today) to members of Gul Plaza Management Committee and the investigating officer (IO) on a petition filed by five shop owners of the mall, seeking to record their statements before the court to include charges of murder and terrorism. Speaking to Dawn , prosecutor Hassan Bhatti said that two applications had been moved by the shop owners before Judicial Magistrate (South) Aasim Aslam. He said the shop owners had already recorded their statements before the IO under Section 161 (examination of witnesses by police) of the criminal procedure code and now they wanted to record their statement before the magistrate. He further stated that the prosecution did not oppose the plea seeking to record their statements before the court. However, he added that the prosecution opposed the plea seeking to include charges of murder and terrorism and treat the incident as the Baldia Factory fire incident. Prosecutor Bhatti told Dawn that he argued before the court that the Gul Plaza fire was a separate incident. He added that in the Baldia Factory fire case, a chemical report had found phosphorus, and there was also an alleged intention behind the incident as the factory owners had not paid the ransom demanded by the accused persons. He added that the Gul Plaza incident was separate and that the fire had broken out unintentionally, as per statements recorded by prosecution witnesses. According to witnesses, he added that a teenage boy was playing with matchsticks, which led to the fire in the mall. Meanwhile, defence counsel Shaikh Jawaid Mir, representing members of the Gul Plaza Management Committee — Tanveer Pasta, Amar Ismail, Muhammad Ramazan and Muhammad Ameen — as well as the owner of an artificial flower shop, Naimatullah, and his over 11-year-old son, Huzaifa, had raised objections to the plea seeking to include murder and terrorism charges in the case. After hearing arguments from all sides, the court issued notices to the suspects and the IO regarding recording of their statements and directed them to appear in person on Saturday (today) for hearing. Regarding the plea seeking to include murder and terrorism charges in the case, the court adjourned the matter until Oct 7. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

items.title: Dried placenta may help men regain erections faster after prostate surgery – Study
items.description: By Sola Ogundipe For men undergoing surgery for prostate cancer, removing the tumour may solve the immediate threat, but it can leave behind another deeply personal problem: erectile dysfunction. Read Also: Mental Health Summit: US-based behaviour specialist to spotlight youth addiction, recovery at Vanguard summit October Researchers are exploring an unusual way to help sexual function return. The approach, according to a publication in New Scientist, involves placing thin sheets of dehydrated human placenta around nerves exposed during prostate surgery. Early evidence suggests the technique may help some men regain erections sooner. The idea is attracting attention because the nerves responsible for erections can be stretched, bruised or damaged during prostate cancer surgery, even when surgeons manage to spare them. Recovery can take months and, in some cases, considerably longer. The placenta-derived material is being investigated as a biological aid to nerve healing. Placental tissue contains a range of growth factors and other biological components that researchers believe could support tissue repair and reduce inflammation around injured nerves. “To help men get better erections, we’re using donations of placentas from women,” said Shirin Razdan, a surgeon at HCA Florida Kendall Hospital in Miami. The principle is based on belief that if the delicate nerves involved in erection can be protected and supported immediately after surgery, they may have a better chance of recovering their function. A review involving thousands of prostate cancer operations has reported an earlier return of erectile function among men who received the placenta-derived treatment. Some studies have reported erections returning within about a week, compared with roughly two weeks among men who did not receive the intervention. The findings, however, need to be viewed with caution. An earlier return of erections doesn’t necessarily mean the treatment restores normal sexual function in every patient. Nor does it prove that the placenta material alone is responsible for all of the improvement observed. An earlier return of erections may be encouraging, but the more important questions are whether men ultimately regain satisfactory erections, how long any benefit lasts, whether sexual function improves enough to affect quality of life, and whether the procedure brings additional risks or costs. The research reflects a growing interest in regenerative approaches to complications of cancer treatment. Prostate cancer surgery is increasingly successful at controlling localised disease, but survival isn’t the only measure of a successful outcome. For many men, being able to return to normal sexual, urinary and social functioning is also an important part of life after cancer. For now, the placenta-derived technique is largely regarded as an emerging approach rather than a proven solution for post-surgical erectile dysfunction. Further research is ongoing. items.title: UE : 6.200 ordres de départ visant des Marocains au T2, 1.180 retours effectifs
items.description: Les autorités des États membres de l’Union européenne ont délivré 6.200 ordres de quitter leur territoire à des ressortissants marocains au deuxième trimestre de 2026, tandis que 1.180 Marocains ont effectivement été renvoyés vers un pays situé hors de l’UE, selon les dernières données de l’Office statistique de l’Union européenne (Eurostat). Les ressortissants algériens restent, pour leur part, la nationalité la plus représentée parmi les personnes visées par ces décisions de départ. Les chiffres publiés par Eurostat, montrent une légère baisse des mesures prises à l’encontre des ressortissants marocains. Le nombre d’ordres de départ les concernant a reculé de 5,1 % par rapport au premier trimestre de l’année. La tendance s’inscrit dans un recul plus large à l’échelle européenne. Au deuxième trimestre, les États membres ont délivré au total plus de 110.000 ordres de quitter leur territoire à des ressortissants de pays tiers, soit une baisse de 3,9 % sur un trimestre et de 12 % par rapport au même trimestre de 2025. Les Algériens en tête des ordres de départ Dans le classement par nationalité, les ressortissants algériens arrivent en tête, avec plus de 10.000 ordres de départ enregistrés au cours du trimestre. Les Marocains figurent également parmi les nationalités les plus concernées, aux côtés notamment des ressortissants syriens, brésiliens et turcs. Le nombre de décisions administratives ne correspond toutefois pas au nombre de personnes effectivement éloignées. Sur les plus de 110.000 ordres de départ recensés dans l’Union européenne, un peu plus de 36.000 personnes ont effectivement été renvoyées vers un pays situé hors de l’UE durant la même période. Cette différence illustre l’écart entre une décision de quitter le territoire et sa mise en œuvre effective, qui peut dépendre de plusieurs facteurs administratifs et juridiques. La France en tête des décisions de départ La France arrive largement en tête des pays membres pour le nombre d’ordres de départ délivrés au deuxième trimestre, avec plus de 32.000 décisions. Elle est suivie par le Portugal, avec 11.190 ordres, puis par l’Allemagne, avec 8.160. À eux seuls, ces trois pays représentent près de la moitié des décisions enregistrées dans l’ensemble de l’Union européenne. La hiérarchie est différente lorsqu’il s’agit des retours effectivement réalisés. L’Allemagne arrive en tête avec environ 8.400 renvois vers des pays situés hors de l’UE, devant la France avec 3.835 et la Pologne avec plus de 3.000. Ces trois États concentrent ainsi plus de 41 % des retours recensés au niveau européen. Les retours sont majoritairement volontaires Les données d’Eurostat permettent également de distinguer les modalités de retour. Plus de 60 % des personnes effectivement renvoyées ont quitté le territoire européen de manière volontaire, alors qu’environ 39,2 % ont fait l’objet d’un retour forcé. La proportion des retours contraints est particulièrement élevée dans certains États membres, notamment au Danemark et en Italie. Ces chiffres concernent les personnes ayant effectivement quitté le territoire et ne doivent donc pas être confondus avec l’ensemble des ordres de départ prononcés durant la période. The post UE : 6.200 ordres de départ visant des Marocains au T2, 1.180 retours effectifs appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Mental Health Summit: US-based behaviour specialist to spotlight youth addiction, recovery at Vanguard summit October
items.description: By Sola Ogundipe A US-based addiction and behavioural health specialist, Dr Daniel Ikpechukwu, is among the experts billed to feature at the 4th Vanguard Mental Health Summit in Lagos, where he will examine Nigeria’s response to young people caught between substance dependence and offending. Ikpechukwu, a Substance Abuse/Behavioral Health Counselor, Alcohol/Drug Clinical Evaluator and Treatment Provider, and Adjunct Professor of Psychology at Georgia Gwinnett College, Georgia, USA, will address how the country can balance accountability with appropriate intervention when substance use is linked to offending. His presentation, titled “Youth Drug Addiction and the Justice System: Advancing Treatment, Rehabilitation and Recovery in Nigeria,” is one of the key sessions at the summit, organised by Vanguard Media Limited and scheduled for Friday, October 9, 2026, at the Civic Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos. Themed “Advancing Youth Mental Health in Nigeria,” the summit has as its sub-theme “Mental Health in a Digital Age: Navigating Social Media, Technology and Wellbeing.” Ikpechukwu’s presentation brings a pressing dimension to the summit’s focus on youth mental health, about what happens when a young person comes into contact with law enforcement and the courts. At the centre of the discussion is whether punishment alone is enough when substance dependence is a significant factor in a young person’s behaviour. Ikpechukwu will examine the psychological, behavioural and social factors that can drive drug use and contribute to harmful behaviour. Nigeria’s national drug-use survey estimated that 14.4 per cent of people aged 15 to 64, about 14.3 million people, had used a psychoactive substance in 2025, even as drug use can disrupt education, employment, family relationships, health and a young person’s prospects. Ikpechukwu will examine how early assessment, appropriate intervention and structured alternatives to incarceration in suitable cases could form part of a more effective response, while recognising that public safety, the seriousness of an offence, individual circumstances and the law must remain central. The summit is expected to deepen discussion on how Nigeria can strengthen early identification, expand access to appropriate services and improve support for young people after treatment or release. Ikpechukwu’s participation brings an international clinical and behavioural health perspective to the discussion. The challenge is to ensure that young people affected by substance dependence are held accountable where necessary while also having access to the care and support needed to rebuild their lives. items.title: The Pinky paradox
items.description: ON Sept 26, alleged drug dealer Anmol alias Pinky and her alleged accomplice Sameer were indicted in a narcotics case registered in 2021. This followed Pinky’s acquittal in three other narcotics cases over the summer. She remains in jail, facing several other cases. Ever since she was arrested in May of this year, Pinky’s case has garnered a ton of media attention; purported voice recordings in which she taunts police over their inability to catch her, and the branding on her alleged product, ‘Queen Medam Pinky’ and ‘Naam hi kafi hai’, have all the ingredients of a gangster movie. Except, of course, that there is a ‘godmother’ at the centre of it all. What then to make of a woman who appears to have made a name for herself in the male dominated gangster world? As a weekly columnist for over a decade, I’ve written regularly about Pakistani women. I’ve written about innumerable cases in which women are beaten down by the system, by men, by in-laws, by their own male relatives, by the economy and by all the forces that coalesce to keep women ‘in their place’. Often, these columns are obituaries. Just two weeks ago, for instance, I wrote about a nine-year-old girl from Swat named Ishmal, whose only mistake was to go to her neighbour’s house as she often did. She was allegedly sexually assaulted and killed. Or let’s remember Hina Javed’s case from just over a month ago — a woman married to a former professor at Nust, who was found dead in a bathroom after allegedly suffering abuse and torture. These are the usual stories of women in Pakistan, and I know you know many more than the ones I have written about. Women trapped in abusive and even torturous marriages because they do not know if they will be able to make it on their own. Or women who have tried to make it on their own and are punished at every turn, landlords rejecting them for not having a man of the house, bosses harassing them because they are seen as available because of their single status. And these are stories of the middle class; poverty exacerbates all of these cruelties even further. Life in Pakistan in 2026 is harsh and Hobbesian for everyone, but for women it is a particular kind of hell. Defiance alone is not a virtue. Then there is Pinky — an alleged cocaine dealer whose lethal product was packaged under her name. Born into a family of modest means with a home in Lyari’s Baloch Para, she finished Class VIII. According to investigators, she then left for Lahore to pursue modelling. According to police, it was from her former husband, a lawyer and alleged drug dealer, that she learned the drug trade. Investigators allege that she went on to manage an extensive cocaine network spanning Karachi and Lahore, using riders, social media, benami accounts, and other intermediaries. She allegedly sold to customers in Karachi’s affluent areas. Her story is unusual, but the allegations against her are serious: drug trafficking is not an act of female emancipation simply because the person accused of running the operation is a woman. Selling drugs is a reprehensible trade. Sadly, many turn to it to escape penury. It is an aspect to reflect on — without turning Pinky’s alleged criminal enterprise into a heroic rebellion. The same poverty and absence of opportunity that can make criminal networks attractive also produce countless victims of the narcotics trade. Pinky must pay for her crimes. Even as I say that, I cannot help but wonder how many of the wealthy and influential people allegedly connected to her network will face similar scrutiny. Police said an initial forensic examination of her phone identified hundreds of contacts, including 300 alleged active customers, as well as multiple bank accounts allegedly used for payments. Will we ever know who among the powerful benefited from or sustained this trade? Pakistani society is often eager to make a woman pay even as it looks askance at the sins of male leaders, politicians, industrialists, and others with power. But equality cannot mean transforming an alleged drug dealer into a feminist heroine. It must mean equal accountability: for Pinky if the charges against her are proved, for those who allegedly enabled her operation, and for the wealthy customers whose money made such a lucrative trade possible. A defiant woman is a rare creature in Pakistan, and one who manages to stay alive while challenging powerful structures may be rarer still. But defiance alone is not a virtue. Pinky’s story may tell us much about gender, poverty, power and hypocrisy in Pakistan. None of that requires us to turn her into a heroine. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy. rafia.zakaria@gmail.com Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

Ravel, su hijo de 19 años, no estaba en la comisaría, ni en los hospitales, ni entre los muertos o detenidos que aparecían en los vídeos que circularon tras la masacre. Mientras sus amigas iban recogiendo los cuerpos de sus hijos, a ella solo le quedaba por comprobar el bosque que separa los complejos de favelas de Alemão y la Penha , en la zona norte de Río de Janeiro. Entre los árboles encontró cadáveres de 10 en 10 y ella gritaba hasta oír su propio eco: “¿Hay alguno con el pelo rojo?”. A las cinco y media de la mañana, atiborrada de tranquilizantes, arañada, sucia y sin haber comido, se fue a casa a ducharse. Su prima le estaba peinando cuando sonó el teléfono: habían encontrado a Ravel. O, mejor dicho, su cabeza. Seguir leyendo
