items.title: Avoiding transparency
items.description: IN January this year, the National Assembly passed a private member’s bill to amend Section 138 of the Elections Act, 2017, which may blunt, if not totally reverse, the legal requirement of making public the submitted annual statements of assets and liabilities by national and provincial legislators by the Election Commission of Pakistan. The amendment would create an exception allowing the presiding officer of a legislature to ask the ECP to keep a member’s statements confidential if the presiding officer determines that publication would pose a serious threat to the member’s life or safety. The bill was forwarded to the Senate but, fortunately, has not yet been passed. Earlier, the ECP was pressured into discontinuing the practice of posting the Gazette Notification of legislators’ statements of assets and liabilities on its website, and people were constrained to purchase a hard copy of the Gazette Notification through a complicated and time-consuming procedure, diluting the intended transparency guaranteed by the law. This is not the first attempt to undermine laws requiring transparent information about elected public officials or about those aspiring to public office. The Elections Act, 2017, was a landmark piece of legislation that included several electoral reforms but, unfortunately, did away with the legal requirement for each candidate for public office to submit some 19 declarations under oath along with nomination papers. The declarations provided and made public information such as candidates’ assets, liabilities, educational qualifications, tax paid, and records of registered criminal cases, if any, against the candidate, along with similar data, to help voters make an informed choice. After civil society reacted to this blatant reversal of transparency, the Lahore High Court, and later the Supreme Court, stepped in. In its June 6, 2018, judgment, the Supreme Court chief justice restored the requirement of public affidavits after journalists filed a public interest petition. Making the assets and liabilities of senior civil servants public has been a contentious issue in Pakistan for a long time. Advocates of transparency argue that public disclosure is vital to combat corruption and track illicit enrichment. Civil servants and certain state institutions often give counterarguments that making their monetary worth public compromises their personal privacy and puts their families at risk of extortion, kidnapping, and targeted harassment. They argue that the media can take asset declarations out of context, leading to unfair public scrutiny or ‘media trials’ before any wrongdoing is proven. There is a trend of undermining processes meant to ensure transparency in public bodies. Senior civil servants also view external demands for transparency as an infringement on their institutional independence or an attempt to weaken their administrative authority. These arguments and counter-arguments are not confined to Pakistan; they are part of a global debate, but it is more pronounced in developing countries like ours. Both sides’ positions may carry weight, but the balance recently tilted in favour of transparency when the IMF put its foot down and demanded that the government ensure senior civil servants’ assets are made public. The Fund’s Governance and Corruption Diagnostic Assessment, made public last November, included 15 priority recommendations for the government. One of them requires the FBR, the Establishment Division, and NAB to strengthen accountability and integrity among high-level federal civil servants by initiating the publication of asset declarations in 2026 and introducing risk-based verification of asset declarations within six months. Ironically, an international agency had to impose this transparency; we ourselves failed to introduce the practice as a voluntary measure of good governance. There is a trend of undermining processes meant to ensure transparency in public bodies. Pakistan has enacted the Transparency and Right to Information (RTI) laws both at the federal and provincial levels. In addition, independent information commissions have been established in Islamabad and the four provincial capitals to adjudicate complaints regarding the denial of information under the Act. Despite this elaborate transparency infrastructure, requests for information have suffered setbacks in some celebrated cases. An Islamabad-based journalist, Rana Abrar Khalid, had submitted an information request to the Cabinet Division in November 2020 seeking details of gifts received, retained and deposited in the toshakhana by then prime minister Imran Khan. The request was denied. The journalist filed a complaint with the Pakistan Information Commission, which upheld the request’s legitimacy and directed the government to provide the information. Instead, the federal government filed a petition with the Islamabad High Court, which dismissed it. The government was planning to approach the Supreme Court when the Imran Khan government was removed through a vote of no-confidence. A request for information about staff strength, vacancies, temporary employees, new positions, gender diversity in the workforce, and the latest approved Service Rules of the Supreme Court, filed under the RTI law in 2019, was declared unmaintainable. Still, the chief justice ‘magnanimously’ asked the registrar to provide the information. Sadly, it set a precedent that superior courts are not covered by RTI laws, although the laws do not explicitly exempt superior courts. In April 2026, citing the Supreme Court precedent, the Lahore High Court refused to disclose its policy on judicial privileges and details of the official vehicles used by judges, even though the Punjab Information Commission had upheld the request. The Commission, however, withdrew its direction to the Lahore High Court to provide the information after the court’s judgement. Transparency is an important ingredient of good governance, and any backsliding on this count will further weaken the quality of governance. Pakistan should review, and reverse, the recent trend of diluting transparency. The writer is the president of Pakistan-based think tank Pildat. president@pildat.org X: @ABMPildat Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

items.title: Who can explain NNPC’s N11.2trn security bill?
items.description: By Hector Igbikiowubo The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited has finally put a number to the black hole that has swallowed Nigeria’s oil wealth for years. In its 2025 audited financial report, the company casually disclosed that it spent a mind-boggling N11.2 trillion to “protect the country’s oil and gas assets on behalf of the Federal Government.” Read Also: How Nigeria declined into criminality, poor governance in 66 years Let that figure sink in. N11.2 trillion. Not billion. Trillion. For a country that is not at war, not under invasion, and not battling a foreign adversary for its oil fields, what exactly was NNPC protecting oil assets from that cost more than one-and-a-half times its entire declared profit for the year? The company declared N7.2 trillion in profit after tax and N34.5 trillion in revenue. Yet it claims to have spent N11.2 trillion on security alone. That means for every N3 the company made as profit, it spent nearly N5 on security. In any serious oil company anywhere in the world, security is a cost element, not the dominant cost centre that dwarfs profit. This is not business; it is an absurdity. Security For What, From Whom? The language in the audited report is deliberately opaque: “other receivables from federation… advance payments to the federation and costs incurred to secure the country’s oil and gas assets” under “an approved framework between the federal government and the group.” What framework? Approved by whom? When was it approved by the National Assembly? What are the line items that make up N11.2 trillion in security expenses in 12 months? Nigeria’s entire defence budget for 2025 – for the Army, Navy, Air Force, fighting Boko Haram, banditry, and IPOB combined – was less than N4.9 trillion. NNPC alone is claiming it spent more than double the national defence budget just to secure pipelines and wellheads. If the Nigerian Armed Forces can attempt to secure the entire territorial integrity of 200 million people for less than N5 trillion, how does a single company spend N11.2 trillion securing oil assets? The Subsidy Shell Game The report contains another sleight of hand. NNPC proudly states that no “energy security expense” – the sanitized term for petrol subsidy – was “recognised” in 2025, compared to N7.13 trillion in 2024. But in the next breath, it admits to a defrayed energy security cost of N8.9 trillion carried over from 2024, which was conveniently “netted off against royalties, tax, and dividends” due to the Federation in September 2025. So Nigerians are still paying for subsidy, just through accounting netting. Royalties, taxes, and dividends that should have gone into the Federation Account to fund hospitals, schools, and roads were simply erased to cover NNPC’s past subsidy bill. Now, with subsidy supposedly gone, a new monster has appeared: N11.2 trillion for security. Nigerians must ask: Is “energy security cost” simply being reborn as “oil asset protection cost”? Is this the new nomenclature for opaque deductions from the Federation? The Questions NNPC Must Answer 1. Publish the Framework: Nigerians deserve to see the full “approved framework” that allows NNPC to spend N11.2 trillion of federation money without appropriation. 2. The Breakdown: Who were the security contractors paid? How much went to private security firms? How much to the military and NSCDC? How much is administrative overhead disguised as security? 3. The Audit: Who audited these security expenses? A receipt for N11.2 trillion cannot be justified by a single line item called “costs incurred to secure assets.” 4. The Result: For N11.2 trillion, did oil theft stop? No. Did pipeline vandalism stop? No. The NUPRC still reports massive crude losses. So what did we secure? The NNPC has morphed from an oil company into a parallel government with its own security budget larger than the nation’s, its own spending framework outside the National Assembly, and its own accounting method of netting off what it owes Nigerians. If NNPC can spend N11.2 trillion protecting oil assets and still declare a N7.2 trillion profit, it means the real revenue was close to N45 trillion or more before this dubious deduction. That N11.2 trillion belongs to the Federation. It belongs to the Nigerian people. Until NNPC opens its books and explains how it spent more protecting oil than the Nigerian military spends protecting Nigeria, Nigerians should treat this N11.2 trillion claim not as an expense, but as a heist in broad daylight. Vanguard News The post Who can explain NNPC’s N11.2trn security bill? appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Talks, at last
items.description: YESTERDAY, the government and opposition finally sat across from each other and talked . A government-led coalition, including representatives of the PPP, and the PTI-led opposition, concluded a round of talks on Friday at the chambers of the National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq in Islamabad. The meeting had been called after the president and prime minister met on Thursday to discuss the national political and security situation. It seemed like a last-ditch attempt at defusing the escalating political crisis ahead of the PTI’s planned march on the federal capital, scheduled for this Sunday. Another round of talks will be held today, with time running out. Neither side had much to say regarding what was accomplished in the first round. Mr Sadiq’s assertion that parliament is the right forum for talks is correct, but the opposition is equally justified in demanding that the government demonstrate its seriousness. There is a trust deficit that needs to be bridged quickly. The government’s constant threats to suspend KP’s elected dispensation over a political protest have escalated hostilities considerably. In that context, both sides did well to start talking. The PTI’s Barrister Gohar Khan called the one-hour meeting “cordial”, which gives hope. The prime minister’s special assistant on political affairs did not share as positive an assessment, however — pointing to the fact that no decisions were taken and there was no clear progress. The PTI also seems determined to keep its protest call intact during the negotiations, while the government wants it cancelled unconditionally. The opposition has already shown flexibility by delaying the march from Sept 27 to Oct 4 — perhaps it can be convinced to consider another extension to give the talks a proper chance. It was not a good omen that the opposition leader in the National Assembly boycotted the sit-down. The fact that the PTI went ahead without him shows that it is putting at least some faith in the process. Opposition leaders said they need to consult former prime minister Imran Khan to finalise their agenda. Permitting a meeting with him at Adiala is an easy, low-cost goodwill gesture for the government and could create a quick breakthrough. The other important items for the PTI are allowing the jailed leader to be moved to hospital and the release of his sisters who were arrested ahead of the planned march. Taking these steps would help ease tensions. The point made by PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari regarding unity against terrorism and hostility from neighbours is a fair one, but national unity alone cannot be a reason to shut down legitimate political dissent. Both sides must step back from ultimatums. The threat of governor’s rule must be taken off the table, and the PTI should drop its ‘we will march no matter what’ stance. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

items.title: How Nigeria declined into criminality, poor governance in 66 years
items.description: By Dele Sobowale “What does corrupting time not diminish? Our grandparents brought forth feebler heirs; we are further degenerate; and soon will beget progeny more wicked.” Homer, 65-8 BC Read Also: NIGERIA @ 66: Scandalised? – How NJC’s hammer fell on judges, justices In 1960, nobody being prosecuted for embezzlement of public funds would have been fielded for the next election by any political party. Today, dozens of suspected criminals – certificate forgers, financiers of terrorists and drug traffickers — are running for the highest offices. No graduate of any university would consider crime as his first choice for employment. Today, thousands of the grandsons of the graduates of 1960 routinely join yahoo syndicates in order to fund lavish life styles as their first option. It is difficult to blame them; when former Governors accused of serious crimes are either Senators or aspiring to be – without the slightest sense of remorse. Our founding fathers – Ahmadu Bello, Nnamdi Azikiwe and Obafemi Awolowo would not believe what the nation they fought for had become in the hands of their political children and grandchildren today. Virtually everything – food supply, education, health, roads, infrastructure and, above all, governance — is in relative decline; compared with 1960. FOOD FIRST “There are people in the world, so hungry, that God cannot appear to them except in form of bread.” Mahatma Gandhi, 1869-1948. The great Indian leader and liberator made that remark before he was assassinated in 1948 at a time when his country, now divided into at least three nations, suffered from food scarcity worse than Nigeria is experiencing now. Certainly, it can also be said that there are millions of people in Nigeria today, so hungry, that God cannot appear to them except either as a loaf of bread or a bowl of cooked rice. I was only four years old in 1948. So, I had to interview those far older than me to know how the food situation was like at the time – in addition to historical research. Surprisingly, Nigeria was then a net exporter of food at a time when almost 99 per cent of Nigerians were illiterates; when the University of Ibadan was just opening its doors to students. All the Nigerian university graduates could not have been more than 1000. Today, UI alone graduates over 5,000 annually. All Nigerian universities throw more than 120,000 into the job market. What is the use of our famed “educated manpower” if we cannot feed ourselves now? In 1960, Nigeria was the largest exporter of vegetable oil; the third largest exporter of cocoa; and imported no grain of rice. Today, Nigeria is the exporter of cocoa; a net importer of vegetable oil and the importer of rice. With each passing year, sustainable food security becomes more elusive. “Nigeria’s fertilizer use shortfall.” VANGUARD, Editorial, September 25, 2026. The comment by the paper should be read by everybody aspiring to lead Nigeria and the states. “The Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security says national fertilizer consumption is about 18.6 kilogrammes per hectare, against 50kg/ benchmark associated with the 2006 Abuja Declaration”. Obviously, twenty years, after the Abuja Declaration, Nigeria has not achieved up to half of its benchmark. Food security will remain a mirage for years to come. MULTI-DIMENSIONAL POVERTY NOW INTRACTABLE “133 million Nigerians poor – NBS, November 18, 2022. In 1960, the population of Nigeria was under 60 million; and less than 30 per cent was categorized as poor – when the country was not a majour oil producing and exporting nation. Instead, Nigeria had a more diversified economy. Today, the nation is again moving towards greater diversification; after decades of operating as a heavily oil-dependent economy. Food insecurity and import-dependence were to worst repercussions of the flight from domestic food production. The decline from a Middle Income economy in the early 1960s and 1970s to the Worlds Poverty Capital in 2018, except for occasional reversals, was gradual and relentless. It continues till today. The figures speak for themselves: 18 million in the 1960s; 133 million in 2022 and approximately 138 million in 2025. That figure is expected to increase in 2026 and for at least a few more years on account of President Tinubu’s poorly articulated reform programme centre around fuel subsidy removal. Nigeria is still trying to assimilate the intentions of Tinubu’s economic programme. RELATIVE DECLINE IN CRUDE PRODUCTION RANKING “A bicycle …once rolling, retains its balance so long as it moves. Without movement, it collapses.” Aleksander Solzhenitsyn, The 1970s and early 1980s can be regarded as the golden years of Nigeria’s ranking in the global crude oil export. The nation was once the sixth or seventh largest world producer and exporter. Refineries were established to process some of the crude and the rest was exported. Under military President Ibrahim Babangida, IBB, crude and fuel were produced and exported for a while. The bicycle was moving. It stopped suddenly; when Turn-Around-Maintenance, TAM, were no longer conducted. Apparently one small mistake; but, the consequences for Nigeria had been devastating. No other Federal Government has been able to keep the refineries open since 1994. The repercussions were obvious for decades as every President promised but did nothing to revive the refineries. They are now scraps of metals and electrical lines. In Nigeria ranks as the eleventh oil exporting nation; and we now import crude from the United States, thanks to Dangote Refinery, which was once our largest customer. Economic disaster cannot be better defined; since the Americans have no intention of returning as buyers of Nigerian crude. HEALTH MANAGEMENT IS UNHEALTHY NATIONWIDE “Health is wealth” is one of the most enduring gems of wisdom handed down to mankind through the ages. Every regional government during the First Republic took public health seriously. Patients paid next to nothing for the best possible treatment available in General Hospitals. In 2026, services in General Hospitals have deteriorated so badly, and those rushing there better have a lot of money; otherwise there is no service and it is seldom the best. Patients to doctor ratio in Nigeria has reached about 300,000 patients per doctor in Nigeria; making it one of the worst in the world. Surprisingly, unprecedented revenue since 2023 has brought no improvement. Quite the contrary; the situation has never been worse. Here is evidence. “Only N36m released from 2025 N216bn health capital budget – Minister.” Report, February 10, 2026 When only about 0.06 per cent of capital appropriations for health are released, the repercussions are inescapable. Several services provided by all health institutions – from Primary Health Centres to Teaching hospitals – grind to a halt. Obsolete equipment are not replaced; care provision is not upgraded; staff morale is low everywhere. The failure in this regard can be measured by the fact that Nigeria is the largest country whose life expectancy has barely moved up for nearly a decade. Expect no change soon. “Why 2026 capital budget may not be implemented this year.” VANGUARD, September 21, 2026 The recent report by VANGUARD has merely re-confirmed a stream of tendency by the Tinubu administration to treat annual budgets with the levity they don’t deserve. With the releases for 2026 deferred until 2027, it is clear that what is broken and un-repaired this year will remain that way until next year, at least. How many lives will be lost? HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT AND THE CONSEQUENCES “The devil finds work for idle hands.” That has been known since the dawn of history. Nigerian secondary and tertiary institutions churn out nearly half a million graduates annually. Most of them, including those who graduated First Class, will finish National Youth Service and end up jobless. But, the international crime syndicates are waiting to employ them. It is now a painful experience to read or watch the news these days. More Nigerian youths than ever before are now employed in cyber crimes – yahoo, romance scams, trans-national money laundering – at home or abroad. Drug trafficking, Ponzi schemes and other forms of internet aided felonies have proliferated beyond anybody’s imagination. Law enforcement is lagging behind in many respects. Nobody now knows how many escape for each one caught and prosecuted. More chillingly, some operate their crime syndicates from inside prison walls. CORRUPTION DESTROYS EVERYTHING “Some public officers take Nigeria’s money ‘every minute”, says Olukoyode. The Cable. “Corruption: EFCC uncovers officials with hundreds of house, millions in assets.” PM News Nigeria, September 28, 2026. When the Chairman of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC, talks about pervasive embezzlement of public funds by public officials, Nigerians should listen. It is almost impossible to be a public servant — federal, state or local government – without being involved individually in crimes or colluding with others to commit larceny. Unknown to most Nigerians, the public service is the greatest crime syndicate in the country today. Public servants steal more funds from the federal, state and local government accounts than any other group of criminals can match. The most casual glance at the Annual Report of the Auditor-General of the Federation, AuGF, for any year, would reveal questionable transactions, now running into trillions, by every Ministry, Department and Agencies, MDAs. Shockingly, the worst offenders are: the Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN, the NNPCL, the Presidency, the Police and the Judiciary. Any nation whose law enforcement officers constitute the apex financial predators is probably beyond redemption. Nigeria’s debt now stands at N166 trillion; a significant percentage of the funds borrowed to improve national welfare and reduce poverty were, and are being, stolen by public servants. INCREASING DEBT BURDEN AND PERPETUAL POVERTY “Yes, we will do anything for the poor man; anything, but, get off his back.” Leo Tolstoy, 1828-1910 “FG seeks fresh $1.5bn World Bank loan.” Report, September 28, 2026 The national debt jumped to N166.79 trillion at the end of June 2026. That should not be surprising. Nigerians were warned about this government. Here is a reminder from 2024. “The DMO said as of March 31, 2024, the country’s domestic and external debts stood at N121.67 trillion ($91.46 billion). Nigeria’s debt rose by N24.33 trillion within three months – from N97.34 trillion ($108.23 billion) in December 2023 to N121.67 trillion ($91.46 billion).” Channels Television. Nigerian government leaders, Presidents and Governors, are addicted to loans the same way drug addicts cannot kick the habit; and become increasingly hooked. What Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala persuaded Obasanjo to do in 2004, that is paid off Nigeria’s external loans was so alien to our government leaders that one late former Governor called her “stupid”. Since then, no President or Governor has repeated it – even when opportunities made it possible. In just two years, the Tinubu administration has increased the national dent by N45 trillion. That is more debt than Nigeria racked up from 1960 to 2015 – when APC’s wind of debt change overwhelmed us. The future has been mortgaged for three generations. Right now every Nigerian owes the world N759,000; for which he had received next to no benefits. On the contrary; higher debts have translated into deepening poverty. Yet, there is more debt is on the way. SECURITY CHALLENGES HAVE NEVER BEEN MORE DAUNTING 3.7M DISPLACED NIGERIANS IN EIGHT STATES Note: 3.7 million Nigerians are reported displaced in March 2026. Only eight states account for 3,341,000 or 91% of them. Borno State, alone, accounts for 46 per cent; and together with Benue, the two states hold 60 per cent of all displaced persons in Nigeria. There are reasons for this situation – which we ignore at our perils STATE NUMBER % OF TOTAL Borno 1,711 46 Benue 500 14 Zamfara 276 8 Katsina 244 7 Adamawa 218 6 Yobe 155 4 Sokoto 118 3 Kaduna 117 3 TOTAL 3,341 91 Source: VANGUARD, March 16, 2026 . Internally Displaced Persons, IDPs, can justifiably be a measure of security in the nation. Behind the 3.7 million people in the camp are several hundred thousands killed, homes and means of livelihood destroyed; families broken and futures blighted. Before 2013, seldom were 30 Nigerians massacred in one day; now, it is a good day for the nation if less than 50 people were killed, inducted, maimed or kidnapped by hoodlums in various categories. Before 2010, the Nigerian state had a near monopoly of the use of lethal violence. Not anymore; today, so many groups compete with state security forces for control of power. And, the bandits are succeeding like never before. Almost every day, the media publishes news of mass murders, kidnapping and destruction of entire communities. Occasionally, Nigerians in particular, and the global community is invited, via live video, to witness victims being slaughtered like cattle. The current administration inherited the disaster bequeathed by Buhari; but, for a few successful rescue operations, has so far failed to improve on the security situation since 2023. This being a year when politics takes precedence over governance, and political intolerance on the rise, there is very little hope for relief until after the elections. ANNUAL BUDGET REDUCED TO A JOKE “Why 2026 capital budget may not be implemented this year.” VANGUARD, September 21, 2026 The 2026 Budget is suffering the same fate as the 2024 and 2025 budgets – written to be discarded as soon as they are presented to the worst National Assembly, NASS, since 1999. The steep decline in budget management started with late President Buhari; who left Nigeria “an economy on the brink of bankruptcy”. Buhari’s economic disaster was founded on incompetent budget preparation; and woeful execution; both of which were concealed by propaganda and falsehood. It was only the failure to redeem the promises made and the extension of budgets, well into the following year, which eventually revealed that capital budgets had not been implemented. In May 2023, the annual budget extension, regularly condoned by the NASS, proved particularly costly to the country. Buhari was forced to disclose that N23.7 trillion had been illegally withdrawn from the Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN. Eventually N30 trillion was discovered to have been withdrawn without the authority of the docile NASS. The collusion between the Presidency and the CBN was unprecedented in Nigeria – even under Abacha’s draconian military rule. Till today, there is no record of how the N30 trillion was spent. National debt took a giant leap forward – with nothing to show for it. Since the 2024 Budget, Tinubu has demonstrated that the worst is yet to come. NDLEA OVERWHELMED BY AVALANCHE OF ILLICIT DRUGS When the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, NDLEA Decree 48 of 1989 was promulgated, Nigeria was regarded as a drug transit country; with low consumption. Today, the country has become a high consumer, producer and exporter of illicit drugs. Drug traffickers are apprehended everyday with large consignments of drugs. To cap it all, two multi-billion drug producing factories have been discovered in the country. From all indications, there might be more. Despite the valiant efforts of the NDLEA, the agency is obviously losing the war. Drug addiction has become so pervasive, it has reached primary schools in some states. PRESIDENT HAUNTED BY HIS US PAST “Tinubu misses UNGA for the third time.” “Jimoh Ibrahim, Nigeria’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations had earlier said Tinubu would attend the 81st UNGA, saying that provisions had been made for him to sit close to Donald Trump, his American counterpart.” Daily Trust, September 21, 2026. Mr Jimoh Ibrahim, without realizing it, was passing fake news. President Tinubu was in France while President Macon was packing his bags for UNGA. The Nigerian President made no plans to go to UNGA. Nobody was fooled by Tinubu’s absence. The whole world is aware of his case in the US and the efforts to conceal the past. The annual United Nations General Assembly, UNGA, is the global biggest political event. Heads of Government of the 193 member nations seize the opportunity to promote their nations, network collectively and individually – even when the reception is hostile. It is quite possible that no President has missed two in a row. Tinubu missing three in a row should be concerning to every Nigerian – including his strongest supporters. Several reasons have been advanced for Tinubu’s absence from UNGA. One is most concerning. It has been alleged that a warrant of arrest might have been obtained for hid detention if he stepped on American soil. President Trump was said to be unwilling to save the Nigerian President the embarrassment, as well as the consequences. As things stand, if re-elected, Tinubu might still not be able to attend UNGA in the future. In the 1970s and 1980s, no President of Nigeria evaded the US. That summarises the external affairs situation. items.title: Walter Mosley visits W.E.B. Du Bois Centre in Accra: A New York Secretary’s homecoming story on where Du Bois spent his final years.
items.description: The W.E.B. Du Bois Memorial Centre for Pan-African Culture sits on First Circular Road in Cantonments, a short walk from the United States Embassy. Dr. W.E.B. Du Bois lived there during the last years of his life, and he is buried here alongside the ashes of his wife, Shirley Graham Du Bois. Du Bois was 93 when he moved to Ghana in 1961 at the invitation of the late President Kwame Nkrumah, who asked him to lead the Encyclopedia Africana, a project to document the history and achievements of African people. He became a Ghanaian citizen and continued working until his death in Accra on August 27, 1963, a day before the March on Washington. Walter Mosley’s Private Tour of the Du Bois Centre. For New York State Secretary Walter T. Mosley, the visit was more than a stop between meetings. He chairs the New York State Commission on African American History and minored in African Studies and African American History at Penn State. The visit was coordinated by Maurice Cheetham, founder of Diaspora Bridge Consulting, an Accra-based firm that connects diaspora leaders with government, traditional, business and cultural institutions in Ghana. Meeting key stakeholders was one of Secretary Mosley’s main goals for the trip, and Cheetham built the Du Bois Centre visit into a programme that also included meetings with civic and community leaders in Accra. Because the campus is under renovation, the bungalow where Du Bois lived was closed to visitors. Instead, Secretary Mosley was escorted on a private tour of the Centre’s photograph exhibit and its document preservation lab. The photograph exhibit traces Du Bois’s life, from his years as a scholar and editor in the United States to his final years in Accra. In the preservation lab, papers, books, and records connected to Du Bois are cared for so they remain available to future students and researchers. President Jerry John Rawlings opened the memorial on June 22, 1985, after Du Bois’s remains were moved there from Christiansburg Castle in Osu. Four decades later, the campus is being renovated, and much of the work of protecting Du Bois’s legacy now takes place in its archives and lab. During the tour, Secretary Mosley also laid a wreath at the tomb of Dr. W.E.B. Du Bois inside the mausoleum. Walter Mosley Meets the W.E.B. Du Bois Museum Foundation. After the tour, Secretary Mosley met with Japhet Aryiku, Executive Director of the W.E.B. Du Bois Museum Foundation, the non-profit leading the redevelopment of the Centre. Formed in 2019, the Foundation works with the Government of Ghana to turn the memorial into a full museum complex with a library, museum, conference centre, art theatre and guest accommodation. Board members have already contributed to restoring Du Bois’s bungalow, and the next phase depends on a wider fundraising campaign. Diaspora Bridge Consulting arranged the meeting to focus on practical ways New York could support the Foundation’s work. Discussions centred on how Secretary Mosley could help connect the Foundation with New York philanthropic foundations that fund history, education and preservation; business leaders and diaspora investors with ties to Ghana; and government and civic networks across New York State with an interest in partnerships in Africa. The New York connection has deep roots. Du Bois built much of his career in New York City, where he helped found the NAACP in 1909 and edited its magazine, The Crisis, for more than 20 years. The Foundation’s partnership agreement with the Government of Ghana was also signed in New York City in 2021.Why It Matters: Du Bois spent his life insisting that the history of African people deserved to be written down, preserved, and taken seriously. The bungalow in Cantonments is where that argument ended for him, and where it continues for everyone who visits. Whether the next chapter includes a world-class museum depends on people deciding to show up: travellers who make the trip, donors who fund it, and officials like Secretary Mosley who are willing to open their networks for it. Visiting the W.E.B. Du Bois Centre: No. 22 First Circular Road, Cantonments, Accra. The campus is currently under renovation, so check which areas are open before you go. Typical hours are Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., and Saturday, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

items.title: Sánchez mide el alcance del malestar social contra la derecha para decidir si convoca ya elecciones
items.description: Estaba escrita y medida, y la frase lo decía todo: “ Hagan lo correcto porque la historia les juzgará antes de lo que creen y con más contundencia de la que se imaginan” . Al escucharla, buena parte del hemiciclo interpretó en ese “antes de lo que creen” que Pedro Sánchez ya tiene totalmente decidido adelantar las elecciones de manera inminente , en la primera fecha posible, el 29 de noviembre. La realidad, según diversas fuentes del entorno del presidente y personas que hablaron con él en la larga jornada en el Congreso, es que Sánchez aún no ha tomado una decisión definitiva, aunque el adelanto electoral inmediato sí está encima de su mesa. Seguir leyendo

items.title: De Ceuta a Sol: a quién favorece y perjudica el cambio de asunto político estrella
items.description: Hasta el miércoles de la semana pasada, no había discusión sobre cuál era el tema político estrella: la inmigración , más aún con Ceuta en carne viva . Y si había un cambio de plano era para darle minutos a la corrupción, la mayoría de las veces por casos que afectan al PSOE . Hasta que, de repente, llega el giro de guion. El desahucio de Maricarmen provoca una manifestación que deriva en una acampada en la Puerta del Sol de Madrid, con réplicas en Barcelona, Sevilla y Málaga, en una movilización que no amaina y que a su vez precipita la aprobación por el Gobierno de dos decretos enviados al Congreso con urgencia. Luego, este viernes, el naufragio de los dos decretos. Y empieza a circular la hipótesis de que Pedro Sánchez podría adelantar las elecciones haciendo campaña con la vivienda por bandera ante el rechazo a las medidas del Gobierno por parte del PP, Vox y Junts . Seguir leyendo

items.title: No más incertidumbre
items.description: Pedro Sánchez sopesa adelantar las elecciones generales, y esta posibilidad electrizó ayer el pleno extraordinario del Congreso en el que la mayoría de derechas formada por PP, Vox y Junts derrotó los dos decretos de medidas urgentes sobre la vivienda. Lo que debía ser un debate sobre las propuestas negociadas por el Gobierno en respuesta al estallido social de la última semana quedó reducido a una confrontación de eslóganes. En una intervención no anunciada, el presidente pronosticó que los partidos que votaron en contra recibirán el castigo de la sociedad “antes de lo que creen y con más contundencia de lo que imaginan”. El líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, respondió fuera del hemiciclo : “Acepto el reto”. Fue un ensayo de campaña electoral, aunque no se haya disuelto el Parlamento ni exista una fecha para la convocatoria a las urnas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Pablo Bustinduy: “Las elecciones, cuando sean, van a ser un referéndum sobre la vivienda”
items.description: Pablo Bustinduy (Madrid, 43 años) atiende a EL PAÍS nada más acabar el pleno del Congreso que ha derogado este viernes los dos decretos sobre vivienda. El ministro de Derechos Sociales, encargado de defender en el hemiciclo el texto que recogía la prórroga automática de los contratos de alquiler, se reconoce cansado, después de un trabajo intenso las últimas semanas. Pero cuando responde, no escatima en palabras y deja clara su indignación por el voto en contra de las derechas. “La posición de Junts es un suicidio político”, sostiene. No se pronuncia sobre si el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, debe convocar elecciones, pero advierte de que los comicios serán “un referéndum sobre la vivienda”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Junts se vuelca en su ideario conservador para protegerse de las críticas por vetar el decreto
items.description: Miriam Nogueras hizo un viaje relámpago de Madrid a Barcelona el miércoles. Estaba invitada a la gala que Pimec, la patronal catalana de la pequeña y mediana empresa, organiza cada año en el Palau Sant Jordi. La cena se celebraba horas después de que el presidente del Gobierno Pedro Sánchez declarara sentirse “razonablemente optimista” de cara a poder validar en el Congreso, este viernes, los dos decretos de vivienda que había diseñado su Consejo de Ministros. En un momento de visible crispación social, con movilizaciones en la calle, el precio del metro cuadrado ardiendo y la crudeza de los desahucios acaparando foco informativo, Nogueras lanzó un puñado de dudas al aire cuando se le preguntó si Junts votaría a favor del nuevo marco normativo: “No tenemos ningún miedo de quemarnos para continuar defendiendo los intereses de las familias catalanas”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Los socios ven el final de la legislatura pero no todos quieren elecciones
items.description: Hay veces, por extraño que parezca, que son los políticos quienes preguntan a los periodistas y no al contrario. Este viernes en el Congreso fue uno de esos días. Se acercaba un informador a algún diputado y este le espetaba: “¿Y tú cómo lo ves?”. Una muestra de la incertidumbre que reinaba por todas las esquinas del palacio de la Carrera de San Jerónimo, antes y después de que se consumase el magnicidio político del Gobierno perpetrado por Junts , a propósito de unos decretos de emergencia para paliar los efectos de la enloquecida escalada de precios de la vivienda. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Mapa | ¿Cuánto ha subido el precio del alquiler en tu calle?
items.description: El alquiler se ha disparado en casi todos los barrios de España en la última década. En el 97% de las secciones censales analizadas, el precio de las rentas se ha encarecido más de un 30% desde 2015 —la inflación en este periodo—, y en dos de cada tres, más del 50%, según una estimación de EL PAÍS a partir de los datos del Ministerio de Vivienda y del portal inmobiliario Idealista. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Yo quiero irme, pero no hay adónde
items.description: Yo me fui dócilmente del centro, hace siete años, porque por 1.000 euros solo alquilaban agujeros y los pisos de 70 metros cuadrados sin reformar costaban más de 300.000. Me vine a Carabanchel Bajo , cerca del hoy deforestado parque de Comillas, allí donde en la posguerra, a trabajos forzados, se levantaron barracones para los perdedores. Vine obligada, y como yo fue viniendo más gente, obligada también, y así expulsamos a otras, que no sabemos dónde se esconden; no las vimos entonces, no las veremos después, cuando lleguemos donde estén ahora y tengan que huir de nuevo, más lejos, más afuera, más nunca. Actualmente, en este barrio que bulle de obra en obra, al que le sobran coches y le faltan servicios públicos y frecuencia de autobuses, donde muchos de los edificios —fruto del desarrollismo— sufren problemas de habitabilidad, humedades y baja eficiencia energética, por 1.000 euros solo alquilan agujeros y los pisos de 70 metros cuadrados sin reformar cuestan más de 300.000. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Construir casas en 12 días? Lo que el problema actual de vivienda puede aprender de lo que ocurrió hace 70 años
items.description: En España faltan viviendas. Esta frase no le pilla de sorpresa a nadie que esté leyéndola, si bien admite unos cuantos asteriscos, porque viviendas hay muchas, unas están vacías, otras están donde nadie quiere vivir, otras son turísticas, otras pertenecen a bancos o fondos o particulares que las usan tres semanas al año, otras están en ciudades donde sí quiere vivir todo el mundo pero cuestan lo que hace 30 años habría parecido una broma de mal gusto. En cualquier caso, y aun contemplando todos esos asteriscos, los datos dicen que entre 2022 y 2025 se concedieron permisos para unas 345.000 viviendas mientras aparecieron unos 604.000 nuevos hogares, y el Banco de España ha calculado un déficit acumulado del orden de 600.000 viviendas en ese mismo periodo de tiempo. Construimos menos de las que necesitamos y, además, construirlas lleva tiempo. Mucho tiempo. Desde que se aprueba un plan urbanístico hasta que la gente recibe la llave de su casa pueden pasar perfectamente entre 15 y 25 años, y eso sin contar todos los servicios que necesita un nuevo desarrollo urbano, y que suele prolongar, durante algunos años más, el estado de erial en el que se encuentra un barrio recién inaugurado. Ya sabes, no vale solo con las casas, también se necesita transporte, canalizaciones, tejido mixto y, en general, todas esas cosas que hacen que queramos –y podamos– vivir en un sitio. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Vincent Cassel: “Hay cosas que son buenas para tu carrera y otras que te gustan: haz siempre lo segundo”
items.description: Hay una generación que no puede separar a Vincent Cassel (París, 59 años) de El odio (1995) y de aquel Vince que se zampaba la pantalla. Aunque han transcurrido más de tres décadas, aquella película de Mathieu Kassovitz exponía ya las costuras de la Francia moderna. Un chaval judío de periferia parisina, inflamado por la frustración, el rencor, el veneno de la exclusión, la sensación de injusticia permanente y las ganas de venganza por la muerte de un amigo a manos de la policía. Vince, pero también Saïd y Hubert, sus amigos del alma, formaban un trío improbable hoy en las banlieues. Un árabe, un negro y un judío unidos por ese premonitorio olor a fractura, exclusión y conflictos de identidad que empezaba a alimentar el odio y avivar el fuego de la extrema derecha. Seguir leyendo Realización: Nono Vázquez. Asistentes de fotografía: Emilio Azevedo y Adrián Wong. Asistentes de realización: Laura Gimenez e Isabel Orozco. Maquillaje y peluquería: Anne Bochon. Dirección de movimiento: Pauline Gudet. Vídeo: Daniele Vaia. Estudio: Paul Le Cacheux Photographer.

items.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones tiene ganas de acción en el Bilbao de ‘Kill Jackie’: “Me buscaron la casa cerca del golf para tenerme feliz”
items.description: El antihéroe central del libro The Price You Pay en el que se basa la serie Kill Jackie no se llamaba ni siquiera Jackie. Era Jack, un hombre. Pero cuando una estrella como Catherine Zeta-Jones se interesa por una adaptación, se hace lo que sea para satisfacer sus necesidades. Incluso participó en el desarrollo del guion como productora ejecutiva. Tan importante acabó siendo la presencia de la actriz, que la intérprete oscarizada por Chicago ha podido utilizar su acento natural galés para diseñar a su protagonista e informar de dónde viene: “Es la primera vez que lo uso en mi carrera. Desde que empecé a trabajar con nueve años, nunca había usado mi voz real, y eso ha hecho que por primera vez estuviera cómoda improvisando o cambiando cosas, porque de normal siempre pienso: ‘tengo que hablar con mi entrenador de habla cómo diría esa frase”, explicaba la actriz en la rueda de prensa celebrada el pasado martes en Bilbao. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Alicia Giménez Bartlett, una rebelde en el corazón del crimen
items.description: Hace 30 años Alicia Giménez Bartlett alumbró un personaje que cambiaría la historia de la ficción criminal en español. Al igual que su creadora, la inspectora Petra Delicado es “peleona, sarcástica, protestona y tocapelotas”; también está dolida y enfadada con el mundo, rota por el dolor de una muerte, la del hombre de su vida. Así nos la presentan en Bajo el cielo infernal (Destino) decimotercera entrega de esta serie policíaca (a la que hay que sumar dos volúmenes de relatos), un libro lleno de rabia y estilo, una obra donde se observan todas las virtudes de una escritora que es mucho más que la creadora de la primera inspectora de policía de la novela negra europea. La entrevista tiene lugar en Vinaroz (Castellón) durante el último fin de semana de agosto. Su casa, el refugio ideado para envejecer junto a su añorado Carlos, ha sido escenario de la tradicional fiesta con la que Giménez Bartlett (Almansa, 75 años) despide el verano. En la piscina, dos labradores espléndidos se dan el primer chapuzón, ajenos a todo. Algunos rezagados parten, no sin antes compartir un último cigarro, una charla, una cerveza. “La amistad para mí es muy importante. Los amigos te entienden o no te entienden, pero hablas con ellos a calzón quitado y sin ningún rol estipulado”, confiesa en los primeros compases de una charla que se prolongará durante dos días, en el despacho donde escribe, en el jardín, por las calles y restaurantes de un pueblo en el que, por encima de una celebridad reconocida, los paisanos la saludan y la aprecian como la amiga de la panadera Mariló o del médico Bismark. Seguir leyendo Bajo el cielo infernal Alicia Giménez Bartlett Destino, 2026 448 páginas. 22,90 euros

items.title: El imparable éxito de las agendas japonesas de Hobonichi: se compran con meses de antelación y mueven millones de euros al año
items.description: El pasado 1 de septiembre no fue un día más para Rita Gallego, fundadora de la papelería Likely, en Madrid . Aquel día comenzaba la venta de uno de los artículos más demandados entre los seguidores de la papelería de diseño: las agendas de Hobonichi, compañía japonesa de referencia en su sector. Esta marca lleva años de continuo crecimiento internacional, pero ha sido en 2026 cuando su expansión ha alcanzado cotas nunca vistas. Según datos de la prensa económica de Japón , los pedidos de estas agendas realizados el pasado mes de agosto por los distribuidores internacionales se incrementaron un 108,2% en comparación con el año previo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Escrito en la cara
items.description: Basta que a uno lo acusen de algo para que se le ponga cara de culpable. Por eso en las fotos de frente y de perfil de las fichas policiales no hay nadie que parezca inocente. Yo quisiera encontrar ciertas fotos mías de hace 52 años que me tomaron en las dependencias de la Dirección General de Seguridad, en Madrid, al día siguiente de la ejecución de Salvador Puig Antich. A las once de la mañana estaba participando en mi primera manifestación antifranquista en la Ciudad Universitaria y antes de la una ya me habían tomado las huellas dactilares y me estaban tomando fotos de frente y de perfil con un flash que empalidecía más aún y aumentaría la cara de susto y de culpa del retratado. Esa es la cara que me gustaría ver de nuevo, y que no se si andará todavía grapada a un expediente en los subsuelos de un archivo de quién sabe dónde. Cómo sería esa cara de 18 años recién cumplidos, de adolescente que se había empezado a dejar la barba y el pelo largo nada más salir de la vigilancia capilar de su padre, de inocente arrojado a la intemperie y la amplitud de un Madrid más habitable en los sueños de provincia que en la torva realidad de las postrimerías franquistas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Fantasmas
items.description: En Buenos Aires hay una zona llamada el Abasto . Toma su nombre del mercado del Abasto, ahora convertido en mall , que funcionó allí durante décadas. A pesar de que el negocio inmobiliario predijo que la presencia del mall iba a transformarlo todo, la zona sigue siendo una versión siglo XXI del lugar que era, un poco sórdido, un poco marginal. A mí me gusta mucho. En la facultad, para la cátedra de Historia del Arte, hice un trabajo acerca de ese edificio que entonces, años noventa, estaba cerrado. Me asomaba a los portones, recorría el vecindario, entrevistaba a la gente. Hasta 2008 viví cerca, en el barrio de Almagro, y fui durante bastante tiempo a tomar clases de teatro en un centro cultural que funcionaba en una escuela pública cercana al mercado, que ya no era mercado y todavía no era mall . Iba y volvía caminando, incluso de noche. Me gustaban y me gustan las calles de adoquines, las veredas en las que hay extraños sauces (un árbol muy campestre, un intruso en la ciudad), el clima un poco provinciano que se vive en ciertos momentos del día. Durante muchos años, cuando regresaba desde el centro hasta mi casa, tomaba el colectivo 26 que pasaba por allí y veía un grafiti que decía: “Los chicos del Abasto no necesitan juguetes. Juegan con las ratas”. Según los datos oficiales conocidos en septiembre , el 44,5 % de los argentinos menores de 14 años se encuentra en situación de pobreza. Según informes recientes de Unicef Argentina, un millón cien mil se encuentra por debajo de la línea de indigencia. El gobierno de la ciudad implementó una campaña bajo el lema Ley y orden , con cartelería en la que se lee “La ciudad sin okupas ”, o “La ciudad sin manteros”, en referencia a los vendedores informales. El grafiti del Abasto desapareció. Supongo que las ratas también. Me pregunto dónde habrán ido los niños. Es posible que la dignidad de las ciudades se mida por la naturaleza de los fantasmas que intenta esconder.

items.title: Sábado pasado por agua: “Nos puede sorprender un chubasco intenso casi en cualquier sitio”
items.description: Agua y más agua y en casi cualquier punto de España. Este sábado prosigue y se expande el fuerte temporal de lluvias, chubascos y tormentas que comenzó el pasado jueves y que aún seguirá al menos hasta el miércoles, con la formación de una dana el domingo que, paradójicamente para el imaginario colectivo que ha aprendido a temerlas, no causará los estragos que tuvo un simple frente el jueves y el viernes . Seguir leyendo

items.title: Dos migrantes marroquíes aseguran que los forzaron a salir de Ceuta: “Nos dijeron que ya se había tomado la decisión de devolvernos”
items.description: Dos migrantes marroquíes de 22 y 25 años que dormían en los asentamientos informales de playa Benítez, en Ceuta, han relatado a EL PAÍS que el pasado martes regresaron a Marruecos porque un traductor de la Policía les dijo que la decisión de devolverles al país vecino “ya se había tomado” y que nadie les ofreció la posibilidad de pedir protección internacional, ni les tomaron información o huellas. “No me preguntaron si quería volver a Marruecos. Me arrojaron en contra de mi voluntad”, mantiene el joven de 25 años. “Nos condujeron hasta entregarnos al Ejército marroquí”, añade el de 22 años. Los migrantes llevaban en la ciudad autónoma desde la entrada masiva del pasado 30 y 31 de julio y creían que les iban a trasladar a un centro de acogida temporal del Gobierno. Sin embargo, aseguran que terminaron en la frontera y horas después metidos en un autobús, con miembros del Ejército marroquí, que los dejaron a cientos de kilómetros de la ciudad autónoma. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Fátima Mansouri: una ‘dama de hierro’ bajo el trono de Mohamed VI
items.description: Preguntada en 2021, al ganar un segundo mandato para la alcaldía de su Marraquech natal y ser nombrada al mismo tiempo ministra de Urbanismo y Vivienda, si se consideraba la “dama de hierro” de la política de Marruecos, Fátima Ezzahra el Mansouri prefirió definirse como una activista que iba “por libre”. Tras recibir el martes la designación del rey como jefa de Gobierno, la líder del Partido de la Autenticidad y la Modernidad (PAM, centroderecha) se ha consolidado a los 50 años como la mujer más poderosa en la historia del país magrebí, que se convierte así en el segundo del mundo árabe en tener a una mujer al frente del Gobierno, después de Túnez. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Kaliningrado, el exclave militarizado ruso encajado en la OTAN que desató la amenaza nuclear de Putin
items.description: Kaliningrado, el exclave militarizado ruso encajado entre Polonia y Lituania, dos países de la OTAN y la UE y un constante foco de tensión entre el Kremlin y la Alianza Atlántica, se ha convertido en el centro de la amenaza nuclear de Vladímir Putin contra los europeos. Esta semana, Moscú ha acusado a la OTAN de querer bloquear Kaliningrado y ha amenazado con utilizar armas nucleares si la organización militar —de la que forma parte España— avanza en ese supuesto propósito. Para el Kremlin, el exclave, que le brinda una estratégica salida al mar Báltico (es el único puerto que puede usar todo el año) y un punto clave en su guerra híbrida contra Europa, es un bastión avanzado. Para la OTAN, supone una pieza que condiciona cualquier crisis en el Báltico porque podría dificultar el movimiento las fuerzas aliadas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: From anger to money and infighting: The comical attack on Standard Group
Mariana Mazzucato, economista: “La vivienda es un derecho humano y la base de todo lo demás”
items.description: La economista Mariana Mazzucato (Roma, 1968) está obsesionada por pisar el terreno, mancharse las manos y ver cómo sus ideas se ponen en práctica y mejoran la vida de las personas. Acaba de regresar de Brasil y de México, después de varias semanas de trabajo con comunidades locales. Recibe a EL PAÍS en su casa londinense de Londres, en el barrio de Camden , con una incomprensible energía en alguien que debería estar aún bajo los efectos del jet lag . Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ana Rujas: “Siento que si no me arriesgo, no funcionará”
items.description: Ana Rujas trae algo denso y reposado a nuestra conversación, una escucha y un modo de hablar propio de quienes han atravesado pasiones y se han entregado a explorarlas en su práctica artística. Reflexionar a través de los años, sin límite o tabú, sobre lo que nos enciende y moviliza, deja una especie de calma. Estos días prepara un papel actoral exigente, donde transforma su cuerpo para contar la vida de la primera boxeadora española en ganar un campeonato del mundo. La serie, de María Cantuel, está producida por Kubik Films. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El comprador de vivienda llega a su límite: cada vez más anuncios bajan sus precios y ha vuelto la negociación
items.description: Los reales decretos ley de vivienda finalmente no han salido adelante en el pleno del Congreso de los Diputados del viernes. Incluían medidas para tratar de aliviar la grave crisis que sufre España, pero no contaban con la aprobación del propio sector inmobiliario, que consideraba que no se atacaba la raíz del problema: “El déficit estructural de vivienda”, señala la Asociación de Promotores y Constructores de España. Nadie en el sector creía que estos decretos fueran a tener un impacto real en los precios del alquiler y, mucho menos, en los de venta. Avisaban de un trasvase de casas del alquiler a la venta, aunque esto tampoco iba a impactar en los precios. “En las principales ciudades la demanda de compra es muy superior a la oferta por lo que esto no iba a afectar a los precios de venta, que ya se están estabilizando por sí solos”, opina José María Alfaro, presidente de la Federación de Asociaciones Inmobiliarias (FAI). Seguir leyendo

items.title: Rot in judiciary deep – Olisa Agbakoba loud on public perception
items.description: By Henry Ojelu, Assistant Judicial Editor In this interview, former Nigerian Bar Association, NBA, President, Dr Olisa Agbakoba, SAN, examines the state of Nigeria’s judiciary, 66 years after independence. He discusses public confidence in the courts, conflicting judgments, judicial appointments, funding, executive influence and the reforms needed to strengthen justice delivery. He also calls for greater autonomy for the NBA and a constitutional approach to the relationship between religion and the state. Read Also: NIGERIA @ 66: Focus On Judiciary – Disgraceful conflicting judgements that taint courts reputation 66 years after independence, how would you assess the Nigerian judiciary, today, particularly when compared with the past? Generally speaking, I am not giving my personal view. I am giving the view of what I see the public saying. It seems to me that the perception of the public is that there is low performance on the part of the judiciary. They judge that from what they see as too much interference and uncertainty in the decisions of the courts, particularly in election petition cases. The public perception is that it is not the place of the judiciary to determine political office holders, such as the President, governors and senators. It is the duty of the people who elect them. But it seems now that the judiciary has taken over that function, and everybody turns to the judiciary to ask, “Who will they elect?” That is not their function. The judiciary should resist the invitation to be lured into becoming an electoral umpire. That is not its function. There are cases I have seen where a judge would take a case and you would ordinarily wonder: “Why is this case here? I am sitting in Jigawa, and this matter concerns a party dispute in Onitsha. Why is it here?” Those are the issues. I think there is a lot that needs to be done to restore public confidence in the judiciary because there are so many fine judges on the bench. There are so many brilliant and distinguished judges serving today. But whether we like it or not, there is a very strong perception by the public that something is wrong. What, in your view, are the major factors responsible for this perception, particularly the conflicting judgments that have become a concern? There are two reasons for that. One is the public perception that judges are no longer following their oath and are influenced by considerations other than judicial considerations. Whether that is so or not, I don’t know. But I have seen evidence of cases that look alike and should be decided alike, yet they receive different decisions. The second problem has to do with competence. To be a judge is not an easy thing. You have to demonstrate competence. In the old days, when my father was around, there were competent people who did not apply for the job. In fact, I know that the first Northern lawyer, Alhaji AbdulRazaq, the father of the current governor of Kwara State, declined to become a judge in 1969. They asked him and he said, “I just can’t afford to be a judge. How much are you going to pay?” That was the quality of the time. It wasn’t a matter of being forced into it. People who wanted to be judges had already made successful careers as lawyers. They didn’t have the temptation to go there to make money. I don’t know if you can speak of that criterion today. Appointment of judges In the appointment of judges, it is very important that we talk about competence. If you do not have criteria for competence, then anybody can become a judge. I have appeared before judges whom I am shocked by how they became judges. If a judge doesn’t understand the rudimentary rules of the law of evidence, how to decide cases or the substantive issues involved, then he will give poor-quality decisions. All these factors have brought into the public mind a very low perception of judges, and that needs to be turned around. How, then, should judges and justices be appointed to ensure competence and integrity? The appointment process should be transparent. I sat on the National Judicial Council, NJC, and we set up criteria for appointment. Unfortunately, those criteria are not being followed. I don’t know whether you are familiar with the objection process in churches when a couple wants to get married. That is the way we should appoint judges. Put it in the newspaper: “The following 10 people have applied to be judges in the Anambra State High Court. Anyone who has any complaint or anything against them, please say so.” Put them through public scrutiny so that anything we have against them will be put on the table. I think that is a very important filter. If the NJC criteria for the appointment of High Court judges, Court of Appeal justices and Supreme Court justices are followed, I think it will go a long way towards dealing with the problem we have. But they are not being followed. That is the problem. Beyond the appointment process, what role should the NJC play in addressing conflicting judgments and other problems affecting the judiciary? The problem with the NJC goes back a long way. The composition of the NJC makes the Chief Justice of Nigeria the almighty power. When I sat on the NJC, nobody could challenge the CJN. Nobody. Because he appoints virtually everybody. The only CJN I can say tried to deal with the structural issues of the NJC was the late Dahiru Musdapher. When he became CJN, he constituted a high-powered 29-man panel to look at all these issues. The main thing we said was that if the NJC structure continued to be what it was, then we cannot have a great judicial policy. Unfortunately, the late Dahiru Musdapher was only six months in office. He was the shortest-serving CJN in Nigerian history. Immediately he retired, all the reforms died. He appointed me to create model rules for the speedy administration of justice, but till today, not one person has remembered what the late Justice Musdapher put in place. The NJC continues to be a body that doesn’t have any staff. It is unbelievable. We are all ex-officio members. The law says there are five NBA members and judges from the six geopolitical zones, and they are all appointed by the CJN. But what about the quality of people who work in the NJC? There is nobody. So, they don’t deal with high judicial policy. There is no thinking about the concept of how to speed up justice. The only CJN I recall who was worried about that was Justice Dahiru Musdapher. Is the lack of a clear response to conflicting judgments also responsible for the public’s concerns about the judiciary? The only issue where speed of justice has relevance is politics. If it is the National Assembly where politicians have an interest, they have created a very fast timeline. Six months and it must be finished. What about commercial cases? What about people on trial for murder who sit on death row for 30 years? When I was a political prisoner in Enugu under Abacha, I met two or three people on death row. One was an 80-year-old man who had been on death row for about 45 years. Nobody cares. The only interest we see in speed is political cases because politicians have an interest. But the NJC ought to have an interest in saying: “If cases don’t go fast, nobody will be interested in going to the courts.” All these rule-of-law things you see are just hype. We need to see a very active NJC. You mentioned conflicting decisions. Has the NJC ever made a statement on it? Has it ever said to judges, “why do you keep giving conflicting decisions?” Nobody can tell what exactly constitutes a pre-election matter. Even me, at 50 years at the Bar, I am not sure that if a client comes to me and asks, “what exactly is a pre-election matter,” that I know. There are too many conflicting decisions. In what cases can the courts determine to remove the chairman of a political party? I don’t know.These very basic issues heat up the polity. You have mentioned the need for speedy justice. What specific changes would you like to see in the way courts operate? The NJC and the constitutionally mandated organ to deal with judicial policy ought to do more about the speed of justice. You have to look at the rules of court and how the courts work. Why are judges still handwriting and taking things down in longhand in today’s technological, digital age? If Mr Justice Jones, who sat in the High Court of Lagos in 1830, were to come back to life today, he would recognise the system and say there has been no change. The entire architecture that underlies the way the legal profession works needs a complete overhaul. Another issue is the relationship between Sharia law and Nigeria’s general legal system. What are the constitutional implications of the continued operation of Sharia alongside the general legal system? The problem is the failure to observe Section 10 of the Constitution. When Sharia law first started in Zamfara, I led a strong team. We lost the case. We argued that the state could not declare that Zamfara was a Sharia state because it conflicted with the doctrine of separation of religion from the state. Nigeria is a secular state. Nigeria is not a secular state for nothing. It does not mean Nigeria ceases to be a religious country. It means that religion is a private matter. It is in the Constitution. But the Constitution is not obeyed. That is the problem. If the Constitution were obeyed, a lot of these conflicts around religion would have been dealt with. That is why I raised the issue that government should not sponsor pilgrimages to Mecca or Jerusalem. There should be nothing like Christian pilgrimage. People criticised me for saying that, but that is what the Constitution says. The problem is that the Constitution is not being obeyed. There is no compliance with the Constitution. How can the judiciary be insulated from executive influence, particularly through funding and infrastructure? It goes back to the NJC. I sat on the NJC and raised this point: the Constitution confers on the NJC a funding structure. But the problem is that the funding structure set out in the Constitution is not being obeyed, and the NJC has not really pushed to have it obeyed. I went to court. I went to three courts and I won all three cases. I raised the issue in the NJC that it has the power to determine its budget. Why doesn’t it take that power? At that time, it was Justice Aloma, the first female CJN. I thought, since nobody would do it, I would do it. I won the cases establishing that the judiciary does not depend on the executive to be funded. Unfortunately, the effort I made and the decisions of the courts have not been implemented. The NJC itself has not helped matters. Neither has the Supreme Court helped matters. There was a case before the Supreme Court on the funding mechanism of the Parliament, the executive and the judiciary. By Section 162(9) of the Constitution, the makers of the Constitution set out parameters for funding. The justices of the Supreme Court said that provision was unconstitutional. That was shocking to me. Judges said that the way they should get money was unconstitutional. My predecessor, Alegeh, after he had been NBA president, went back to the Supreme Court and we again raised the issue that the Supreme Court does not have the power to declare the Constitution unconstitutional. It cannot, unless the National Assembly amends it. The NJC sends an estimate to all branches of the judiciary across Nigeria. They gather together what is called an estimate and it is sent to the National Assembly for appropriation, not to the executive. But what is going on now is that the NJC sends it to the executive, and somebody in the Ministry of Finance may then decide that the judiciary’s budget will be, for example, N100 billion. That is not their job. It is the job of the NJC to determine its budgetary allocation. That is the problem. And that is why Wike is building houses for them and they are gratefully accepting them. Is that his job? It is the job of the judiciary to create a budget where it takes care of itself—its salaries, housing and courts. If a judge has collected a house from the executive, the public perception becomes: “Can this man really do justice in my case?” You have raised concerns about judicial autonomy. What reforms would you prioritise to address these problems? I would focus on the competence of a judge being properly weighed and subjected to public scrutiny. That is the area I would focus on, so that the person who becomes a judge is entitled, not only in law but by public confidence, to be called a judge. Once the quality of a judge goes up, the judge is not interested in who you are. He does his job without fear or favour, then we are good. But if the judge is influenced by what he is going to get or fear of executive condemnation, then we don’t have a judiciary. That is the most important thing: the quality of the individual judge sitting on the bench. You know what it was to be a judge in the old days? A judge was seen as a god. My father was Chief Justice, and you couldn’t just come to our house. Who were you to approach our house? Even the Commissioner of Police in Enugu at that time couldn’t just come and see my father. He would come to the gate and sign the visitors’ book, saying, “My Lord, I am here to ensure that your safety and security are secured,” and he would go away. My father never went to any social function. There was total seclusion. Today, it is strange. So, we need to go back to the period when a judge was found worthy in character and learning to occupy the bench.That would be my priority. Apart from the quality of judges, what other reforms would you like Nigerians to see? Funding. Judges must be free from executive control of their funding. They must be totally free. The constitutional provision that provides the framework for funding the judiciary should be a top priority. I should not need Wike to build me a house, nor should I need the executive to assign a budget for me to build courts. Once the judiciary controls its budget, that is the second important thing. With quality judges and proper funding, I think you will see that judges will not be afraid. The words “without fear or favour” are very heavy words. The reason judges of old could dispense justice without fear or favour was because they were protected. They didn’t have anything to lose, either in terms of their emoluments or whatever. There was a judge in a case in Benin who gave a decision adverse to the interest of the government. He was transferred from Benin to Maiduguri as punishment. Other judges would see what happened to him and become afraid. So, judges must be able to do their work without fear or favour. The Constitution needs to guarantee their tenure of office. Look at how Justice Onnoghen, the CJN of Nigeria, was removed and nothing happened. Yet, the Constitution gives him protection. I was the one who defended him at the NJC trial against the way he was removed. Finally, as a former NBA President, you have also called for greater autonomy for the legal profession. What changes would you like to see in the NBA? I don’t even sit on the body that disciplines lawyers, yet I am their president. It is ridiculous. So, please don’t assume that the NBA is what you think it is. It has a powerful voice, but I think two things should happen. Either the system should free the NBA and allow it to operate like ICAN. ICAN controls its own examination. There is no law school for ICAN; it has its own examination process and nobody controls it. For us, everybody goes to law school. The NBA is too constrained by government bureaucracy and, as a result, it is not anywhere near as influential as people think. That is why, for me, the NBA cannot do much unless to play an advocacy role. But I want the NBA to have the sort of power that its equivalent in London has. If a lawyer misbehaves in the United Kingdom, you complain to the professional body. If it finds that your complaint is justified, it can impose the relevant punishment, including striking the lawyer’s name off the roll. But in Nigeria, by the time you go through the hierarchy and get to the Legal Practitioners Disciplinary Committee and all of that, the whole process is muddled in statutory bureaucracy. We should regulate ourselves. Everything about the law profession should be done by us, not the government.We should determine the curriculum that lawyers require. We should determine the discipline that is required. We should determine the excellence that we will bestow on those found worthy of it. That is when you will have a strong NBA. When there is misconduct, the decision should be taken at the local bar. If a lawyer in Lagos misbehaves, the Nigerian Bar Association, Lagos Branch, should be able to deal with it. Vanguard News The post Rot in judiciary deep – Olisa Agbakoba loud on public perception appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: EU agrees to release diesel stocks after US pressure
items.description: BRUSSELS: European countries agreed to release diesel stocks on Friday after the White House pressured governments to do so, in a bid to cool surging fuel prices linked to the Iran war. “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked diesel oil. The process will begin immediately,” President Donald Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. Trump’s statement followed talks on Friday among EU governments, who discussed a proposal by France for European countries to release 50 million barrels of diesel, and for International Energy Agency members to release 50m barrels of crude oil, according to sources. Under the proposal discussed by European governments, Europe would release part of the diesel volumes in a 20-day period, responding to Trump’s demand for a rapid release of fuel stocks. French President Emmanuel Macron chaired a videoconference with G7 leaders on Friday afternoon to discuss the energy situation, the Elysee Palace said. It was not immediately clear if G7 countries had agreed to France’s proposal on the volumes of fuel to be released. US diesel futures extended their price losses after reports of the stock release discussions, and were down more than four per cent to $4.4491 a gallon. Benchmark European diesel futures fell by over $100 a metric ton. The discussions underscore growing pressure on Europe as Trump considers a potential ban on US diesel exports to help lower domestic fuel prices ahead of Nov 3 midterm elections. In weighing its response, the EU needs to balance the need to ease soaring fuel costs against preserving emergency reserves to safeguard against uncertain supply from Gulf producers due to disruptions caused by the Iran war. French President Macron spoke with Trump overnight, emphasising the need to work together to combat rising fuel prices and ensure the global availability of refined products, the Elysee Palace said. France currently holds the G7 presidency. US pressure on Europe According to sources, the Trump administration had told Germany and France to draw down emergency diesel inventories or face a potential US diesel export ban. The US had demanded that large European countries release 100m barrels of diesel within a 20-day window, the sources said. Global diesel supply has been hit by the Iran war and a Russian ban on exports after Ukraine damaged many of its refineries. Chinese refiners have also suspended fuel exports to bolster domestic stocks. The proposed 50-million-barrel release equates to approximately 17pc of the EU’s total emergency stocks of diesel and gasoil, Eurostat data showed. It reflects around 3pc of the bloc’s annual consumption of the fuel. Europe used to rely on Russian and Middle Eastern diesel imports, but has increasingly relied on imports from the United States in recent years. “Having been caught dragging their feet on promised strategic stock releases earlier this year and now jarred by possible US export restrictions, European countries will likely release more diesel and possibly crude from their stocks,” said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy Group. “European strategic stock releases are a necessary, if not sufficient, condition to prevent US export restrictions, which would still remain on the table given acute political anxiety in the White House about high pump prices.” Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026
