items.title: Vol spécial pour Buenos Aires : Le Burkina Faso affronte l’Argentine au terme d’un périple mouvementé sans leurs piliers habituels
items.description: Malgré des incertitudes logistiques et l'absence de plusieurs piliers de l'équipe, la rencontre amicale internationale entre le Burkina Faso et l'Argentine aura bel et bien lieu dans la nuit du samedi 3 octobre 2026 à Buenos Aires. Après avoir quitté Casablanca ce vendredi soir à bord d'un vol spécial, la sélection nationale dirigée par Amir Abdou aborde ce choc fortement diminuée. Pour combler ces défections de dernière minute, le sélectionneur a fait appel aux jeunes de la sélection A', transformant ce défi majeur en un test grandeur nature pour les talents locaux. Le duel international entre les Étalons du Burkina Faso et l'Argentine se tiendra comme prévu. Les doutes qui entouraient le calendrier de déplacement ont été levés vendredi soir avec le départ effectif de la délégation burkinabè depuis Casablanca à bord d'un vol spécial affrété vers Buenos Aires. Ce vol direct permet à l'équipe nationale de rallier la capitale argentine juste à temps pour disputer la rencontre programmée dans la nuit du samedi 3 octobre 2026. Une sélection handicapée par l'absence des cadres Sur le plan sportif, la préparation de cette affiche prestigieuse s'est apparentée à un véritable casse-tête. Le sélectionneur national, Amir Abdou, doit faire face à un handicap majeur : composer son effectif sans plusieurs cadres habituels de l'équipe, absents du déplacement. L'absence de ces éléments d'expérience constitue un défi supplémentaire au moment d'affronter une nation majeure du football mondial. Face à ces défections, le staff technique a choisi de réagir en faisant appel à la réserve nationale. Plusieurs joueurs issus de la sélection nationale A' ont été appelés en renfort pour compléter le groupe. Pour ces jeunes athlètes, ce déplacement inattendu représente une opportunité en or de faire leurs preuves au plus haut niveau international et de défendre avec fierté le maillot national. Une détermination intacte malgré l'adversité Bien que le défi s'annonce particulièrement difficile face aux Argentins, la volonté du groupe reste inébranlable. Amir Abdou et ses hommes entendent aborder ce rendez-vous avec gravité et sérénité, déterminés à livrer une prestation honorable et à représenter dignement le « Pays des Hommes intègres ». items.title: Boeing 737 MAX software bug ‘not a safety concern’ – Regulators
items.description: A software bug that delayed the US certification of Boeing’s 737 MAX 10 aircraft does not pose a safety concern, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said Friday after an investigation. The glitch was found in a cockpit software update to the plane model and can cause an automated navigation feature to fail when planes shift their approach to landing. “Following a thorough review, a panel of FAA safety experts on Friday determined a software issue in certain Boeing 737 MAX flight computers is not a safety concern,” the US regulatory agency said in a statement. The FAA’s review board reached this conclusion about the software bug’s safety “because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous.” “As with any situation, the FAA will consider appropriate action if it receives new information about this issue.” Boeing will also send a bulletin to airlines detailing the issue and instructing employees how to recognize and respond to the situation should it take place. “We will continue to follow the lead of the FAA as our engineers work on the next software update,” Boeing said in a statement to AFP. The aerospace giant on Monday said it had “informed all 737 operators about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario.” Boeing on Friday added that it was working to formalize a procedure with airlines that would allow pilots to restore automated flight guidance in case the glitch occurs. Despite the FAA review, neither the regulator nor Boeing said whether the certification process for the 737 MAX 10 would be unfrozen. The model is the last of four 737 MAX planes to receive regulator certification to enter service. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Monday at a press conference that the MAX planes certified by the FAA thus far are safe but that “we will be delaying the 10 until… we’re satisfied we don’t have an issue here.” Vanguard News The post Boeing 737 MAX software bug ‘not a safety concern’ – Regulators appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Bourse de Casablanca : une semaine dans le rouge
items.description: La Bourse de Casablanca a clôturé la semaine du 28 septembre au 2 octobre dans le rouge, son indice principal, le MASI, reculant de 2,89% à 17.303,69 points (pts). Le MASI.20, qui reflète la performance des cours des 20 entreprises les plus liquides, a perdu 2,99% à 1.249,35 pts et le MASI ESG, indice des entreprises ayant la meilleure notation ESG selon Moody’s ESG Solutions, a lâché 3,07% à 1.280,56 pts. Le MASI Mid and Small Cap, qui mesure la performance des petites et moyennes entreprises cotées à la Bourse de Casablanca, a diminué de 3,27% à 1.679,86 pts. Sur le plan sectoriel, les indices « Ingénieries et biens d'équipement industriels » (-7,69%), « Matériels, logiciels et services informatiques » (-7,01%) et « Loisirs et hôtels » (-5,94%) ont accusé les plus fortes baisses. Les secteurs « Industrie pharmaceutique » (+2,73%) et « Sociétés de placement immobilier » (+1,26%) ont réalisé les uniques performances positives. Les échanges ont dépassé 1,6 milliard de dirhams (MMDH), réalisés essentiellement sur le marché central « Actions » et dominés par les transactions sur Attijariwafa bank (21,7%), Sodep-Marsa Maroc (15,66%) et SGTM (13,73%). La capitalisation boursière s'est établie à plus de 1.019 MMDH. Aux valeurs individuelles, les plus forts replis ont été enregistrés par Stokvis Nord Afrique (-27,84% à 46,18 DH), Fenie Brossette (-12,36% à 319,9 DH), HPS (-10,66% à 570 DH), Zellidja (-9,96% à 250,3 DH) et Stroc Industrie (-9,32% à 159 DH). À l'inverse, les plus fortes hausses ont été affichées par BMCI (+4,18% à 573 DH), Cartier Saada (+4,1% à 18,8 DH), Maghreb Oxygène (+3,68% à 392,95 DH), Aluminium du Maroc (+3,19% à 1.909 DH) et Sothema (+2,94% à 350 DH). The post Bourse de Casablanca : une semaine dans le rouge appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Capital blockade chokes Karachi Port operations
items.description: KARACHI: Pakistan’s effort to keep supporters of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan out of the capital has led to a pileup of shipping containers in the nation’s main port of Karachi, 1,400 kilometres away. Truckers are refusing to drive north, for fear their vehicles will be seized and the containers used to barricade Islamabad ahead of an Oct 4 march on the city planned by Imran’s Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) opposition party. “Right now, going toward Punjab is like committing suicide,” said driver Javid ur Rehman, 35, who has halted such journeys, referring to Pakistan’s most populous province. “The police seize the vehicles and snatch the containers, and then we are left distressed.” Containers pile up as truckers halt northbound trips ahead of PTI march Steel shipping containers, packed with sand and welded together, have lined the roads into Islamabad for weeks, in preparation against a march, postponed from Sept 27, to demand Khan’s release from prison. The former prime minister was jailed in 2023 after being ousted by parliament. All convictions but one have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. His party remains under state scrutiny that has suppressed participation in recent protests, however, “This is not the way to stop protests,” said Rana Mohammad Aslam, president of the Karachi Goods Carrier Association. Authorities began stopping vehicles around Sept 5, weeks before the original march date, he said. Pakistan’s home, information, commerce and finance ministries did not respond to requests for comment. Punjab police and the provincial home department also did not respond. The containers are positioned ready for placement at key entry points into Islamabad, a capital region larger than the southeast Asian city state of Singapore. Transporters battling rising prices say they cannot afford to have trucks seized. Police requisitioned more than 2,000 vehicles in September ahead of the march, they added, many still loaded with cargo and held for days with little or no compensation. Their reluctance is leaving containers piling up at Pakistan’s main trade gateway, Karachi. The disruption was affecting routes to Islamabad, the military city of Rawalpindi, and the cities of Jhelum, Peshawar and Attock, Aslam said. Some operators had halted journeys beyond Gujranwala in Punjab, while others took alternative routes. Transporters mounting bills The bills are mounting for those whose containers have been seized, as daily demurrage charges on one such container alone can run into Rs30,000 to Rs40,000 ($110 to $150), Aslam said, adding to losses from missed deliveries and idle trucks. Consumer prices rose 10.26pc in September from a year earlier, while the transport price index climbed 27.43pc, the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics said on Thursday. Operators are struggling to pay drivers and maintain their fleets, as international shippers still expect payment regardless of the reason for the delay, Aslam said. He said he was holding talks to find a solution, but transporters could stage their own protest if complaints go unanswered. For Pervaiz Khan, 50, the risk was enough to keep a load of chemicals parked in Karachi. “Right now, my vehicle is loaded, but I am not going,” said the father of five, adding that he had loaded his cargo of chemicals by night. “We depart from Sindh, and the moment we enter Punjab, that’s when our troubles begin.” Drivers stranded near Islamabad regretted lost days of work or earnings. “If the roads open, our children’s livelihoods will open up,” said Sagheer Ahmed, 51, who added that his children, awaiting him at home, relied on his earnings. “If not, we will just keep standing.” Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

items.title: Govts should be allowed to complete their terms: CM Maryam
items.description: LAHORE: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz has said governments that perform well should be allowed to complete their five-year terms, arguing that the lack of policy continuity in Pakistan remains a major hurdle to development. She was addressing a delegation of the National Command Authority Senior Officers Leadership Course on Thursday, according to an official handout. Speaking on the occasion, she said Pakistan’s “excellent image and new face” had emerged before the world during the recent conflict with India, adding that the army and other security institutions were rendering invaluable services for the country’s defence. The chief minister said good governance and performance were essential to tackling internal security threats. “We are Pakistanis first, regardless of whether we belong to Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan or Gilgit,” she said, stressing the need for continuity in national policies. Credits PML-N’s extended rule over Punjab for ensuring policy continuity, leading to better governance; Azma says policies should not be sacrificed to ‘political changes’ Building on her argument for political continuity, CM Maryam said governance standards had improved because the PML-N had remained in government in the province for longer periods. She also claimed that terrorism had been brought under control in Punjab, but acknowledged that the threat had not disappeared, adding that the provincial government remained prepared for any possible attacks. The chief minister said the province previously had around 70 areas regarded as “no-go areas”, but claimed that there was no such area now. “I am responsible for the safety of 140 million people, so I had to take decisions that had not been taken before,” she said. Referring to criticism of her government, CM Maryam said there were occasions when she had to choose between “protecting myself or protecting the people”, adding that she had always prioritised the public. The chief minister said she had no personal grievances against anyone, and did not seek credit for herself. “I ensure 100 per cent merit in Punjab, and neither accept recommendations nor do people now approach me with recommendations,” she said. Listing her administration’s ‘achievements’, she said the government had strengthened security infrastructure, particularly in border areas, by establishing fortified posts and providing weapons and night-vision cameras. She also highlighted round-the-clock surveillance to detect terrorist activity. The chief minister said the Punjab government had established separate groups for administration and law and order and that special attention was being given to crimes against women and children. She said the government had dismissed around 1,000 police and revenue officials as part of measures against corruption and claimed that sustained action had created a fear of the law among officials demanding or accepting bribes. The chief minister said the government had established virtual police stations for women unable to visit police stations, particularly victims of domestic violence, claiming that hundreds of thousands of cases had been dealt with through the system. In a subsequent statement, Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari also stressed the importance of policy continuity, saying that CM Maryam’s “clear stance is that governments may change, but the national vision and policies aimed at public welfare should not change”. She insisted that the country’s development was not the responsibility of any single province, government or political party; rather, it is a shared responsibility of all. “Policies formulated for the country’s development and public welfare should not be sacrificed to political changes.” Ms Bokhari said that if a policy introduced today is abandoned or changed tomorrow merely because of a political change, the country cannot move forward. “Pakistan needs a consistent national vision and continuity of policies instead of short-term political agendas,” she noted. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

items.title: PTI to begin march from south KP tomorrow
items.description: PESHAWAR: PTI Khyber Pakh­tun­khwa Secretary Information Shaukat Yousafzai said on Friday that the party’s protest march would start from the southern districts and be led by Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. “The march on October 4 will take place at any cost,” he said in a statement issued here. He said the procession from the southern districts would be led by the chief minister, while the procession from Malakand Division would be led by PTI provincial president and MNA Junaid Akbar Khan. He said processions from the southern districts, Peshawar, Malakand and Hazara would converge in Swabi, adding that preparations for the march had been completed and a shortage of resources would not be a hindrance. Shaukat Yousafzai says CM Afridi will lead procession Mr Yousafzai said the success of the government-opposition negotiations would depend on the government’s attitude. He said the PTI had been demanding access to incarcerated party founder Imran Khan, his transfer to a hospital and early hearings of his cases. He described PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan as a mature and conciliatory person who would find a way forward. “So far, I can call the government-opposition negotiations encouraging,” he said. He said both sides had presented their respective positions during Friday’s negotiations, adding, “Let’s see what happens next.” He further said the final destination of the protest march was Islamabad. “Governor’s rule is not the solution to the problems; it will make the situation even more serious,” he said. He said suggestions for imposing governor’s rule or an emergency were being made by non-political people in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. If the government wanted to improve the situation, he added, it should immediately allow a meeting with Imran Khan. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

items.title: Some institutions have become hurdles to performance: Naqvi
items.description: LAHORE: The country’s system is in need of a reset, as some departments and institutions have become hurdles to ‘performance’, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Friday. The security czar, who had whipped up a political storm when he called for the formation of new administrative units in the country a few months ago, urged the business community to support the government’s efforts in this regard. Mr Naqvi made the remarks while speaking to businessmen in Lahore – reminiscent of his original tirade at the Pakistan Economic Summit in July. “As far as federal institutions are concerned, we do receive your complaints from time to time. It seems that some departments and institutions have become hurdles in the way of our performance. So whenever possible, we try our best to correct the things,” the minister said. Revives earlier call for ‘system reset’, seeks support from business community “I will not speak more on this and I don’t want to go into detail, as there are many things and we achieved many of them. But at this time, this country’s system needs to be reset, and we cannot do that until we have your support,” he reiterated. He hoped that whenever the system is reset, things will much improve. The interior minister, who has recently made several whirlwind trips to Iran as part of the country’s efforts to find a diplomatic solution to the ongoing hostilities between Iran and the US, also spoke at length about the neighbouring country’s progress despite decades of sanctions. In his words, those who hadn’t been to Iran thought of it as a war-torn country, with destruction everywhere. “The people who visited Iran with me returned astonished after seeing the scale of development in a country that has been suffering under sanctions for many years,” he said. “You name anything – their auto industry is manufacturing everything locally. I agree that export-led growth is necessary for this the country’s [economic uplift], but at the same time, we need to reduce our imports through local manufacturing,” he said, requesting the business community to come up with proposals related to both exports and imports. He stressed the need to learn from Iran’s economic development. “If they can do this despite sanctions for 30-40 years, we can do much more than them. And it is easy for us,” he maintained. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

items.title: Exposition gouvernementale : Le Camarade ministre d’État en charge de la guerre ouvre le « Dialogue avec le Peuple » sur les enjeux de défense et de sécurité
items.description: ‎Le Camarade ministre d’État, ministre de la Guerre et de la Défense patriotique, le Général de division Célestin Simporé, a animé la première séance du « Dialogue avec le Peuple », dans l’après-midi du vendredi 2 octobre 2026, au Pavillon du Soleil Levant du SIAO. Cette activité de l’exposition gouvernementale a permis aux citoyens d’interroger directement le ministre d’État sur leurs préoccupations en matière de défense et de sécurité. ‎ ‎Organisée dans le cadre de la deuxième phase de la troisième édition des Journées nationales d’engagement patriotique et de participation citoyenne (JEPPC), cette séance avait pour thème « Gouvernance et sécurité nationale : le peuple debout ». Elle s’inscrit dans la volonté de rapprocher l’action gouvernementale des populations, en associant la présentation des réalisations et des réformes aux échanges directs avec les citoyens. L’exposition gouvernementale se tient du 2 au 9 octobre 2026. ‎ ‎Dans sa déclaration liminaire, le ministre d’État a présenté les grandes orientations de son département, notamment le renforcement des capacités nationales de défense, la mobilisation des Volontaires pour la défense de la Patrie (VDP) et les actions de sécurisation du territoire. ‎ ‎Les échanges ont ensuite porté sur des préoccupations concrètes : l’accessibilité de certaines localités, la sécurité aux frontières, le recrutement des réservistes, la lutte contre le grand banditisme et les possibilités de formation militaire. ‎ ‎Un participant de la commune de Bourzanga a évoqué les difficultés d’accès à certaines zones et demandé un accompagnement pour les populations confrontées aux difficultés de la saison agricole. En réponse, le ministre d’État a indiqué que des travaux sont en cours. Il a également annoncé qu’il échangerait avec le ministère concerné pour examiner les possibilités d’assistance. ‎ ‎Des participants du Sud-Ouest et de Mangodara ont sollicité un renforcement de la sécurisation de la frontière avec la Côte d’Ivoire ainsi qu’une augmentation du nombre de VDP. Le ministre d’État a assuré suivre les évolutions de la situation aux frontières. Tout en soulignant la complexité de cette question, il a appelé les Burkinabè à contribuer à la sécurisation du territoire national. ‎ ‎Concernant le recrutement des 100 000 réservistes, il a précisé que les capacités d’enregistrement seraient progressivement renforcées grâce à la nouvelle plateforme et au déploiement de dispositifs dans les régions. ‎ ‎Interpellé sur le grand banditisme, le ministre d’État a indiqué que des stratégies sont en cours pour combattre cette forme de criminalité. Il a également invité les habitants d’une même localité à mettre fin aux querelles internes. ‎ ‎La formation militaire a constitué un autre sujet des échanges. Un élève du Prytanée militaire de Kadiogo a exprimé ses préoccupations concernant l’ouverture des bourses au grand public, estimant qu’elle pourrait réduire les possibilités offertes aux élèves de l’établissement. Le ministre d’État a expliqué que cette mesure répond à la volonté de donner une chance au plus grand nombre de Burkinabè désireux d’intégrer les forces armées. ‎ ‎S’agissant des formations à l’étranger, il a défendu le renforcement des capacités nationales de formation. « L’Afrique ne doit plus envoyer ses meilleurs à l’extérieur, car l’Afrique a besoin de ses meilleurs pour développer le continent », a-t-il déclaré. Il a insisté sur la nécessité de former les cadres en tenant compte des réalités nationales, afin qu’ils puissent mieux servir la Nation. ‎ ‎À la jeunesse, le ministre d’État a adressé ce message : « Tout ce qui se fait aujourd’hui, c’est pour vous ». ‎ ‎Cette première séance du « Dialogue avec le Peuple » a ainsi donné aux citoyens l’occasion de faire entendre leurs préoccupations et d’obtenir des éclairages sur les orientations du Gouvernement en matière de défense, de sécurité et de formation militaire. ‎ ‎DCRP/Primatur L’article Exposition gouvernementale : Le Camarade ministre d'État en charge de la guerre ouvre le « Dialogue avec le Peuple » sur les enjeux de défense et de sécurité est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Coopération Burkina Faso – Banque mondiale : Le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ et Ousmane DIAGANA scellent un partenariat stratégique « aligné »
items.description: Ce vendredi 2 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou, le Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ, a reçu en audience une délégation du Groupe de la Banque mondiale conduite par son Vice-président pour l’Afrique de l’Ouest et du Centre, Ousmane DIAGANA. Selon les informations diffusées par la Direction de la communication de la Présidence du Faso, cette rencontre a permis d'officialiser les grands axes d'un nouveau cadre de partenariat stratégique, axé sur la création d’emplois et le soutien à des programmes véritablement transformateurs pour le pays. Ce vendredi 2 octobre 2026, la Présidence du Faso a été le théâtre d'échanges de haut niveau entre le Chef de l'État, le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ, et une délégation de la Banque mondiale emmenée par son Vice-président pour l’Afrique de l’Ouest et du Centre, M. Ousmane DIAGANA. L'audience a été consacrée à la présentation des grandes orientations du nouveau cadre de partenariat stratégique liant le Burkina Faso au Groupe de la Banque mondiale. Approuvé il y a à peine trois mois par le Conseil d'administration de l'institution financière, ce texte vise à structurer une coopération vaste et diversifiée couvrant plusieurs secteurs clés. À cette occasion, M. DIAGANA a également présenté la nouvelle équipe technique de la Banque mondiale chargée du suivi opérationnel des programmes dans le pays. Au sortir de l'audience, le chef de la délégation a précisé les ambitions centrales de cet engagement renouvelé. L'objectif principal de ce cadre stratégique est d'accompagner le Burkina Faso à convertir la résilience extraordinaire démontrée par le pays ces dernières années en opportunités réelles de développement socio-économique. Cette dynamique doit se traduire de manière concrète sur le terrain, notamment à travers un soutien direct à la création d’emplois pour les populations locales. Au cours des discussions, le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ a exprimé avec clarté sa vision ainsi que les priorités stratégiques du gouvernement burkinabè. Tout en partageant ses appréciations sur les interventions déjà déployées sur le terrain, le Chef de l'État a insisté sur la nécessité pour la Banque mondiale d'appuyer le pays par le biais de programmes réellement transformateurs. Face à ces exigences, M. Ousmane DIAGANA s'est réjoui de constater un « alignement total » entre les propositions formulées par l'institution financière et les orientations politiques fixées par le Présidence du Faso. L’article Coopération Burkina Faso – Banque mondiale : Le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ et Ousmane DIAGANA scellent un partenariat stratégique « aligné » est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

Doctors cannot run drug stores without licence: FCC
items.description: • Observes Pharmacy Act and Drugs Act perform different legal functions • Sets aside 2023 PHC order restraining regulatory action ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) on Friday ruled that a registered medical practitioner (doctor) may prescribe and dispense medicine to his own patient within the scope of Section 31(4)(a) of the Pharmacy Act 1967, but cannot maintain a medical store or retail drug outlet without a licence under the Drugs Act 1976. The FCC issued the ruling while setting aside a June 5, 2023 order of the Peshawar High Court’s D.I. Khan bench, which had restrained regulatory action against registered medical practitioners allegedly running medical stores and dispensaries. The FCC ruled that registration as a doctor does not exempt them from the licensing requirements of the Drugs Act. A two-judge FCC bench, headed by FCC Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan and comprising Justice Ali Baqar Najafi, issued the verdict while taking up an appeal moved by the secretary of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa health department. The controversy arose when respondents, including Dr Muhammad Rizwan Rajpoot, who were registered medical practitioners, were found maintaining dispensaries/medical stores within their respective clinical establishments and allegedly stocking and vending pharmaceutical drugs without possessing the requisite drug sale licences. This culminated in an inspection conducted on Jan 21, 2020, during which the drugs were taken into custody through Form-6 and consequential show-cause notices were issued. The respondents invoked the constitutional jurisdiction of the PHC, challenging the legality of the regulatory action. Their writ petition was allowed by the high court through its impugned judgement of June 5, 2023. While setting aside the PHC order, Chief Justice Aminuddin observed that registration with the medical regulatory body and registration under the Pharmacy Act perform different juridical functions. Holding them otherwise would amount to judicially engrafting upon the licensing regime, an exemption which the rule-making authority itself had not enacted, said the nine-page judgement authored by the FCC chief justice. During the hearing, the FCC framed three core questions: whether the drug inspector had lawful authority to inspect and take action under the Drugs Act; whether registration as medical practitioners, coupled with Section 31(4)(a) of the Pharmacy Act 1967, gave them an unfettered right to stock and sell drugs without a licence; and whether the high court was justified in intervening at the show-cause stage. On the first question, the court held that Sections 17 and 18 of the Drugs Act empower inspectors to inspect premises, take samples, and search and seize drugs. Section 19 prescribes the procedure, including issuance of a receipt in Form-6. The FCC noted that no case had been established that the inspector concerned lacked appointment, territorial competence or authorisation. Drawing a distinction between the Pharmacy Act and the Drugs Act, the judgement observed that Section 31(4)(a) of the Pharmacy Act merely creates an exception allowing a registered medical practitioner to dispense medicine to his own patients or serve his own prescriptions. It does not authorise him to establish or maintain a medical store or retail drug outlet without a licence under the Drugs Act. “The legal effect of an exception cannot be enlarged beyond the prohibition from which it operates,” the judgement explained, adding that Section 23(1)(c) of the Drugs Act clearly provides that no person shall sell any drug except under a licence, and the expression “no person” admits of no occupational exception for registered doctors. The FCC emphasised that the Pharmacy Act was primarily concerned with regulation of the profession and practice of pharmacy, constitution of pharmacy councils and registration of pharmacists. Section 31(1) prohibits practice as a pharmacist by an unregistered person. Subsection (4)(a), upon which the respondents rested their entire claim, merely carves out an exception from that prohibition in favour of a registered medical practitioner who dispenses medicine to his own patients or serves his own prescriptions. Whereas the objective of the Drugs Act was to regulate the import, export, manufacture, storage, distribution and sale of drugs, Section 23(1)(c) employs language of unmistakable amplitude by providing that no person shall sell any drug except under, and in accordance with, the conditions of a licence issued under the Act. The expression “no person” admits of no occupational exception merely on account of the seller being a registered medical practitioner. The judgement pointed to the specialised mechanism under the Drugs Act, including the Provincial Quality Control Board and the Drug Court, which should examine technical and factual questions before judicial review. It clarified that Section 11 of the Drugs Act is not a conventional appellate remedy but part of the statutory machinery. The FCC also disapproved the argument that Article 18 of the Constitution protects the respondents from licensing requirements, stating that the right to enter a profession or trade was expressly subject to qualifications prescribed by law, and regulation through a licensing system was constitutionally permissible, especially for pharmaceuticals linked to public health. “Constitutional jurisdiction is essentially corrective and supervisory; it is not ordinarily a substitute for a fact-finding forum specially constituted under statute,” it observed. The FCC regretted that constitutional jurisdiction in the present case was exercised prematurely and upon an erroneous construction of the governing enactments. “The petition, therefore, merits conversion into an appeal and acceptance, with the result that the impugned judgement is liable to be set aside and the parties relegated to the statutory process for determination of the show-cause proceedings in accordance with law,” the court ruled. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

items.title: ‘God has given us another chance’ – Nigerian returnees narrate South Africa ordeal
items.description: By Esther Onyegbula For Eze Pauline Ijeoma, stepping onto Nigerian soil was more than a homecoming. It was a return to a place where she hoped she could finally live and work without fear. After years in South Africa, where she said xenophobic attacks, police detentions and difficulties running her food business had made life increasingly difficult, Ijeoma was among 105 Nigerians who returned to the country in the second batch sponsored by the Redeemed Christian Church of God, RCCG. “I would say that we are so grateful and we are so happy to be home because there is no place like home,” the Imo State indigene said. “No more xenophobic, no more attack, no more police, no more problems. No more killings. So, we are so happy.” Ijeoma’s relief, however, came against the backdrop of painful experiences she said she endured during her stay in South Africa. ‘I left in 2013’ “I left Nigeria in 2013, went home and came back again in 2023. It wasn’t like that before. But silently, they always do it. This period, it was so hard,” she said. According to her, the situation affected her ability to earn a living as a food seller, as she became apprehensive about going out to conduct her business. “I don’t go to business because every time you go to business, you come back with your food. I’m a food seller,” she said. “So, it is very horrible for now. I don’t sell because anytime you go out, police will arrest you. And you sell it inside the cell.” She also recounted the emotional burden of witnessing Nigerians lose their lives and the difficulties she said she faced during encounters with the police. “Because seeing our brothers dying every time. Every time, police will arrest you for doing nothing. Even going to business is a problem,” she said. Ijeoma, who disclosed that her husband died in South Africa, said she took to food vending as a means of survival but alleged that police harassment made it increasingly difficult to operate. “My husband passed away in South Africa. It was not easy, that’s why I started selling food,” she said. “Every time police will detain, asking for your papers or whatever. Even if your papers are complete, they will still fine you, fine one thing or the other to ask you, in order to extort money from you.” For her, the return to Nigeria has therefore brought a renewed sense of hope. “We are so happy that we are alive to come back. We are so grateful to God and the people who made it possible for us to be among the people,” she said. ‘Rescue’ Another returnee, Chukwuma Augustine Ayoka, also from Imo State, described the return as a rescue after what he said was a difficult period for Nigerians in South Africa. “I’m so excited. I give all glory to God for them to come to our rescue,” Ayoka said. He expressed appreciation to RCCG for sponsoring the return of Nigerians, including families, children and individuals. “Lifting 500 people, including fathers, mothers, children and single ones from South Africa under xenophobic attack, afrophobic attack, it’s not easy. So it’s only by the grace of God,” he said. According to Ayoka, the situation had affected businesses and the ability of some Nigerians to move freely. “Although it was not a war zone, but with the case of xenophobia attack, afrophobic attack, with the killings, we have no other choice than to come back,” he said. “They close our businesses, destroy our businesses, loot our businesses. Life became terrible. You can’t even get out of your house. So we have no other choice than to seek for rescue.” RCCG Ayoka, who said he returned alone, added: “Redeem came to our rescue and at the end of the day, we are here through the grace of God and through the help of RCCG.” The Chairman, RCCG Task Force for the Reception of Nigerian Returnees from South Africa, Pastor Belemina Obunge, said the church’s intervention followed a “Save Our Soul” appeal from Nigerians in South Africa. Obunge said the intervention was approved by the church’s General Overseer, Pastor E.A. Adeboye, after the plight of Nigerians stranded in South Africa came to the attention of the church. He said the initiative was designed as a humanitarian contribution to the efforts of the Federal Government to bring Nigerians in distress back home. “Basically, there was a Save Our Soul clarion cry by Nigerians in South Africa. It was echoed by the High Commission in South Africa. It got to the ears of our Heavenly Lord, the General Overseer, and he, being who he is with a heart of compassion, had determined that the church should intervene,” Obunge said. He explained that the church resolved to sponsor the airlifting of 500 Nigerians from South Africa. “By the grace of God, the first set of 100 had been brought in. This second set of 105 is now being brought in,” he said. According to him, three more batches are expected to arrive as the process continues. Obunge said the returnees should see their arrival in Nigeria as a new beginning rather than the end of their journey. “What we are telling them, they are not forgotten. They should realise that this is a new beginning. God has a plan for them. They should connect with God,” he said. He also encouraged the returnees to deploy the skills and experience they acquired abroad in rebuilding their lives in Nigeria. “Once they begin to take advantage of the skills, the talents, and what they’ve learned over the years and put it in practice here in Nigeria, one thing is clear, the best is yet to come,” he said. Obunge stressed that the humanitarian intervention was not restricted to members of RCCG. He said the returnees were selected regardless of their religious or ethnic backgrounds. “Our national anthem says, ‘no tribe and tongue may differ. In brotherhood we stand.’ We believe in that anthem,” he said. “Those being brought are of different tribes, different tongues, different religions. Definitely, they are not all members of the Redeemed Christian Church of God. In fact, we don’t even know if any of them is a member of the Redeemed Christian Church of God. “They are wonderful, glorious, spectacular Nigerians, and by the grace of God, they are part of those that we have an assignment towards.” The returnees Obunge said the latest batch comprised 55 adults, 45 children and five infants, bringing the number already brought back under the RCCG initiative to 205. He said the church expected to receive about 295 to 300 more Nigerians, subject to the completion of the required processes by the Nigerian High Commission and South African authorities. According to him, the returnees are profiled by the Nigerian High Commission before the relevant South African authorities complete their procedures for their return. A representative of the Head of Operations, National Emergency Management Agency, Lagos Operations Office, said NEMA and other government stakeholders had been involved in receiving Nigerians returning from South Africa. The official described the RCCG intervention as a complement to the Federal Government’s efforts. “This is the second batch of returnees being sponsored by the Redeemed Christian Church of God,” the official said. “As you are aware, NEMA and other stakeholders have been in the forefront representing the Federal Government, receiving Nigerian returnees from South Africa. And the RCCG has come to also complement the effort of the Federal Government.” The official explained that the returnees’ details were being documented to facilitate possible government assistance and follow-up. “If you observe from the arrival from South Africa, part of this process is to have their details, by registering them, getting their names and contacts and their other details. And this is for further assistance going to the extended later,” the official said. The official added that the information would help the government contact the returnees when necessary and provide further assistance. NEMA, according to the official, would also facilitate the transportation of the returnees to their respective states to enable them reunite with their families. For Ijeoma, the journey home represents an opportunity to begin again after years of uncertainty. “My expectation, by the grace of God, is that God will help us the way He has been with us, protecting us. If we can survive there, in our own homes, we will make more, by the special grace of God,” she said. Vanguard News The post ‘God has given us another chance’ – Nigerian returnees narrate South Africa ordeal appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 66 Years After Independence: How to make Nigeria great again – Prof Falode
items.description: By Clifford Ndujihe, Politics Editor Nigeria’s political, economic and security crises are not isolated problems but manifestations of a deeper structural malfunction in the way the country organises democracy, federalism and education, Professor Adewunmi Falode has said. Falode, Professor of International Relations and Strategic Studies and Director of the Centre for Peace and Strategic Studies, CPSS, at the Lagos State University, LASU, Ojo, said Nigeria could overcome its seemingly intractable challenges if it stopped importing political models wholesale and began designing institutions around its own history, realities and peculiarities. Delivering LASU’s 115th Inaugural Lecture, titled “Bespoke Solutions: Reimagining, Reifying and Realigning the Wheels of the Nigerian State,” recently, he identified democracy, federalism and education as the three major “wheels” that must be realigned to put Nigeria firmly on the path of stability, development, peace and national integration. Of his prescriptions included a single, non-renewable seven-year tenure for elected public office holders, a decentralised centre with stronger and fiscally empowered states, and free and compulsory primary and secondary education. Falode also called for the domestication of Nigeria’s democratic and federal systems, arguing that the country had for decades operated institutions that were not sufficiently adapted to its social, historical and economic circumstances. His central argument was that Nigeria’s problem was not a lack of resources or ideas but the failure to align the country’s political and socioeconomic institutions with its realities. He said: “Nigeria’s democracy is alien, expensive and exclusionary. It has failed to deliver its dividends in the First, Second, Third and Fourth Republics.” Costly four-year democratic cycle Falode picked holes in Nigeria’s four-year, two-term presidential and governorship system, which he said encourages permanent electioneering, litigation and political manoeuvring at the expense of governance. Under his proposed arrangement, elected public officials would serve one non-renewable seven-year term. He argued that the existing system leaves little time for effective governance because politicians spend substantial periods dealing with election petitions, positioning for another election and managing political battles. How? “The presumed winner uses two out of four years fending off petitions, five months to govern, and the remaining one and a half years preparing for reelection,” he said, adding that Nigeria’s democracy has become an expensive cycle in which enormous public and private resources are expended during elections, while the aftermath is frequently followed by litigation, political tension and, in some cases, violence. Rising cost of polls Falode cited the escalating cost of elections as evidence of the problem. He recalled that the 1983 federal elections cost about N2 billion, while Nigeria budgeted N1.5 billion for the 1999 elections, N42 billion in 2011, N108.8 billion in 2015 and about N242.2 billion for the 2023 elections, with post-election litigation and other associated expenses not fully captured in the figures. He lamented that despite the huge resources committed to elections, the process often ended with disputes that required judicial intervention. “The shocking thing was that at the end of such elections, where humongous money had been expended, with countless lives lost and businesses destroyed, it would still take the intervention of the judiciary for the wheel of democracy to be realigned and readjusted,” he said. Why seven years? Falode’s seven-year proposal is designed to create a longer period of uninterrupted governance while removing the incentive for incumbents to divert public attention and resources towards securing a second term. He argued that the proposed arrangement could provide about four years of stable governance, with the remaining period accommodating electoral preparations and litigation. He cited countries that operate variations of single-term arrangements and urged Nigeria to study such models rather than assume that the American system it adopted is necessarily suitable for Nigeria. “Nigeria will have to tweak its constitution to allow for a single term of seven years,” he said, but stressed that the reform must be achieved constitutionally and democratically. The post 66 Years After Independence: How to make Nigeria great again – Prof Falode appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Mbah lists projects yielding Enugu money
items.description: * Says ‘We’re fastest growing state in revenue generation yet less than 13 % comes from taxation Editors of print, broadcast and now online platforms were wowed once again by the giant strides of Governor Ndubuisi Mbah when they visited the Coal City for the Annual Conference of the Nigeria Guild of Editors last week. Enugu also hosted the conference last year and repeated the project tour that made some editors wish Mbah could be hired by their states as they do in football. Work on the New City that will sit on 10,000 hectares, the new secondary schools, Enugu Ranch, Pine Forest, a tourism centre, Enugu International Hospital were among the sites they beheld. Former Governor of Ogun State, Segun Osoba, President of the Guild of Editors, Eze Anaba were full of praises for Mbah, arguably the star governor of the southeast east and one of the best performing governors in Nigeria. At the end of the tour, the editors asked the governor about the continuity of the huge projects at the end of his tenure, the transformation of the Enugu economy among other questions. As usual, he was eloquent in his answers. Excerpts: Let me once again restate how grateful we are as government and people of Enugu to have the honour of hosting you for the second year in a row. We truly understand the value, and we do not take it for granted. I’m also grateful that two days ago I invited you to explore Enugu, to go out and see for yourselves what we’ve done in Enugu. Thank you that you were able to take up that invite. I’m interested to know what you saw. What surprised you? What disappointed you? What doesn’t add up? And the questions that you may have raised. You know, I just wanted to get feedback. But again, for us, what you saw, the security, the transports, the investments, tourism, and all that, they are all interconnected. They are mutually reinforcing. They’re all designed to achieve a common objective. When we took office, we laid out a blueprint. One was to grow the economy of the state exponentially, but also to eradicate poverty and to create a state where people can live, work, invest and build futures. What I said to them when I was campaigning was that I was tired of seeing young people leave Enugu after their education to go elsewhere to look for work. The idea was for us to create something here that will keep people here so they can create wealth here, find employment, live here, have a satisfying life here without necessarily going out. We don’t want our boys only to come back to Enugu when they want to attend funerals or weddings. Those projects in themselves are not the end point. They’re actually the means for us to achieve that, and if you notice, if we talk about them, you see how they are designed to achieve, for example, the investment in the tourism is to help us attract 3 million people into Enugu. So, we’re currently doing six massive tourism sites. I understand you saw one. You went to the pine forest where we’re doing the zip line. We’re also doing the cable car at Opatu, 5.6 kilometer cable car. We’re also recasting the Nsude pyramid. It has a history of over 2,000 years. We have the ledger, iron smelting site. That, again, with a history of over 4,000 years. So, we’re preserving these things, trying to make sure that they become an icon that will bring people here. There are a whole lot of things. Even in the transport sector, we got ourselves into aviation because we want to create connectivity to the state, and we want people to have access to this place with ease. It’s all designed towards growing the economy exponentially, but also eradicating poverty. That would tell the story about our intervention in the social sector, intervention in education, in healthcare. It’s almost, as I always say, insane. Doing over 7,000 classrooms within two and a half years. But when you hear 7,000 classrooms, it’s not even about the classroom. That doesn’t tell you the story about the 464,000 furniture items that we also had to procure to go with the 7,000 classrooms. The solar system, the data and all that. They are not for political acclaim. Our hope is that whoever comes after would have to build on what they see because these things are, for example, our intervention in education is not about the structure. If you go to any of the smart green schools, you see that the future tells a difference. It underscores the fact that our children are entering into a different world. Not the one we lived 40 years ago where we went to school with chalk and blackboard. We recognise that in designing the smart school to capture the evolving 21st century skills. This is what these kids must be exposed to. So, once these kids begin to learn what we now call experiential learning, you cannot take them back to the rot system of learning where you teach them to memorise and write. We’re hoping that once we’ve raised the bar, that whoever comes thereafter would just build on it because the citizens would demand for that because they would have been used to that. In any case, we’re now doing the heavy lift. The capital expenditure we’re carrying now. We’re hoping that whoever comes subsequently will be focusing more on the operating cost. Which we know is sustainable in terms of what we have done. In terms of growing the revenue of the state. You may already know that in terms of revenue generation, we are the fastest in the country in terms of the speed of growth. We ended last year with N406 billion from N25 billion we started in 2023. We are only behind Lagos and Rivers in terms of IGR. We tell people that a lot of that doesn’t come from tax because there is this narrative that has been framed – that we’re overtaxing our people. It’s just a three part of it. Less than 13 per cent of our IGR comes from taxation. Over 87 per cent we get from the businesses we’re building. We’ve activated all our moribund companies, and they are all running. The United Palm Products. The Sunrise Flower Mill. The Niger Gas. The Presidential Hotel. The International Conference Centre. The terminals. These are major revenue generators. And they have created employment. We are making money from them. And that was our commitment to pluck the leakages and activate, revive all the Moribund industry. And that’s where the revenue is coming from, not from taxation. The approach, as you said, security is difficult for you to insulate yourself from your neighbours. But what we’ve also done in terms of making sure that our borders are well-policed is that we also have a line of sight of those coming into our states from the different gateways. Whether you’re coming through the formal or informal gateway, we can see you, we know you and we know when you’re leaving. But there’s also this conversation around peer review, which is something that is going on now. And we’ve had a number of my colleagues who have come to, of course, see what we’re doing here. And the whole idea is for us to, at some point, also have an integrated system. Where we can have a common command and control centre for the entire South-East. Not just for intelligence, but also for operations because what tends to happen is if you have tension in a certain location, once you neutralise that, you see those people migrating to other areas. We’re mindful and it’s a work in progress. It’s something that we do hope to achieve. In terms of the South-East integrated development, we’re lucky that federal government, the president, approved and signed into law the South-East Development Commission. And that’s somehow now driving these South-East common projects. For example, the SEDC is working on the pressure gas pipe to all the major cities in the South-East. They’ve taken ownership of that. It was something we were working in isolation. But since the coming into force and the operationalisation of the South-East Development Commission, that project is back to life. In fact, the integrated South-East railway line is also back. They are currently trying to find funds for that project. I think that we must commend the president for signing the SEDC into law and operationalising and also funding the SEDC because they are now taking up these projects of common interest in the South-East. Again, on our part in Enugu, we’re also doing our bit in making sure that the airport, which we believe should be a major gateway for the entire South-East, the international wing, as you may already know, has been concessioned. And we are trying to make sure that the investor gets it operationalised. We are working on that. In terms of our partnership with federal government, we are actually partnering with federal government in several ways, particularly with the road infrastructure. The road you drove through today, I think when you are going through the Enugu-Abakaliki Road, the flyover on that road is being done by federal government. But the dualisation is being done by the states. So the state is doing the 22-kilometre stretch, we’re dualising it, and then federal government is stepping in. And then you can see that they have also done the Enugu-Onitsha Expressway. That was almost a road that was impossible to get done, but we now can drive easily to Onitsha with ease and quite a whole number of interventions. So we have quite a good synergy with the federal government, and we also use this opportunity to commend the President for his interest in the South-East, and quite a lot of intervention has taken place since he assumed office. The Enugu-Port Harcourt Expressway now, the whole one carriage of that entire stretch is completely done. The post Mbah lists projects yielding Enugu money appeared first on Vanguard News .

It also stated that this will be critical in assisting the firm to drive growth in 5G mobility as well as in fulfilling its aspirations to the home connectivity in Ghana It continued that MTN Ghana will keep the market informed of material developments as it advances the rollout of the newly awarded spectrum and high-speed 5G services aimed at enhancing customer experience across the country. “The company appreciates the continued support of its shareholders and other stakeholders as it undertakes this strategic investment,” it added.

NPL: How three authors turned pain, history and faith into poetry
items.description: By Prisca Sam-Duru The 2026 edition of the Nigeria Prize for Literature nears its climax parading three poets, three different obsessions, but one common urgency — to hold a mirror to Nigeria. James Ngwu Eze writes against fear and silence. Tares Oburumu interrogates the colonial name we still bear. Ogaga Ifowodo asks a disturbingly simple question: Why does God need a gun? These three voices; authors of Unbind Me Now, Flora’s Love Colony and Why Does God Need a Gun? — are the finalists for the 2026 Nigeria Prize for Literature, worth $`100,000 and sponsored by Nigeria LNG Limited. They emerged from 223 entries to make a longlist of 11, and finally, a shortlist of three. The winner will be announced this October. Ahead of the final verdict, the trio spoke about their journeys, during an interview following the 2026 Book Party organised by CORA in partnership with NLNG, where excerpts from the 11 longlisted books were performed by young poets. The Nigeria Prize for Literature, established in 2004, rotates yearly among Prose Fiction, Poetry, Drama and Children’s Literature. Its Advisory Board is chaired by Prof. Akachi Adimora-Ezeigbo. James Ngwu Eze: Poetry As Protest For Eze, Unbind Me Now did not start as a book. It started as outrage. He had been gathering poems since 2019, but Nigeria’s relentless cycle of violence including Lekki Toll Gate, farmer-herder clashes, Ruga, kidnappings, insecurity, pushed him into what he calls a creative outburst. “When there is terror, people’s freedom shrinks,” Eze said. “People woke up every morning expecting a horrible breaking news. It became a deadly experience for everybody.” The title itself is a demand. The poetic voice speaks for the displaced, the bereaved, the violated; people asking to be unbound, not tomorrow, but now. Why poetry? Because, he says, poetry compresses what a novel would take chapters to say. “The poet has the gift of compressing emotions into a few lines of verse with the right emotion,” he noted. Eze never imagined he would make the final three from 223 entries. He calls it “an act of God.” He insists he does not write for prizes and is already working on a new collection. He credits NLNG for giving poetry glamour and visibility. “NLNG has glamorised poetry and made it attractive to everyone,” he said. Making the longlist before, he added, opened doors for him. His counsel to young poets: Read, relentlessly. Tares Oburumu: The Woman Who Named Nigeria Oburumu’s curiosity began with a name — Flora Shaw. Who was Lord Lugard’s wife who coined the name Nigeria? That question led him into the archives of amalgamation and beyond, into a full tracing of Nigeria from its colonial conception to its present contradictions. “I needed to trace Nigerian history from the beginning, from the origin to present day,” he said. Flora’s Love Colony is therefore a post-colonial inquiry, examining how colonialism still shapes our politics and identity. Writing since 2010, Oburumu — who studied Philosophy and Religion at the University of Benin — grew up with classics like Things Fall Apart, Chike and the River and Treasure Island. But books were scarce. He did not have real access to them until he was 14. In his primary school, pupils sometimes sat on mud floors. That memory drives him. After winning an earlier prize, he started building a library for his hometown primary school. If he wins the `$100,000, he wants to complete it. “The first thing that came into my mind was that there comes an opportunity to finish my project and do something for the children,” he said. For young writers, his advice is blunt: Reading shapes a writer more than writing. Stay consistent and passionate. Ogaga Ifowodo: When Faith Carries a Rifle Ifowodo’s title is a question that answers itself. Why Does God Need a Gun? If God is all-powerful, why do humans kill to defend Him? The idea was conceived during the revision of his collection, particularly a sequence of 26 poems titled From the Forest of a Million Demons, Leah Sharibu Lifts the Veil. The poet persona gives voice to victims of terrorism and abduction, echoing Chibok and Dapchi. It confronts religious intolerance, fundamentalism and the dangerous belief that those who worship differently deserve less life. Making the final three, for him, is validation that his work has found an audience, after 223 entries. But Ifowodo is philosophical about winning. “Winning is not in itself an ultimate judgment on your work,” he said. Some prize-winners fade; some overlooked books endure. He is currently working on three projects: a work of fiction, his detention memoirs, and a new poetry collection that may explore love. If he wins, he plans to endow a poetry prize at Federal Government College, Warri, where he wrote his first poem in 1982. Beyond the $100,000 For all three finalists, the prize is bigger than money. It is visibility, recognition, and a louder microphone for urgent conversations about insecurity and freedom, colonial hangovers, and faith weaponised into violence. items.title: Agadir : levée de l’interdiction de collecte et commercialisation de coquillages
items.description: Le secrétariat d’État chargé de la Pêche maritime a annoncé, vendredi, la levée de l’interdiction sur le ramassage et la commercialisation des produits conchylicoles collectés au niveau des zones conchylicoles classées Douira-Sidi R’bat et Tamri-Cap Ghir, relevant de la circonscription maritime d’Agadir. « Le Comité Technique chargé du suivi du milieu marin et des produits conchylicoles a examiné les résultats d’analyses effectuées par l’Institut National de Recherche Halieutique (INRH) au niveau des zones conchylicoles classées Douira-Sidi R’bat et Tami-Cap Ghir (Région d’Agadir) » , indique le secrétariat d’État dans un communiqué, précisant que les résultats des analyses ont montré une stabilité des milieux et une purification totale des moules au niveau desdites zone. Par ailleurs, il est recommandé aux consommateurs de ne s’approvisionner qu’en produits conditionnés, portant les étiquettes sanitaires d’identification et commercialisés dans les points de vente autorisés (marchés officiels). Les produits conchylicoles colportés ou vendus en vrac ne présentent aucune garantie de salubrité et constituent un danger pour la santé publique, avertit le secrétariat d’État. items.title: 2026 UN Day of Older Persons: Senior citizens want monthly stipends, free transport
items.description: A group of elderly Nigerians, under the umbrella of Global Veterans has called on the Federal, state and local governments to make adequate budgetary provisions for the welfare of senior citizens, including monthly stipends and free transportation, beginning with the 2027 fiscal year. The seniour citizens also advocated the establishment of special welfare centres across Nigeria’s 774 local government areas where elderly people can access essential drugs, medications, food items and other household necessities at subsidised rates. They made the call at a programme organised by Global Veterans to commemorate the 2026 United Nations International Day of Older Persons, with the theme, “The Age of Longevity: Rethinking Systems for Longer Lives.” Speaking at the event, the Convener of Global Veterans, Mr Victor Oluwadamilare said growing old in Nigeria was increasingly becoming a difficult experience characterised by want, deprivation, bitterness and abandonment. He said the economic realities confronting the country had placed additional pressure on elderly citizens, many of whom were suffering silently because of the cultural tendency among African parents to conceal their difficulties According to him, “one of the hardest things in Nigeria right now is not just being poor, it is growing old in difficult times.” He therefore appealed to all tiers of government to include comprehensive welfare programmes for senior citizens in their budgets from 2027. He proposed that Nigerians aged 60 and above should be considered for monthly stipends and other forms of social support, while free or heavily subsidised public transportation should also be introduced to ease the burden of mobility on elderly citizens. He further called for the establishment of dedicated centres in all 774 local government areas to provide affordable access to medicines, food and other basic necessities. Prince Ade Adekanmbi, Special Adviser on Media to former Governor Rashidi Ladoja, said society must change the way it views older people, stressing that they should not be regarded merely as dependants. Adekanmbi said elderly citizens should instead be recognised as partners in national development, given their wealth of experience and contributions to society. He urged government and other stakeholders to continually review systems affecting older citizens, particularly healthcare, pensions, social protection, housing, transportation, digital inclusion and access to essential services He said healthcare deserved particular attention because longevity without access to affordable and quality medical care could turn longer life into a burden rather than a blessing. “After decades of service, our senior citizens deserve a retirement that allows them to live with dignity,” he said, stressing the need for a pension system that goes beyond mere survival. The Chairman of the Nigeria Union of Pensioners, Oyo State chapter, Pastor Ayo Oshuntade, questioned the kind of society Nigeria was building for its citizens to live longer. He said longevity should not simply mean adding more years to people’s lives, but ensuring that those years were lived with dignity, purpose and adequate support. “What kind of society are we building for people to live longer life? Longevity doesn’t mean only to live long but to live more life with dignity and purpose to those years,” Oshuntade said. Former Chairman of the Campaign for Democracy, Comrade Mashood Erubami, also attributed the difficulties faced by many Nigerians in old age to inadequate provision of essential public services. Erubami argued that government’s failure to provide basic services had contributed to the inability of many citizens to live healthy and fulfilling lives into old age. A lecturer at Ajayi Crowther University, Oyo, Dr Samson Owolabi, advised elderly people to maintain healthy relationships with people within their neighbourhoods and communities. He encouraged senior citizens to develop friendships and social networks that could provide companionship and reduce isolation. Owolabi also advised them to remain reasonably principled while avoiding rigid attitudes that could negatively affect their wellbeing. He urged the elderly to pay attention to their personal welfare, including eating and dressing well, and to prioritise their basic needs when spending their resources. He also advised them to avoid becoming excessively entangled in what he described as “spiritual legover.” The speakers collectively stressed the need for a coordinated national framework for ageing, arguing that government policies on healthcare, pensions, transportation, housing and social protection must recognise the growing population of older Nigerians. They maintained that supporting senior citizens should be treated as a social responsibility and a matter of dignity, rather than charity, particularly as economic pressures continue to affect vulnerable members of society. items.title: FAAN, Bi-Courtney differ on approach to aviation revenue
items.description: By Dickson Omobola Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria, FAAN, and Bi-Courtney Aviation Services Limited, operators of the Murtala Muhammed Airport Terminal Two, MMA2, have recommended different approaches to growing the country’s aviation revenue, with the airport management agency advocating a comprehensive review of taxes, levies and charges. Although FAAN said there was a need for transparency and a review of the revenue structure across the aviation industry, the terminal operator pushed for a growth-driven model that prioritises lower charges and increased passenger traffic. The different positions emerged at the 30th Annual Conference of the League of Airport and Aviation Correspondents, LAAC, themed ‘Towards Sustainable Aviation Industry: Balancing Government Revenue Demands with Sector Growth,’ held in Lagos. Speaking during a panel session at the conference, Managing Director of FAAN, Olubunmi Kuku, represented by the agency’s Director of Finance and Accounts, Ayodele Olatiregun, said despite improvements in aviation revenue and domestic passenger traffic since the COVID-19 pandemic, international traffic had remained the major driver of revenue in the sector. Kuku, who said the contribution of domestic passenger traffic to the overall revenue base remained relatively low despite a slight improvement in passenger numbers over the last five years, called for a comprehensive review of all taxes, levies and charges in the air transport sector. However, she said all stakeholders must be ready to make their figures available to facilitate the process. She said: “One thing I will also say from this other side of the divide is, in the last five years, post-COVID pandemic, there has been improvement in the revenue generation in aviation as a whole. But, unfortunately, data shows that most of this is actually driven by international traffic, rather than local traffic. So, yes, there has been slight improvements in passenger traffic at a domestic level, in terms of contribution to the cake, or to the base, it is not really representative. What I will say, in essence, is, I understand the fact that there are several charges from the perspective of who pays them. That’s the airline. But from the airport perspective, everything that we have done is in line with international regulations. “Of course, we know that aviation is highly regulated. But when we talk about other levies and taxes, it’s very important that the cost of doing business is something that airlines will always find a way to bring the issues to the fore. And it’s not only in the aviation sector. I feel that it makes absolute sense for there to be a consolidated and comprehensive review of all the taxes, levies and charges as it affects the aviation industry. And when I say aviation industry, I mean not just the airlines, government itself and its agencies, the ground handling companies and every other entity or sector working in the industry as a whole. “I believe it’s an ongoing conversation that needs to be had. But it is also very important that we also think through it because information is required to make such decisions. And that information is not publicly available. I believe not just government. For transparency’s sake, I feel all stakeholders, and I believe FAAN inclusive, should be ready to put out their numbers out there for proper review.” Meanwhile, Acting Chief Operating Officer of Bi-Courtney Aviation Services Limited, operators of the Murtala Muhammed Airport Terminal Two, MMA2, Remi Jibodu, urged government to view aviation as an economic multiplier rather than primarily as a source of revenue. Jibodu said lower charges could encourage growth in passenger traffic and other aviation-related activities, which would eventually expand government revenue. Jibodu said: “It is better for you to have one per cent of 1 billion than 10 per cent of 100 million. The truth about it is that if you look at the figures globally, I think Airports Council International, ACI, said we are going to be growing globally by four per cent. Africa, because we have not even reached the maturity level, is going to grow by about five to six per cent. Recently, AOG came up with a report during this last summer, and they said that Africa grew by about seven per cent, which is very high. “The driver for that is actually the domestic market in Nigeria, which drives that figure in Africa. What I’m trying to say, basically, is that the numbers, if you look at the numbers, mean there is going to be consistent growth even beyond 2050. Now, if you want it to grow and not be stunted, the way to go is to look at the mathematics and say, I will charge a little from many, or not so much from a few. Now, the second point of view, basically, is that when you now take this advice, what will happen is that, for instance, let me give you MMA2. On a daily basis, we entertain no less than 15,000 people, both passengers and customers. And what am I saying? Within these 15,000 people, you have passengers. “They are a dynamic population, so they are not unique. So, it’s going to evolve on a daily basis. What it means, basically, is that you’re going to have expansion in cargo, ground handling, travel agencies, infrastructure, and so many aspects, in terms of employment and revenue. What it means is that the multiplier effect for the economy is going to be that the government is going to make more money at the end of the day. And the growth of the industry will be very significant, especially in Nigeria and Africa. A lot of people are looking at us to see how we can grow this figure. Government will eventually make the money. That is just the bottom line of it. But what is important is that the industry also grows while government is also making money.” The post FAAN, Bi-Courtney differ on approach to aviation revenue appeared first on Vanguard News .
