Mini-réseaux solaires photovoltaïques : Le secteur privé sensibilisé aux nouvelles normes nationales à Bobo-Dioulasso
items.description: L’Agence Faso Véneem, en collaboration avec l’Agence burkinabè de normalisation, de la métrologie et de la qualité (ABNORM), a organisé, ce 2 octobre 2026, à Bobo-Dioulasso, un atelier de vulgarisation des normes nationales au profit du secteur privé. Cette activité, qui s’inscrit dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre du Projet national « Africa Minigrids Program » (PN-AMP), vise à renforcer la connaissance et l’appropriation des normes applicables afin de garantir la qualité, la sûreté et la fiabilité des équipements solaires. Après Ouagadougou, c’est au tour des acteurs du secteur privé de Bobo-Dioulasso de bénéficier de cette session de sensibilisation. L’atelier a réuni différents acteurs intéressés par le développement des solutions énergétiques solaires. Il vise à contribuer à la structuration d’un marché crédible et durable des équipements solaires au Burkina Faso. Il s’agit notamment de permettre aux professionnels du secteur de mieux connaître les exigences techniques et normatives afin de faciliter leur prise en compte dans leurs activités. Présent à l’atelier, Drissa Coulibaly, directeur régional des Mines et des Carrières du Guiriko, a invité les acteurs à tirer pleinement profit de cette formation. Pour lui, la normalisation ne doit pas être perçue comme une contrainte administrative supplémentaire, mais plutôt comme un outil de qualité, de sécurité, de protection du consommateur et de structuration du marché. « La qualité d’un mini réseau ne dépend pas d’un seul intervenant, elle se construit tout au long de la chaîne de valeur » , a déclaré Drissa Coulibaly. Pour les organisateurs, la connaissance et le respect de ces normes constituent des éléments importants pour garantir la qualité, la sûreté et la fiabilité des équipements solaires utilisés sur le marché national. Prenant la parole, Mahamed Saraba, représentant de l’ABNORM, a précisé que la tenue de cette session s’inscrit dans le cadre de l’élaboration de 11 nouvelles normes nationales relatives aux mini-réseaux solaires photovoltaïques. « Après élaboration nous avons décider d’approcher ces normes au niveau du terrain à travers les acteurs privés le dans le but de les vulgariser sur son utilisation » , a-t-il ajouté. Par ailleurs, le développement des énergies renouvelables, notamment de l’énergie solaire, nécessite des équipements répondant à des exigences de qualité et de sécurité. La vulgarisation des normes nationales apparaît ainsi comme un moyen de renforcer les capacités des différents acteurs de la chaîne. À Bobo-Dioulasso, cette rencontre devrait permettre aux participants d’échanger avec les spécialistes sur les normes applicables aux différents composants des mini-réseaux solaires photovoltaïques. Roger Ouédraogo, coordonnateur du PN-AMP, a invité les participants à s’approprier ces normes afin d’améliorer la confiance des consommateurs et la rentabilité de leurs ouvrages électriques. Seydou Konaté, gérant de la société Faso Dambé Plein d’Énergie et Services, a remercié les organisateurs pour la mise en place de cet atelier. Selon lui, cette formation leur permettra de travailler avec davantage d’assurance dans la mise en œuvre de futurs projets. À l’issue de cette activité, les organisateurs espèrent un changement de mentalité à travers une meilleure utilisation des normes, qui permettront d’assurer la qualité des composants et la durabilité des mini-réseaux photovoltaïques. L’article Mini-réseaux solaires photovoltaïques : Le secteur privé sensibilisé aux nouvelles normes nationales à Bobo-Dioulasso est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: John Boadu: The leader our party needs at this time – Amb. Edward Akwasi Boateng
items.description: From abroad, I have followed with considerable interest the keenly contested national elections within our party. The intensity of the campaign reflects the passion of our members and the importance of the choice before us. All the candidates have offered valuable ideas and deserve commendation for their commitment to the NPP. As delegates prepare to vote on Saturday, October 3, our overriding consideration must be the future of the party and the demanding journey towards 2028. The NPP was decisively defeated in the 2024 elections. We must now reunite, rebuild and restore confidence, discipline and hope. I do not make this endorsement lightly. I have worked with all the candidates and know them personally and professionally. After careful reflection, I believe John Boadu’s experience, institutional knowledge, temperament and willingness to listen make him the leader best suited for this moment. He understands the Party—from the grassroots to the national leadership—and can reconcile its competing interests and traditions. As National Organiser and later Acting General Secretary from 2014 to 2016, he helped rebuild our organisational machinery and contributed significantly to the historic 2016 victory. His candidacy is not about returning to the past. It is about applying the lessons of experience to renew the party, reconnect its leadership with the grassroots, rebuild trust and forge the broad coalition required for victory in 2028. After Saturday, I hope all the candidates will rally behind him, because each has something valuable to offer the Party. Delegates must ask: who can best work with the Flagbearer, unite our people and prepare the Party for the task ahead? For me, the answer is clear. I respectfully urge delegates to elect John Boadu as National Chairman.

items.title: Octobre Rose : le traitement du cancer du sein reste un défi au Mali
items.description: Octobre Rose, mois consacre a la sensibilisation et a la lutte contre le cancer du sein, a debute hier. Au Mali, les activites mettent l'accent sur la sensibilisation et le depistage gratuit. Malgre ces initiatives, l'acces aux soins et aux traitements reste difficile pour de nombreux patients. Selon Faye Kadiatou Kante, presidente de la Ligue malienne de lutte contre les cancers, le manque de specialistes constitue l'une des principales difficultes dans la prise en charge des patients. Le coût des medicaments et des examens represente egalement un obstacle. « On n'a pas assez d' oncologues . Non seulement les medicaments coûtent cher, mais aussi les analyses. On n'a qu'une seule radiotherapie au Mali. Maintenant, la radio ne fonctionne pas » , deplore-t-elle. La prise en charge du cancer reste ainsi confrontee a des difficultes liees a la disponibilite des equipements, des specialistes et des medicaments. Des subventions de l'etat et une demande croissante La presidente de la Ligue malienne de lutte contre les cancers releve toutefois des avancees dans la prise en charge de la maladie. Elle cite notamment les subventions accordees par l'etat depuis 2009 pour faciliter l'acces aux medicaments. « Moi, je peux dire qu'il y a eu des changements, parce que l'etat a toujours fait des subventions, de 2009 jusqu'a maintenant » , explique Faye Kadiatou Kante. Elle constate egalement une augmentation de la demande en medicaments, qu'elle met en lien avec le nombre croissant de nouveaux cas. Selon elle, les produits subventionnes, qui pouvaient auparavant rester longtemps disponibles dans les hopitaux, sont desormais rapidement utilises. Une meilleure sensibilisation au depistage Autre evolution relevee par la presidente de la Ligue : la prise de conscience des populations. Elle estime que davantage de personnes comprennent desormais l'importance de consulter dans les structures de sante pour se faire soigner. Cette evolution constitue, selon elle, un changement important dans la lutte contre le cancer au Mali. a rappeler que la sensibilisation et le depistage precoce restent au cœur des activites d'Octobre Rose. items.title: Pour soulager les éleveurs de Richard-Toll, la CSS mise sur le niébé fourrager
items.description: La Compagnie sucrière sénégalaise (CSS), historiquement connue dans l'exploitation de la canne à sucre, a emblavé 145 ha de niébé fourrager à Richard-Toll, offrant un véritable soulagement aux éleveurs de la zone. Soutenue par les autorités, cette initiative enrichit les sols, améliore l'alimentation du bétail et confirme l'ambition d'aller bien au-delà des 600 ha dans les prochaines campagnes. La Compagnie Sucrière Sénégalaise (CSS) reste historiquement associée à la canne à sucre. Pourtant, elle vient de confirmer, pour la deuxième année consécutive, son engagement dans la production de fourrage. Cette saison, 145 hectares de niébé fourrager ont été emblavés, un geste salué comme un véritable « ouf de soulagement » par les autorités et les éleveurs. Mme Ndama Thiam, chef de poste vétérinaire de la commune de Richard-Toll et représentante du Ministère de l’Agriculture, de la Souveraineté alimentaire et de l’Élevage, indique qu’on peut dire qu’il y a un « ouf de soulagement ». Dans une zone où cohabitent production de viande, de lait, bovins et petits ruminants, l’amélioration de l’alimentation du bétail constitue un enjeu majeur. « Avec la politique de notre Ministère dans la zone, nous pouvons atteindre l’amélioration de l’alimentation du bétail », souligne-t-elle. De son côté, Amadou Ndiaye, coordonnateur opérationnel des activités agricoles à la CSS, détaille l’opération. Le choix du niébé n’est pas anodin. Cette légumineuse valorise l’azote de l’air, enrichit le sol et offre un fourrage très appétant, particulièrement riche en protéines, prisé par les bovins de la zone. « Ça contribue beaucoup à améliorer l’alimentation du bétail au niveau de Richard-Toll », insiste-t-il. L’investissement est conséquent. Des dizaines de millions de francs CFA ont été mobilisés pour ces 145 hectares. Après avoir disposé d’un semoir lors de la première édition, la CSS a acquis le sien propre cette année, pour plus de 20 millions de francs, en plus de tracteurs, de personnel et de gasoil. Le ministère a apporté un appui décisif avec plus de trois tonnes de semences, malgré les difficultés à trouver des graines de qualité à cette période. L’objectif initial de 600 hectares n’a pas été atteint en raison de contraintes, mais l’ambition demeure : dépasser ce chiffre dans les prochaines campagnes. En diversifiant ainsi ses cultures, la CSS ne se contente pas de produire du sucre. Elle contribue à sécuriser le fourrage local, à soutenir les éleveurs et à renforcer la résilience d’une filière essentielle pour le nord du Sénégal. Un partenariat public-privé qui porte déjà ses fruits et promet davantage. Tidiane SOW (Correspondant)

items.title: Burkina-Banque mondiale : Le nouveau Cadre de Partenariat Pays 2026-2031 lancé
items.description: La ministre déléguée chargée du Budget, Fatoumata Bako/Traoré, représentant le ministre de l’Économie et des Finances, Dr Aboubakar Nacanabo, a présidé, ce vendredi 2 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou, la cérémonie officielle de lancement du nouveau Cadre de Partenariat Pays (CPF), établi entre le Burkina Faso et le Groupe de la Banque mondiale pour la période 2026-2031. Le CPF 2026-2031 constitue la nouvelle feuille de route de la coopération entre le Burkina Faso et le Groupe de la Banque mondiale pour les cinq prochaines années. Il s’inscrit dans un nouveau cadre de partenariat couvrant les quatre pays du Sahel central, à savoir le Burkina Faso, le Mali, le Niger et le Tchad. En lançant ce nouveau cadre ce vendredi, les deux parties ont réaffirmé leur volonté de renforcer leur partenariat sur la base d’une responsabilité partagée, d’une exigence commune de résultats et d’engagements clairement définis. Selon la ministre déléguée chargée du Budget, cette approche implique « une attention particulière à la qualité des projets, à la célérité de leur exécution, à l’efficacité des ressources mobilisées et au suivi régulier de leurs impacts ». Pour la représentante du ministre en charge de l’Économie, le CPF 2026-2031 doit avant tout constituer un instrument au service de résultats concrets. « Sa mise en œuvre devra se traduire par des investissements structurants dans les secteurs prioritaires, tels que la santé, l’éducation, l’énergie, l’agriculture, les infrastructures, mais aussi par un renforcement durable de nos capacités nationales à concevoir, à mettre en œuvre et à évaluer nos politiques publiques », a-t-elle soutenu. Des détails à venir sur Minute.bf.

La direction du festival salue l'acceptation par l'artiste Mohamed Ali Ben Jemaa de cette fonction honorifique, estimant que sa présence constitue une contribution artistique et symbolique majeure à cette édition, qui vise à soutenir la création cinématographique, à renforcer la présence du cinéma tunisien et à mettre en valeur le rôle des femmes et des jeunes dans le 7e art. Le festival poursuit également son ouverture sur les expériences cinématographiques arabes et internationales, en favorisant les échanges artistiques et en créant des espaces de dialogue et de rencontre entre les artistes et cinéastes de Tunisie et du monde entier. items.title: Baffour Awuah: EOCO arrested, detained MP after hours of waiting, questioning – Afenyo-Markin
items.description: Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin has detailed the circumstances surrounding the detention of Manhyia South MP Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah after he voluntarily reported himself to the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO). According to Mr Afenyo-Markin, the MP arrived at EOCO at 10:47 a.m. on Thursday, October 1, accompanied by his lawyers and some parliamentary colleagues, but was made to wait several hours before questioning began. Speaking to the media on Friday, October 2, after visiting the MP in custody, the Minority Leader said Mr Awuah was initially told he would be seen within 15 minutes. “That 15 minutes turned into some 3 or 4 hours. So, not until after 2 pm when EOCO officials finally invited him to the interrogation room,” he said. Mr Afenyo-Markin said the Manhyia South MP was then made to wait for another 30 minutes before being asked to complete a personal profile form. According to him, EOCO officials subsequently left, saying they needed clearance from the Director of Operations. He said investigators later returned and asked Mr Baffour Awuah to provide an overview of a case his law firm handled for SIC Life in 2018. “He complied,” Mr Afenyo-Markin said, adding that the process of providing the overview ended at about 4 p.m. It was at that point, he said, that EOCO officials informed the MP that he was under arrest. “They officially tapped his shoulders and said he was under arrest. So, to them, it was at 4 pm after all of that that they effected an arrest,” he said. Mr Afenyo-Markin said EOCO subsequently took Mr Awuah to his law office in Dzorwulu for a search. He said the MP cooperated with the search but alleged that some documents unrelated to the investigation, including vehicle documents, were taken. “So, no document was taken in relation to the case under investigation,” he said. According to the Minority Leader, the MP returned to EOCO at about 7:30 p.m. and was again taken to an interrogation room, where he waited for about an hour. He said investigators later informed Baffour Awuah that they needed to undertake further work and would therefore detain him. The MP was subsequently taken to the cells at about 8 p.m., despite protests from his lead counsel, Samuel Atta Akyea. Mr Afenyo-Markin said the following morning, investigators informed Baffour Awuah that a team would be assembled to begin a second phase of the process, with the expectation that the MP could secure bail by midday. He said, however, that no investigator attended to him until after 2 p.m., when EOCO indicated that it wanted to search his residence. Mr Baffour Awuah’s detention forms part of an ongoing EOCO investigation into transactions involving SIC Life Savings and Loans. The MP reported himself to the agency on October 1 after the Accra High Court issued a warrant for his arrest. The investigation has been linked to suspected financial loss, dissipation of public funds and money laundering, although the allegations remain under investigation. Mr Afenyo-Markin’s account comes as the Minority continues to raise concerns about the manner in which the MP has been treated by EOCO.

items.description: Day after day, the Israeli-occupied village of Mansouri, perched on a green hill a few kilometres south of the coastal city of Tyre, is slowly disappearing. Already heavily damaged during the war, it is now quite literally being wiped off the map, in a final twist of cynicism, during the ceasefire.

items.title: EOCO court warrant authorised search of Baffour Awuah’s law firm, not residence – Afenyo-Markin
items.description: Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin has questioned the Economic and Organised Crime Office’s (EOCO) decision to search the residence of Manhyia South MP Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah, claiming the court order obtained by the agency was specifically for a search of his law firm. Mr Afenyo-Markin said the issue arose on Friday, October 2, after EOCO informed the detained MP that investigators intended to search his residence. Speaking to the media after visiting Mr Awuah in EOCO custody, he said the MP found the decision puzzling because, according to him, the court order obtained by EOCO specifically authorised a search of the MP’s law firm in Dzorwulu. “The court order that was procured by EOCO was very clear that they should only search his office, his law firm at Dzorwulu,” he said. Mr Afenyo-Markin said the court had also directed that the order be served on the Speaker of Parliament, Alban Bagbin. He explained that the Speaker would then use Parliament’s internal processes to serve the order on Mr Awuah, after which the MP could make himself available to EOCO. According to him, Mr Awuah therefore questioned why investigators were seeking to extend the search to his private residence. “He found the decision to search his house quite curious. So he inquired that the order of the court was specific to a search to be conducted in his office. So why his residence?” Mr Afenyo-Markin said. The Minority Leader’s comments come after EOCO took the Manhyia South MP to his former law firm on Thursday as part of its investigation into transactions involving SIC Life Savings and Loans. Reports at the time indicated that investigators also intended to search his residence. Mr Awuah had voluntarily reported to EOCO on October 1, accompanied by his lawyer, Samuel Atta Akyea, following the issuance of an arrest warrant by the Accra High Court. EOCO had told the court that it had exhausted reasonable means of securing the MP’s voluntary attendance and was concerned that relevant documents could be concealed, altered or destroyed.

items.title: Pakistani national charged with defrauding US Postal Service of $126m
items.description: A Pakistani national has been charged with defrauding the United States Postal Service (USPS) of $125 million by selling counterfeit postage labels online, it emerged on Friday. According to a press release by the US Attorney’s Office of the Southern District of Florida, issued on Monday on the website of the Department of Justice (DOJ), a federal grand jury returned an indictment charging a Pakistani national, a 33-year-old from Khanewal, with operating “an unauthorised website that allegedly sold more than five million counterfeit US postage labels”. According to court records, these were sold at a fixed rate, “typically $2 per label”, regardless of the size, weight or destination of the package in question. This allowed customers to post items for cheap at rates “far below legitimate USPS prices”. The statement also pointed out that the website used for this purpose was not authorised to sell USPS products and services. The investigation revealed that over 5,200 individuals used the website to buy more than 5.1m counterfeit shipping labels. The losses caused to the service as a result were reported to be over $126m, the press release highlighted. “Through the work of the US Postal Inspection Service and our prosecutors, the website has been shut down, the domain seized, and federal charges brought against its alleged operator,” US Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida said, according to the press release. He termed the alleged scheme “simple but massive”. According to the statement, the accused is charged with “one count of conspiracy to defraud the US and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps; five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels; and four counts of wire fraud”. If convicted, he faces a maximum of five years in prison on the counts of conspiracy to defraud and sell counterfeit postage stamps, as well as 20 years in prison for each count of wire fraud. “An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law,” the DOJ added. In February, two Pakistani nationals were indicted in the US for their alleged role in a $10m healthcare fraud scheme that targeted Medicare and private insurance programmes.

items.title: NPP delegates conference: 3,000 to 4,000 police personnel deployed for security in Kumasi – Anthony Karbo
items.description: The New Patriotic Party (NPP) says between 3,000 and 4,000 police personnel have been deployed to provide security for its National Delegates Conference and elections at the Baba Yara Sports Stadium in Kumasi. Chairperson of the party’s Organisation Committee, Anthony Abayifaa Karbo, said the police deployment would cover traffic management, security at hostels accommodating delegates and guests, as well as security within and around the stadium. He commended the Inspector General of Police (IGP) and the Ashanti Regional Police Command for their cooperation and support ahead of the conference. Speaking to Accra-based Citi News in Kumasi, Mr Karbo said preparations for the conference, scheduled for Saturday, October 3, were far advanced, with delegates already arriving and settling into their designated hostels. He said public address systems were being installed at the venue, while security personnel had been positioned around the stadium. Mr Karbo also expressed confidence in the conduct of the aspirants and delegates, noting that the contestants had been cooperative throughout the process. He urged delegates to conduct themselves responsibly to ensure a smooth and successful conference. “We’re very much ready for tomorrow; you come around, you see the police and arrangements so far. I’m sure we’re ready; delegates are arriving at their hostels. “The IGP has been fantastic so far; his regional command has been cooperative with us, and they have worked hard to deploy about 3,000 to 4,000 police force to help us with security arrangements and traffic within the hostels and also the stadium,” he said. Mr Karbo reiterated the party’s commitment to ensuring that the National Delegates Conference proceeds smoothly.

items.title: Ethiopia accuses Sudan of backing opposition, reshuffled hope for Idris’s govt, tribal violence engulfs South Darfur, military opens road to West Kordofan, China on Sudan’s coast
items.description: Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . Sudan’s government is taking a long hard look in the mirror, and they don’t like what they see, sources close to Prime Minister Kamel Idris and the Transitional Sovereignty Council told Mada Masr this week. Ushered in on a promise of hope a year ago, Idris’s government has faced significant issues. Some of those come down to war-time trials, but infighting and attempts to delimit the remit of a civilian government backed by a powerful and intrusive military council have been persistent issues. Now the government is considering a reshuffle of ministerial and gubernatorial appointments to address executive imbalances and shortfalls, particularly on economic and service-related issues, according to a source in Idris’s office. While Idris and the TSC may see an administrative reshuffle as a way to address war-time woes, the armed movements that signed the 2020 Juba peace agreement insist that any bureaucratic rearrangement must not change the power-sharing agreement inked in the South Sudanese capital. For now, the reshuffle is all just talk. But the movements do not view it in isolation from the larger reshaping of the political landscape of recent months, a leader in one of the Juba armed movements told Mada Masr, particularly as the planned national dialogue will have to address their relationship with the government. Outside military-controlled areas, the Rapid Support Forces have also been dealing with internal discord over the last two weeks, though the dispute they are presiding over has a decidedly less understanding and diplomatic tenor. Throughout September, deadly inter-tribal clashes have engulfed South Darfur. With heavy weapons in hand and grappling with a faltering rainy season, tribes in Gereida, about 90 km south of Nyala, and in southern parts of Nyala itself, have become embroiled in violent confrontations. The RSF has tried to step in to calm the situation, deploying troops to prevent it from continuing to spiral out of control. As residents look on to see how effective these immediate tamping down measures will be, civil society and RSF sources agree that the much more difficult problem will be halting the spread of heavy weapons into residential communities, which allows competition over water, pasture and farmland during droughts to become increasingly militarized. On Sudan’s battlefields this week, the military cleared the last major RSF defensive positions in North Kordofan, effectively opening the West Kordofan front. These losses have triggered yet another defection from the paramilitary group, as Al-Tayeb “Waheedo” Mohamed Ahmed arrived to Omdurman, saying he left after witnessing “tragedies” and “collapse” within the RSF’s ranks. But while frontline battles remain consequential, drone warfare continues to figure in Sudan’s conflict. RSF drones struck targets in Gezira and North Kordofan over the week, reaching fuel infrastructure east of Wad Madani and multiple sites in Obeid, where at least six civilians were killed. This week also saw a series of tense diplomatic exchanges. The first came at the UN General Assembly’s debate on Monday, with the United Arab Emirates and Sudanese delegations engaging in tug-of-war over the narrative on Sudan’s conflict. A former official said the spat does not necessarily signal another diplomatic rupture. But the second tense diplomatic moment could prove more consequential. Ethiopia, recently plunged into another civil war, accused Sudan of abetting opposition fighters then took the more drastic diplomatic step of expelling Eritrean and Egyptian diplomats. While wars and their fallout dominate the headlines this week, Sudan is taking steps toward a post-war future. And as with previous attempts to attract foreign powers to Khartoum, this future projection involves lucrative real estate on Sudan’s Red Sea coast. But instead of Russia or the UAE, this time, it is China that is coming in to revive the Abu Amama port project, two years after Sudan cancelled a memorandum of understanding with an Emirati-led consortium to execute the project. *** After TSC review, Idris prepares for govt reshuffle, Juba armed movements to join talks Prime Minister Kamel Idris and the members of the “Government of Hope.” Courtesy: The Government of Hope. Prime Minister Kamel Idris has begun holding consultations in recent days in preparation for reshuffling his government just over a year after it was formed, sources close to the premiership and the TSC told Mada Masr. The talks, which sources said cover several ministries and state governorships, follow an earlier decree ordering a review of government appointments made in recent months, which alarmed the armed movements that signed the 2020 Juba peace agreement over fears that their guaranteed share of executive power under the terms of the deal could be reconsidered. The ministries under review are mostly economy- and service-focused, while governors are being judged largely on how they have restored services in military-recaptured states. The final lineup is yet to be agreed. The reshuffle would be the first major review of the “Government of Hope” since it was completed last summer and is expected to affect ministries held by the armed movements, chiefly the Finance Ministry, the sources said. The movements’ positions in the government were themselves secured under political pressure. Idris had initially proposed a cabinet of non-partisan technocrats, but after months of deadlock, the TSC intervened and pushed him to preserve the movements’ positions under the peace agreement. A year later, the TSC is again directly involved, this time in monitoring and assessing the performance of ministries, including some of those held by the same movements it had helped keep in government. The review comes as Khartoum is still trying to turn military gains into evidence of a functioning state. Over the past year and a half, the government has brought millions of Sudanese back to areas recaptured by the military under a “ voluntary return ” campaign, promising that institutions and basic services would follow. But war-related needs continue to consume public money. The pound is collapsing, while the productive sectors that might replenish the treasury with domestic income or foreign currency remain badly damaged or outside government control. Across the areas where people have returned, basic infrastructure is still damaged. The reshuffle is a review of who is responsible for managing that gap. According to a source in Idris’s office, the changes are aimed at addressing what the government sees as imbalances and shortcomings in the performance of the executive branch, particularly on economic and service-related issues. The Finance Ministry is therefore among the portfolios under particular scrutiny, the source said. It is held by Gibril Ibrahim, the leader of the Justice and Equality Movement and the longest-serving finance minister in Sudan’s history. His Cabinet position was itself the product of the political settlement the TSC pressed Idris to accept. So far, the reshuffle remains a set of negotiations rather than a settled list of departures. No final decisions have been made on which ministers will leave or who will replace them, according to the source in Idris’s office and a source informed of the talks. Idris is approaching the process as a reorganization of the executive branch rather than a wholesale change of government, the source in the prime minister’s office said, with some ministers expected to stay on to complete work already underway and others potentially moving or getting replaced over performance problems or overlapping responsibilities. According to the source informed of the consultations, the health and digital transformation and communications portfolios are not expected to change. The rest are being assessed before a final lineup is agreed, with both political considerations and the performance of the ministries in question taken into account, the source said, citing information available to him. The Juba movements are part of those negotiations. Their representatives hold several of the ministries under review, and consultations with them are a central part of the process, he added. The movements’ 25-percent share of executive power remains in place, the source stressed, meaning changes to individual ministers do not necessarily reopen the quota itself. The movements currently hold several ministries, including finance, human resources and social welfare, federal governance, minerals, and infrastructure and transport. Still, the movements are watching the reshuffle against a broader political landscape that is already in flux. A JEM leader told Mada Masr that the movement and other Juba signatories continue to regard the peace agreement as the framework for their participation in government. Any change to that arrangement, he said, would have to be discussed among the parties to the agreement. JEM does not object to reviewing ministries or changing ministers, he said, provided that the changes are based on performance and the need to improve the government’s work, and are made in consultation with the movements. That worry is unfolding as Khartoum moves toward an internal dialogue over the shape of the transitional period. The movements do not see the reshuffle as separate from that process, the leader said, because the coming political discussions will also have to address the relationship between the government and the armed movements. Their participation, he added, should not be reduced to a question of who holds which ministry. The push for a reshuffle did not begin entirely inside the prime minister’s office. The TSC spent a period monitoring the government’s performance and discussing its findings with Idris, according to a source close to TSC Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. TSC member Ibrahim Gaber followed ministries tied to production and the economy, while TSC member Shams Eddin Kabbashi monitored other executive portfolios, the source said. Their assessment identified persistent problems with production, revenues and public services and pointed to a need to reorganize some portfolios and replace officials in specific positions. Those findings are now feeding into the reshuffle, including the discussions over the Finance Ministry, as the government grapples with mounting economic pressures. The question of who will hold the ministry is being considered alongside the broader review, the source said. The TSC’s interference is itself part of the questions the reshuffle is meant to address. The source close to Burhan rejected the idea that the TSC was taking over the government, saying its monitoring was part of following priority files during the war and amid diminishing public resources. In practice, however, the boundary has remained blurred since the government’s formation. The attempt to give the executive branch a civilian face has never resolved the military leadership’s role in governing it. The TSC’s discussions with Idris following its review covered the government’s ability to implement decisions, relations between federal ministries and states and overlapping responsibilities among government bodies, the source close to Burhan said. A source close to the prime minister said the first government left unresolved the relationship between ministers from the armed movements and Idris’s executive program, the extent to which the TSC would be willing to step back from running executive affairs and the division of responsibilities between the federal government and the states. Those questions are now on the table as part of the reshuffle talks, the source added. The reshuffle is also expected to extend beyond the federal cabinet to the state governorships, with Khartoum emerging as a particular focus of the discussions, according to the source close to Burhan. The capital has become the clearest test of the government’s ability to restore basic services after the war. Federal institutions moved back to Khartoum in January, but the city’s infrastructure remains badly damaged. Electricity and water networks, roads, bridges, government buildings and health facilities all require repair, while unexploded ordnance and other remnants of the fighting continue to obstruct access and delay restoration work. The return of the government has also come alongside the return of large numbers of residents, who moved into areas relatively less damaged by the war, thus putting extreme pressure on infrastructure meant to serve a smaller population. Parts of Khartoum, Bahri and Omdurman, the three cities that make up the capital, continue to face severe shortages of services, while the reopening of markets and public institutions has remained uneven. That has made the management of the return an important part of the discussion over the governors. The source close to Burhan said several governors could be replaced, with particular attention on Khartoum State. Their performance is expected to be assessed in part on their ability to manage the return of residents, restore services and revive economic activity. Any changes to the governors are expected to accompany the federal reshuffle, with responsibilities between the center and the states potentially redistributed according to their ability to implement reconstruction and service restoration programs, according to the source informed of the consultations. Names have been proposed for some positions, but Idris has yet to make final decisions. According to the source in his office, Idris wants to complete discussions with the relevant parties before submitting the new lineup for approval. The source close to Burhan said the reshuffle should produce “greater harmony” between the government and the TSC in managing economic and service-related issues in the period ahead. *** Weeks of tribal violence in South Darfur leave communities in precarity Effects of the drought on agricultural land in Sereif, South Darfur, September 23. Courtesy: Darfur Victims Support via X. Heavy weapons in the hands of local groups, weakened controls on the use of force and a failed rainy season have converged to push South Darfur into a month of deadly inter-tribal clashes, including in and around Nyala, the seat of the RSF’s parallel government. At least 16 people were killed and dozens wounded in clashes between Massalit and Fallata communities in Gereida, about 90 km south of Nyala, after a dispute in a market earlier this month escalated into fighting across the town, medical sources and residents told Mada Masr. Hundreds of residents fled, fires broke out in residential areas and in a displacement camp, and the violence later spread to the farmland north of the town, where farmers were also caught up in it. The harvest season brings the two predominantly agricultural communities into close contact in Gereida’s markets, where farmers sell their crops and people from surrounding villages converge, giving rise to frictions. This year, poor rains and a weak harvest have added to the pressures around those interactions, according to a senior RSF source in the office of South Darfur’s governor. The fighting began on September 19 in Abuja market, when a dispute between a Massalit and a Fallata turned violent. Armed men from both sides quickly joined, and the fight spread into nearby neighborhoods, with light and heavy weapons in use, a medical source in Gereida said. Twelve people were killed and dozens wounded that day, according to the source. The town’s health facilities, already limited, took in casualties throughout the fighting. Some of the seriously wounded were taken to Nyala, while others stayed in Gereida because the roads out of town were too dangerous due to the clashes, he said. Tribal administration leaders stepped in to defuse the situation and RSF security personnel intervened overnight to separate the two sides, a police source in Gereida told Mada Masr. The calm lasted only a few hours. On September 20, armed groups attacked from the town’s eastern and western sides, and fighting spread again, the source said. Heavy weapons and Kalashnikov shots could be heard across Gereida, while forces stationed in the town took up positions at its entrances and outskirts to prevent the fighting from spreading further, he added. Four more people were killed and 23 wounded in the renewed clashes, according to a second medical source in Gereida. Some of the casualties were shot inside residential areas, the source said. Local leaders continued working to end the fighting and return the bodies of the dead to their families, said Sulaiman Abdel Rahman, a South Darfur notable. Reinforcements arrived from Buram, south of Gereida, along with civilian protection forces from Nyala, to separate the two sides and prevent another escalation, he said. The two days of fighting displaced residents mainly from western and northern Gereida, where the clashes were concentrated, Abdel Rahman said. Fires also broke out in parts of the Babanusa neighborhood and in the Abyad displacement camp to its east, destroying homes and property. The market stayed closed throughout the fighting, said Ahmed Rizgallah, who lives in Gereida. Movement between the town, surrounding villages and Nyala also stopped as armed personnel took up positions to the north, east and west of the town. The security deployment brought an uneasy calm to Gereida. But it also changed where the violence was taking place. With armed security forces in the town, the fighting moved into the surrounding farmland. On September 21, clashes broke out north of Gereida, where some farmers live and where other residents had sought refuge from the violence in town. Several farmers were killed and wounded, Rizgallah said. Some families who had been staying in the farmland returned to Gereida, while others could not make the journey safely and moved farther away, to places such as Um Dubban and Um Rakouba, he added. A Gereida locality official said a total of 412 people fled the town for areas within the Gereida and Tulus localities. For communities that depend on farming and trade, displacement, the shuttered market and blocked roads mean the damage extends well beyond the immediate violence, a community source added. Community leaders and security forces are working to prevent a new outbreak, but another Gereida resident said people see the situation as liable to flare up again at the slightest friction, with armed men still present in and around the town. The senior RSF source in the governor’s office said that the spread of heavy weapons among local groups, together with the erosion of the controls that once governed the use of force within communities, means that even a minor dispute can quickly escalate into a wide-scale confrontation, faster than the authorities or tribal administration can contain it. The violence in Gereida was preceded by further tribal violence inside Nyala itself. In early September, members of the Salamat said on social media that Shurafa was a subclan of the Salamat. The claim set off an argument online between members of the two groups, according to an official in South Darfur. The dispute soon moved beyond social media. Small groups of Salamat began attacking Shurafa members in the western part of Sereif, southern Nyala, including at coffee shops and other gathering places, according to the residents. The attacks escalated into armed clashes, with both sides using light and heavy weapons. For several days, the violence remained concentrated in western Sereif, where armed groups could move in and out through areas beyond the RSF’s close control, the official explained. That changed on September 16, when the clashes reached eastern Sereif. The fighting spread through Sereif’s residential areas. Homes were burned and looted, and families fled to other parts of the district or stayed indoors as gunfire continued, a resident of Sereif said. At least 10 people were killed and others wounded, the official said. Sereif is divided by Wadi Barly into eastern and western sections. The RSF has a stronger presence in the east, while the west has fluid boundaries that it cannot police closely. When the fighting reached eastern Sereif, the RSF was able to intervene, deploying forces around the affected neighborhoods, according to the official. But the violence flared again the following day as armed men from both sides arrived from outside Sereif, he said. RSF personnel once again separated the two sides and detained around 30 people involved in the clashes, an RSF military source said. The larger clashes have since subsided, but residents told Mada Masr the violence has not fully stopped. Skirmishes continue, particularly in western Sereif, and armed deployments have restricted movement across the area. Many of those who fled have been reluctant to return. One resident said families are waiting to see whether the RSF can keep armed groups from moving back in before deciding whether it is safe to go home. A South Darfur civil society source said in both Nyala and Gereida “weapons were the key factor in turning a limited dispute into a wider confrontation. Security forces in the area only intervened after the fighting had spread.” The senior RSF source said authorities are deeply concerned by the successive clashes, particularly because security and climate pressures are converging during this time. As the drought intensifies competition over water, pasture and farmland, resources that already fuel conflict across Darfur every year, the spread of arms makes it far easier for local disputes to escalate, he said. In his view, an intervention should include halting the spread of heavy weapons into residential and rural areas and swiftly activating the conflict mitigation mechanisms of tribal administration and local authorities before clashes widen and trigger displacement and disrupt the farming season. *** Military captures RSF’s last major defensive positions in western North Kordofan The military captured Mazroub, the RSF’s final major defensive position in western North Kordofan, on Friday morning after what it described as fierce battles, opening the way toward northern West Kordofan. The military had imposed a three-sided siege on Mazroub over the past week, after retaking nearby Sodary on September 25, according to a military source and a former officer who spoke to Mada Masr before the fall of Mazroub. The RSF had been preparing for a direct assault on Mazroub, concentrating troops and vehicles there. Instead, the military moved on Sodary first. When the town fell, the RSF was left defending Mazroub with fewer options for movement, the former officer said. The RSF subsequently reinforced Mazroub, sending additional troops and vehicles on Saturday that took up positions to its west, a second military source said. According to the first military source, the group had recognized that losing Mazroub would effectively end its presence in North Kordofan, while also threatening its positions in northern West Kordofan and its remaining defensive line across the wider Kordofan region. The capture of Sodary followed heavy fighting that caused significant losses to the RSF in personnel and equipment, the source said. Their remaining forces withdrew west toward Um Bader and from there, south toward Wad Banda in West Kordofan, while military and allied forces continued advancing toward Um Shuru, southwest of Sodary. The town is strategic because it sits along routes linking North Kordofan with West Kordofan and North Darfur, including the Arbaeen Road, the desert route connecting the two regions. Its capture helps the military further secure the Saderat Road, which runs through North Kordofan from North Darfur toward Omdurman, as well as areas retaken by the military over the past months. Mohamed Didan, the spokesperson for the military’s special operations forces in West Kordofan, said the loss of Sodary would disrupt RSF supply lines and leave its remaining forces in northern North Kordofan increasingly isolated. According to the former official, the military’s broader advance in North Kordofan is taking place along three axes: west from Sodary toward Abu Zaeima, Hamra al-Sheikh and Um Bader; from west of Bara toward Mazroub and Um Kiredam; and from west of Obeid toward Khawi and Nuhud in West Kordofan. The western Obeid axis had previously been a risky route for the military. The RSF surrounded the area from three sides, leaving any advancing force exposed in a confined battlefield where it could be vulnerable to ambushes, the former officer said. Sodary’s capture changes that position. And with Mazroub now in the military’s hands, the RSF would face pressure from several directions while its supply routes are cut. The resulting pressure could force the group to withdraw from towns and areas in northern West Kordofan, particularly because, he said, the RSF has less experience holding positions under siege. *** RSF launches drone attacks on Obeid, Wad Madani Aftermath of an RSF drone strike on the University of Kordofan’s dormitory in Obeid, North Kordofan, October 1. Courtesy: Sudan Tribune via X. RSF drones struck targets in Gezira and North Kordofan over the week, reaching fuel infrastructure east of Wad Madani and multiple sites in Obeid, where at least six civilians were killed. In Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, more than 15 drones struck different parts of the city on Thursday, including a shelter at the University of Kordofan’s dormitory, a security source told Mada Masr. He said the drones were launched from RSF-held Ghubeish in West Kordofan. The Sudan Doctors Network said the attacks killed five people and wounded 47 others. The Thursday attacks followed strikes on other parts of Obeid earlier in the week. The Olympic Stadium in the northern Wadi Elias neighborhood was struck on Monday, followed by an attack with three suicide drones on an events hall in the city on Tuesday evening, a state official told Mada Masr. The United Nations said at least one civilian was killed. An activist in Obeid told Mada Masr that the military had been using the stadium as a military facility since the start of the war. The strike triggered an explosion at an ammunition and weapons depot inside it, he added. Several buildings near the stadium were damaged, including the Sheikan College, according to the official. The drone attacks had reached Gezira on Sunday, targeting fuel storage facilities in Um Alila, east of the state capital, Wad Madani, according to a police-affiliated field source. The drones hit fuel tankers at the site, triggering a large fire and sending columns of smoke into the sky, the source said. The facilities are among the main fuel storage sites serving Gezira and central Sudan. Three other drones crashed before exploding in agricultural fields in the village of Wad al-Bar al-Khawalda, in the Wad Raeya administrative unit, he added. The following day, Gezira’s state security committee, headed by Governor Al-Taher Ibrahim, inspected the fuel facility and said the damage was limited, adding that it would resume operations within days. *** RSF unit from North Kordofan defects to military A force of 50 RSF fighters under the command of Al-Tayeb “Waheedo” Mohamed Ahmed announced its defection on September 25, marking the third such breakaway from the paramilitary group in Kordofan in recent months. According to a military source who spoke to Mada Masr, the force arrived from the North Kordofan battlefronts in Omdurman, where Waheedo was received alongside several military commanders and members of a committee responsible for coordinating the affairs of RSF defectors. In his first statements to the press, Waheedo said he left the RSF after witnessing the “tragedies” and “collapse” within its ranks. He called on those still fighting with the group to follow suit. The latest defection follows the arrival in September of 200 RSF fighters under Abu Bakr Dahloub , the group’s intelligence chief for special missions in North Kordofan’s Hamra al-Sheikh and the Egypt-Libya-Sudan border triangle. In July, RSF field commander Hussein al-Dodo defected with 280 fighters. He had commanded one of the RSF’s units in Bara. *** Sudan rejects Ethiopian accusations of backing armed opposition As fighting escalates across three northern Ethiopian regions between the federal military and armed opposition groups, the Sudanese military and Foreign Ministry have rejected accusations from Addis Ababa that Khartoum is supporting Ethiopian opposition armed factions. In a video statement on September 25, Ethiopian National Defense Force Chief of General Staff Birhanu Jula accused Eritrea of acting as an intermediary between external powers and the newly formed alliance of armed groups in an effort to destabilize and weaken Ethiopia, saying the current security challenges were part of a broader strategy by what he described as the country’s “historical” and “contemporary” adversaries. “Neither Eritrea nor the Tigray People’s Liberation Front can achieve anything on their own, even if they are allied, unless they are backed, supported and supplied by Sudan, Egypt and other external powers,” he said. The statement came days after the TPLF declared a “defensive war” against the Ethiopian government, as clashes between federal forces and a newly formed opposition alliance, the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival , spread across Tigray, which borders Sudan and Eritrea, and into the neighboring Afar and Amhara regions. The Sudanese military rejected the accusations on Sunday, calling them “baseless” and saying Sudan respects international law, the principles of good neighborly relations and the sovereignty of other countries. It also turned the accusation back on Ethiopia, saying it has information and evidence that the RSF continues to receive support via Ethiopia, including training and supplies, and that Ethiopian territory is being used for military activities, including drone operations. The military called on Ethiopia to exercise accuracy and responsibility and to address such issues through dialogue and official channels. The day after, the Sudanese government reinforced the military’s response through the Foreign Ministry, which also rejected the accusations, describing them as “arbitrary” and saying they had “no basis or evidence.” The ministry said the Ethiopian military chief’s remarks were an attempt to “drag Sudan into the internal conflicts engulfing Ethiopia.” From Khartoum’s perspective, the significance of the Ethiopian statements goes beyond the direct accusation that Sudan is supporting the Tigray front, a Sudanese diplomatic source told Mada Masr. The source said the statements came as the Ethiopian government seeks to explain the emergence of a new military alignment inside the country as the result of outside interference, rather than as a development rooted in Ethiopia’s own political and security crisis. Bringing Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea into that narrative gives Addis Ababa a regional frame for the conflict, the source said. Khartoum is wary of that framing because it could turn the Sudan-Ethiopia border, already marked by longstanding territorial and security disputes, into another arena of Ethiopia’s internal conflict, the source said. Sudan wants to maintain its stated position that its territory will not be used as a launchpad for activities targeting neighboring countries, he added, while retaining the right to respond to any activity it considers a threat to its security. The military shares the immediate concern of a spillover, according to a Sudanese military source informed of the assessments of Sudan’s General Command. As the fighting expands, Ethiopia’s western border with Sudan is increasingly becoming part of the conflict’s military calculations, the source told Mada Masr. The military also sees the accusation itself as an attempt to redirect attention from the support the RSF receives from Ethiopia and toward a Sudanese role in Ethiopia’s internal conflict, he added. Any claim that Sudan is supporting Ethiopian armed factions, the source stressed, should be accompanied by specific evidence from the ground, something Addis Ababa has not provided in the statements made by its military chief. On Thursday, the Ethiopian Foreign Ministry announced it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital of Asmara and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats in Addis Ababa persona non grata, ordering them to leave within 48 hours. The ministry said the step was “in response to Eritrea’s direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia.” The move marks one of the sharpest diplomatic escalations between the two countries since they restored relations in 2018. Asmara responded later in the day by announcing it had severed all diplomatic ties with Addis Ababa, citing what it described as “Ethiopia’s deplorable acts of hostility.” Addis Ababa also took action against Cairo on Thursday afternoon, declaring a member of the Egyptian diplomatic mission in Ethiopia persona non grata and ordering him to leave within 48 hours. Egypt responded in kind, expelling the Ethiopian embassy’s advisor in Cairo. *** Sudanese-Emirati war of words at UN General Assembly Foreign Minister Mohie Eddin Salem during his speech at the UN General Assembly, 28 September. Courtesy: The UN. The Sudanese and Emirati delegations took the floor one after the other at the UN General Assembly’s debate on Monday, setting out competing visions for an end to Sudan’s war, before turning on each other in two rounds of increasingly heated exchanges after the general debate concluded. Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohie Eddin Salem opened by expressing regret that he was the one addressing the General Assembly, rather than Transitional Sovereignty Council and Sudanese military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, whose United States visa was denied. Salem called for “comprehensive, equitable and expeditious reform of the international system” and urged countries to refrain from “the use of force or the threat thereof in international relations” and from imposing coercive measures on the basis of political disagreements. The visa denial has been read within Sudanese official circles as an attempt to pressure the government over its resistance to a truce proposal Washington is now pushing, Sudanese officials told Mada Masr last week. Salem said the government “categorically rejects any attempt to impose external solutions, dictates or agendas on our people.” The Sudanese people, he said, “should determine their own future without influence or pressure.” Khartoum, he said, has begun its own political process that will lead to free and fair elections. Then the UAE took the floor. On Sudan, Minister of State at the Emirati Foreign Ministry Khalifa Shaheen al-Marar said his country has stressed the need to “end the humanitarian catastrophe,” and called for “a permanent and unconditional ceasefire that would bring an end to the civil war,” followed by “a comprehensive and credible political process led by civilians.” The resulting government, he said, should be independent of both parties to the conflict and extremist groups. “The future of Sudan must be decided solely by the Sudanese people,” Marar said, calling on the international community to press the “leaders of the Port Sudan authorities” and the RSF, as parties to the conflict, to engage seriously with international initiatives. Sudan exercised its right to reply. Its representative, Al-Harith Idriss , accused the UAE of contributing to the humanitarian catastrophe Marar had referenced “through continuous support to the terrorist militia,” referring to the RSF. The UAE’s “claim to be neutral and innocent,” Idriss said, “will not aid in covering their crimes and their atrocities where they are in a bloodied partnership with the RSF.” He went on to cite evidence of Emirati support for the RSF, including financing, training and military supplies. Idriss also took issue with the UAE’s reference to the Sudanese government as the “Port Sudan authorities,” saying the language was out of place at the UN forum, before turning to a wider attack on Abu Dhabi and its own regime. He also accused the UAE of “leading an international campaign to expand the scope of the arms embargo to target the Sudanese Armed Forces,” referring to the US draft resolution discussed at the Security Council last month that sought to expand the Darfur arms embargo to cover all of Sudan and include Sudanese state institutions. The UAE came back with its own right to reply, accusing the Sudanese military of using chemical weapons and saying it would not “be lectured” by a military government that had committed war crimes against its own population. The two sides went back and forth twice, turning the General Assembly floor into a direct diplomatic confrontation over the war, the legitimacy of Sudan’s government and the role of the UAE. A Sudanese diplomatic source told Mada Masr that the escalation should not necessarily be understood as a step toward another diplomatic rupture. Rather, it reflects how both sides are using international forums to exert pressure and reinforce competing narratives of the war. Khartoum wants the international discussion to focus on foreign support for the RSF and rejects equating the military with the paramilitary force. Abu Dhabi, meanwhile, is pushing for a political process that would keep both sides of the war out of the next government, the source said. Khartoum also rejects the UAE’s role in the international effort to end the war, arguing that Abu Dhabi cannot act as a mediator while being, in Sudan’s view, a party to the conflict. The UAE is part of the US-led Quad on Sudan — alongside Egypt and Saudi Arabia — which has backed several ceasefire proposals rejected by Khartoum. The confrontation at the General Assembly is only the latest chapter in a dispute that has increasingly spilled into international forums since the war began, the source said. Sudan has repeatedly taken its accusations against the UAE to the Security Council and International Criminal Court, while Abu Dhabi has continued to deny them. *** Sudan turns to China for Red Sea port after scrapped UAE deal Two years after Sudan cancelled a memorandum of understanding with a UAE-led consortium to build Sudan’s Abu Amama port , the government is reviving the project with a major Chinese port company, Hassan Gaafar, the deputy head of the state-owned Sea Ports Corporation and head of its Higher Committee for the International Conference on Seaports, told Mada Masr. Sudan has begun taking practical steps toward building the port, Gaafar said. Studies are expected to be completed and construction to begin by the end of 2027, he said. The move is part of a broader expansion of Sudan’s economic ties with China, as the government looks to Beijing for investment in ports, energy and infrastructure, according to Sudanese government and diplomatic sources. China Harbour Engineering Company signed an agreement with Sudan in July to develop existing ports and build new ones, while other Chinese companies are in talks over electricity and infrastructure projects, a Foreign Ministry source said. Abu Amama lies about 200 km north of Port Sudan, near the Mohamed Qol and Marsa Oseif port localities, along the Red Sea coast and close to major shipping routes. The area has deep waters, reducing the need for extensive dredging and allowing it to accommodate large vessels and cargo ships. The details of the proposed arrangement with China, including financing, the length of any concession and who would operate the port, have yet to be formally announced. The Chinese-backed version of the project is being developed as part of a different government approach to Sudan’s ports, according to a Finance Ministry source informed of the ports file. Rather than being part of a single, large investment package, Abu Amama is now being presented as part of a government push to expand Sudan’s port capacity and improve its ability to move imports and exports. The government is exploring an investment model that would link the port more closely to Sudanese trade and exports, the source said. The UAE deal, signed in December 2022, was considerably broader. Under the agreement, a consortium comprising AD Ports Group and Invictus Investment was to develop, operate and manage Abu Amama, with announced investments of up to US$6 billion. The package included a free trade zone, an agricultural project and a $300 million deposit at the Central Bank of Sudan, according to the Sudanese government announcement at the time. For the UAE investors, Abu Amama’s location was a central part of the appeal, the Finance Ministry source said. The port could serve as an outlet for Sudanese exports and imports and connect the coast to agricultural and mining production areas and overland transport networks, he added. The project would have given Sudan another port alongside the Port Sudan complex, while giving the UAE-led consortium a long-term role in developing and operating a facility on a major global shipping route, the source said. The government cancelled the agreement in November 2024, as relations between Khartoum and Abu Dhabi deteriorated after Sudan accused the UAE of backing the RSF in the war. At the time, Finance Minister and JEM leader Gibril Ibrahim told reporters that, following the UAE’s support for the RSF, “there is no [Sudanese] entity that could even think about giving a port to the UAE, not even a single centimeter of land.” A Sudanese government source told Mada Masr that the cancellation was part of a broader reassessment of the country’s economic relationship with the UAE since the war. Ports, the source said, have since become part of Sudan’s political and security calculations in its foreign relations, alongside their role as commercial infrastructure. A diplomatic source informed of Sudan-UAE relations said Abu Dhabi may view the transfer of Abu Amama to a Chinese partner as part of Sudan’s wider economic realignment following the political crisis between the two countries. The main question for the UAE, the source said, would be whether the new arrangement will reproduce any of the rights granted to the UAE-led consortium under the original agreement, including long-term operating rights or ownership of related assets. The project comes as Sudan’s economic ties with China expand. Chinese cooperation has increasingly extended into infrastructure, energy and ports in recent months, while Sudan is looking for long-term investment to rebuild infrastructure damaged by the war and sees its ports as a key route back into foreign trade, a Sudanese diplomatic source and the government source said. Under the potential Chinese model, the first phase could focus on building the port’s basic infrastructure, followed by expanding its operating capacity and connecting it to transport networks and areas producing goods for export, the government source said. But much of the project’s success will depend on what happens beyond the port itself. A maritime transport expert told Mada Masr that Abu Amama could ease pressure on existing facilities if it were connected to roads and railways capable of moving goods from production areas to the coast. Its economic viability would depend not only on the depth of the water, the expert said, but also on the cost of building berths, container terminals, warehouses and logistics zones, as well as the transport links connecting the port to Sudan’s interior. The port could handle agricultural exports, livestock, minerals and imports, but serving those markets would require a logistics network extending well beyond the construction of the quay itself, the expert said. That broader challenge is part of why the government is looking at the ports sector as a pillar of post-war economic reconstruction. The International Conference on Sudanese Ports opened in Port Sudan on September 27, bringing together experts and institutions from Sudan, China, Egypt, Spain and Norway to discuss investment, infrastructure, supply chains, digital transformation and public-private partnerships. A government official participating in the conference told Mada Masr that Sudan wants to move away from reliance on its existing ports toward a more diversified network along the Red Sea, combining the expansion of current facilities with new ports capable of handling trade. Reviving Abu Amama with a Chinese partner is part of that effort, the official said, allowing Sudan to draw on Chinese experience in building and operating maritime infrastructure. *** Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . The post Ethiopia accuses Sudan of backing opposition, reshuffled hope for Idris’s govt, tribal violence engulfs South Darfur, military opens road to West Kordofan, China on Sudan’s coast first appeared on Mada Masr .

items.title: Commercialisation de produits SOFTCARE au Sénégal : les députés examinent le rapport de la Mission d’information parlementaire
items.description: La séance plénière de l’Assemblée nationale, tenue ce vendredi 2 octobre 2026, a été consacrée à l’examen du rapport de la Mission d’information parlementaire relative à la commercialisation des produits de marque SOFTCARE au Sénégal. Les députés ont ouvert une plénière vendredi, pour examiner le rapport de la Mission d’information parlementaire relative à la commercialisation des produits de marque SOFTCARE au Sénégal. Instituée en application de l’article 51 du Règlement intérieur de l’Assemblée nationale, cette Mission, mise en place à l’initiative de la Commission de la Santé, de la Population, des Affaires sociales et de la Solidarité nationale, avait pour objectif d’établir de manière « impartiale, contradictoire et documentée », explique une note de l’Hémicycle, les faits relatifs aux décisions successives de retrait puis de remise sur le marché des produits SOFTCARE. A lire aussi : Affaire Softcare : une mission d’information parlementaire officiellement installée « Installée le 5 décembre 2025, la Mission a mené ses travaux jusqu’au 2 avril 2026. Elle a conduit 20 auditions et effectué une visite de terrain sur le site industriel de SOFTCARE à Sindia, en auditionnant notamment les responsables de l’Agence sénégalaise de Réglementation pharmaceutique (ARP), les représentants de l’entreprise, les administrations concernées, les organisations professionnelles, les associations de consommateurs ainsi que des experts », renseigne le texte. En fait, les travaux ont bénéficié de l’appui technique de la Direction des Services de Planification, de Contrôle et d’Évaluation des politiques publiques (DSPCEPP) et des assistants parlementaires, notamment pour la collecte et l’analyse documentaire, la préparation des auditions et la consolidation des constats. Plusieurs insuffisances relevées dans le rapport Selon la note de l’Assemblée nationale, le rapport relève plusieurs insuffisances techniques, administratives et institutionnelles. Ceci, notamment en matière de traçabilité des matières premières, de gestion des non-conformités, de coordination entre services et de cohérence de la communication institutionnelle. « La Mission constate que des matières premières périmées ont bien été identifiées sur le site de SOFTCARE. Toutefois, au regard des éléments matériels et documentaires disponibles, elle estime qu’il n’est pas possible, à ce stade, d’établir avec certitude leur utilisation dans le processus de fabrication des produits finis », rapporte l’Hémicycle. Renforcer durablement le dispositif de régulation et de contrôle des produits de santé Au-delà du cas SOFTCARE, le rapport met ainsi en évidence la nécessité de renforcer durablement le dispositif de régulation et de contrôle des produits de santé, cosmétiques et d’hygiène. Parmi les recommandations formulées figurent notamment l’achèvement du cadre réglementaire, le renforcement des pouvoirs d’inspection, la modernisation des systèmes de traçabilité, l’amélioration de la coordination interinstitutionnelle, le renforcement des capacités scientifiques et la mise en place d’un suivi parlementaire régulier des réformes engagées. À travers l’examen de ce rapport, l’Assemblée nationale réaffirme ainsi sa volonté d’exercer pleinement sa mission constitutionnelle de contrôle de l’action gouvernementale, dans une démarche fondée sur la rigueur, la transparence, la redevabilité et l’évaluation des politiques publiques. Mariama DIEME

KGL Foundation commits $200,000 to support juvenile football for the next two years
items.description: The KGL Foundation has announced a commitment of $200,000 to the Ghana Football Association (GFA) as part of its support for juvenile football. The financial commitment is set to last for the next two years, starting with the launch of the 2026 KGL U-17 Inter-regional Colts Championship. The launch of the Colts tournament took place in the Conference Room of the KGL House in Labone, Accra, with key stakeholders present. President Kurt Edwin Simeon-Okraku, Executive Council Members, and top officials of the KGL Foundation were all in attendance. The initiative, which was first launched in 2021, has been the bedrock to unlocking young talents in Ghana and giving them the platform to display their potential. Speaking at the launch on Friday, Okraku lauded KGL for their continuous support towards the development of young talents. “We are here to reaffirm the marriage between the Ghana Football Association and the KGL Foundation,” he said. “Over a six-year tenure, we have produced amazing talents not only for local clubs but also for our various youth national teams. Today, I am proud to say that a lot of the products from these championships have represented Ghana at the U-17 level on the international stage, courtesy of the KGL Foundation.” The championship is also aimed at promoting talent discovery, fostering regional unity, supporting youth development, and nurturing future stars from the district level to the national phase. This year, KGL will provide each participating team with 60 kits (30 home jerseys and 30 away jerseys). The teams will also receive footballs, bibs and cones. As part of efforts this year, KGL will also provide educational scholarships to some of the best players from the competition. Ashanti Region were crowned champions for the second time last year following a 2-1 victory over Western Region.

items.title: Poutine assiste aux manœuvres «Centre-2026» et met l’accent sur la préparation, les nouveaux armements et la coopération militaire
items.description: Vladimir Poutine s'est rendu le 2 octobre sur le polygone militaire de Tchebarkoul, dans la region de Tcheliabinsk, ou il a suivi la phase finale des exercices strategiques « Centre-2026 » et des manœuvres « Interaction-2026 », organisees dans le cadre de l'Organisation du traite de securite collective. Ce polygone est un vaste terrain d'entraînement militaire ou les soldats peuvent s'exercer avec differents types d'armements, notamment des armes legeres, de l'artillerie, des systemes de roquettes, des missiles et des moyens aeriens. Prevus par le programme de preparation des forces armees russes, les exercices « Centre-2026 » constituent un dispositif strategique de commandement et d'etat-major. Ils servent notamment a entraîner les responsables militaires et les etats-majors a diriger de grandes formations de troupes dans differents scenarios operationnels. Lances le 28 septembre et prevus jusqu'au 3 octobre, ils se deroulent en deux etapes et mobilisent plus de 47 000 militaires sur onze polygones ainsi que dans les eaux de la mer Caspienne. Plus de 2 000 equipements et systemes d'armes sont engages, dont 90 appareils aeriens et 77 navires de combat ou de soutien. a Tchebarkoul, Vladimir Poutine a observe les manœuvres depuis un point de commandement, pris connaissance des rapports militaires et examine plusieurs modeles d'armements, de drones et de systemes robotises. Il s'est egalement entretenu avec des attaches militaires etrangers presents sur le site. Renforcer la preparation face aux menaces exterieures L'un des principaux buts des manœuvres est d'ameliorer les capacites de commandement des etats-majors dans un scenario d'agression exterieure. « L'objectif principal des exercices est d'ameliorer les competences du personnel dirigeant des etats-majors de tous niveaux dans le commandement des troupes lors de la reponse a une agression exterieure », a declare Vladimir Poutine. Le scenario porte notamment sur des operations dans la direction strategique d'Asie centrale ainsi que sur la securite militaire dans la zone de la mer Caspienne. Le president russe a egalement souligne que les participants utilisaient de nouveaux armements et equipements en tenant compte, selon ses termes, de l'experience acquise dans le cadre de l'« operation militaire speciale ». Cette experience est ainsi integree a la preparation des unites et aux differentes sequences des manœuvres. Le vice-ministre russe de la Defense Iounous-Bek Evkourov a presente a Vladimir Poutine le deroulement du scenario simule et les differentes phases de l'exercice. Les exercices « Centre-2026 » sont menes parallelement a « Interaction-2026 ». Ce dernier est un exercice de commandement mene dans le cadre de l'OTSC, qui associe notamment des unites de plusieurs etats membres de l'organisation. Les deux series de manœuvres se deroulent dans une meme situation operationnelle afin de travailler la coordination entre les forces participantes. Une cooperation militaire elargie avec les partenaires La participation internationale constitue un autre volet important des exercices. Des representants de 41 etats y prennent part sous differentes formes, un niveau de participation presente comme inedit pour « Centre-2026 ». La Bielorussie, la Chine, le Kirghizstan, la Mongolie, le Pakistan et le Tadjikistan ont envoye des contingents militaires. Le Kazakhstan et le Congo participent avec des groupes operationnels, tandis que 33 etats sont representes en qualite d'observateurs. Cette presence etrangere accompagne les manœuvres conduites dans le cadre de l'OTSC et les differentes sequences de cooperation entre les forces participantes. a l'issue des exercices, Vladimir Poutine a mis l'accent sur l'importance des echanges entre militaires de differents pays. Il a estime que ces echanges renforcaient la confiance entre les armees participantes. « Quand les militaires communiquent entre eux, cela signifie que la confiance se renforce entre les militaires et entre les etats qu'ils representent », a declare le president russe. Il s'est egalement dit convaincu que l'experience acquise pendant « Centre-2026 » et « Interaction-2026 » permettrait d'ameliorer l'efficacite de la reponse des forces participantes.
